Aldi Talk is one of the most popular prepaid options in Germany, and for good reason. You can buy a starter kit at any Aldi Nord or Aldi Süd supermarket for around **€2.99** — and it comes with a small starting credit.

**Best monthly package:** The "Kombi-Flat L" at around **€12.99/month** gives you 15 GB of LTE data, unlimited calls and SMS within Germany, and flat rates to many international destinations including Morocco.

### 2. Lidl Connect (Vodafone Network)
Lidl Connect is excellent if you want Vodafone's broader rural coverage. Starter kits cost around **€3.99** and the SIM is available in every Lidl branch.

**Best monthly package:** Around **€12.99/month** for 15 GB LTE data with a Vodafone signal — useful if your Ausbildung is in a smaller town like Würzburg or Rostock where O2 coverage can be patchy.

### 3. Congstar (Telekom Network)
Congstar runs on Telekom — the strongest and most reliable network in Germany, especially in rural areas. It's slightly pricier but the signal quality is noticeably better.

**Best monthly package:** The "Prepaid Allnet Flat M" starts at around **€15/month** for 8 GB, or you can go for the L option at **€20/month** for 20 GB. Order online at [congstar.de](https://www.congstar.de) and the SIM ships to any German address — or to someone who can receive it for you.

### 4. fraenk (Telekom Network, app-only)
fraenk is a newer digital brand, also on Telekom's network. It's completely managed through an app and costs a flat **€10/month** for 7 GB — no store visits needed. Ideal if you want Telekom quality at a low price and are comfortable managing everything on your phone.

### 5. Lebara (Vodafone Network)
Lebara is a favorite among people who make frequent calls to their home country. Their plans include international call minutes to Morocco, often at no extra charge.

**Best monthly package:** Around **€12.99/month** for 15 GB data plus international calls — perfect if you're calling family back in Casablanca or Marrakech regularly. Order at [lebara.de](https://www.lebara.de) and get the SIM mailed to you.

### 6. EDEKA smart (O2 Network)
EDEKA smart is worth mentioning because starter kits are literally at the supermarket checkout. If you arrive in any major German city, there's almost certainly an EDEKA nearby. Plans start from **€7.99/month** for 5 GB.

## How to Compare Plans: What Numbers Actually Matter

Don't just look at the price. Here's a practical checklist when comparing prepaid plans:

- **Data volume:** For daily use (maps, WhatsApp, YouTube in the evening), aim for at least **10 GB/month**
- **Network:** Telekom has the best rural coverage; O2 is cheapest in cities; Vodafone sits in between
- **International calls:** Does it include calls to Morocco, or do you pay per minute (often €0.09–€0.29/min on basic plans)?
- **EU roaming:** All German SIMs must include EU roaming by law — so you can use your data in Spain, France, etc. at no extra cost
- **Contract type:** Monthly cancellable (monatlich kündbar) = flexible; some "prepaid" plans auto-renew and can trap you
- **Activation:** Can you activate online, or do you need to go to a store? Online is faster and easier when you first arrive

## How to Buy and Activate a Prepaid SIM in Germany

Here's the step-by-step process:

1. **Choose your provider** based on the comparison above
2. **Buy the starter kit** — either at a supermarket (Aldi, Lidl, Rewe, dm) or order online to a German address
3. **Register online** (Freischaltung) — German law requires ID verification for all SIM cards. You'll need your passport or Moroccan national ID
4. **Complete identity verification** — most providers use VideoIdent (a short video call with an agent) or PostIdent (visit a Deutsche Post branch with your ID). VideoIdent takes about 10 minutes
5. **Choose your monthly package** — do this in the provider's app or website
6. **Top up your credit if needed** — buy top-up vouchers (Aufladekarten) at any supermarket or online via the provider's website
7. **Your SIM is active** — usually within 1–2 hours of verification

## Costs at a Glance: 2026 Price Overview

| Provider | Network | Monthly Price | Data | International Calls |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Aldi Talk | O2 | €12.99 | 15 GB | Included (select countries) |
| Lidl Connect | Vodafone | €12.99 | 15 GB | Paid extra |
| Congstar | Telekom | €15–€20 | 8–20 GB | Paid extra |
| fraenk | Telekom | €10 | 7 GB | No |
| Lebara | Vodafone | €12.99 | 15 GB | Morocco included |
| EDEKA smart | O2 | €7.99 | 5 GB | No |

All prices approximate and subject to change. Always check the provider's current website before purchasing.

## What People Get Wrong About Prepaid Plans in Germany

This is where many newcomers lose money or end up with no service:

**Mistake 1: Buying at the airport.** Airport kiosks sometimes sell overpriced starter kits or tourist packages with tiny data limits. Walk five minutes to an Aldi or Lidl instead.

**Mistake 2: Not registering the SIM.** German law (Telekommunikationsgesetz) requires ID verification. If you skip this step, your SIM will stop working after a short period. Always complete the VideoIdent or PostIdent step.

**Mistake 3: Assuming "prepaid" means no automatic renewal.** Many German prepaid plans auto-renew your monthly package. If you don't top up enough credit, it won't renew — but if you have credit sitting there, it will. Check the auto-renewal settings in the app.

**Mistake 4: Ignoring rural coverage.** If your Ausbildung is in a city like Munich or Berlin, any network works fine. But if you're in a small town in Bavaria or Saxony, Telekom is often the only network with reliable indoor coverage. Pay a few euros more for Congstar or fraenk.

**Mistake 5: Forgetting to set international calling rates.** Some people call Morocco without checking rates first and get a shock on their balance. Lebara and Aldi Talk's higher packages include international calls — stick to those if you call home often.

**Mistake 6: Not checking if the SIM works as an eSIM.** If you have a newer iPhone or Android, you might be able to use an eSIM (digital SIM with no physical card). Providers like fraenk and Congstar support eSIM — this means you can activate service before you even land.

## Which Plan Is Right for You?

- **Best overall value:** Aldi Talk Kombi-Flat L (€12.99, 15 GB, O2 network)
- **Best for rural areas:** Congstar on Telekom (€15–€20, reliable everywhere)
- **Best for calling Morocco:** Lebara (€12.99, international calls included)
- **Best budget option:** fraenk (€10, Telekom network, app-managed)
- **Easiest to buy in person:** EDEKA smart or Aldi Talk (supermarket pickup)

## Conclusion

Getting the right prepaid SIM card in Germany is one of the simplest things you can do to make your first weeks smoother. The best plans in 2026 sit between €10 and €20/month, give you 7–20 GB of data, and can be activated entirely online. Choose based on your location, how often you call Morocco, and whether you need Telekom's superior rural coverage.

Once you're settled and ready to think about the bigger picture — like writing your Ausbildung application or building a professional CV — book a free consultation to learn German and move to Germany successfully. Our team can help you prepare the right documents from day one. Visit our [CV builder](/cv-builder) or [Anschreiben generator](/anschreiben-generator) to get started.

faqs.question: Can I buy a German prepaid SIM before arriving in Germany?
faqs.answer: Yes. Providers like Congstar, fraenk, and Lebara let you order a SIM online and ship it to a German address — such as your employer's or a contact's address. Some also offer eSIM activation, meaning you can set up your German number before you even board the plane.

faqs.question: Do I need a German bank account to get a prepaid SIM?
faqs.answer: No. Prepaid SIMs in Germany require no bank account. You pay upfront with cash (at a supermarket) or with an international credit card online. You only need a valid passport or national ID for the mandatory identity verification step.

faqs.question: Which prepaid network has the best coverage in Germany in 2026?
faqs.answer: Telekom has the widest and most reliable coverage, especially in rural areas and smaller towns. O2 (used by Aldi Talk and EDEKA smart) is excellent and affordable in cities. Vodafone (Lidl Connect, Lebara) sits in between. If your Ausbildung is in a rural area, choose Congstar or fraenk for Telekom coverage.

faqs.question: How do I top up (aufladen) my prepaid SIM in Germany?
faqs.answer: You can buy physical top-up vouchers (Aufladekarten) at any Rewe, Aldi, Lidl, dm, Rossmann, or Edeka supermarket — just ask at the checkout. You can also top up directly in the provider's app using a credit card. Typical top-up amounts are €10, €15, €20, or €30.

faqs.question: Are calls to Morocco included in German prepaid plans?
faqs.answer: It depends on the plan. Lebara explicitly includes calls to Morocco in several of their packages (from €12.99/month). Aldi Talk's higher-tier packages also include international calls to select countries including Morocco. Always check the provider's full list of included countries before assuming — basic or entry-level packages usually do not include international calls.

rw-49.title: Home Internet in Germany: DSL, Kabel, and Glasfaser Explained for Newcomers
rw-49.summary: Choosing home internet in Germany — DSL, Kabel, or Glasfaser — can be confusing. Here's exactly what you need to know before you sign a contract.
rw-49.content:
Setting up home internet in Germany is one of the first practical challenges you'll face after moving — and it can feel surprisingly complicated. Between unfamiliar technology names like DSL, Kabel, and Glasfaser, German-only provider websites, and contracts that lock you in for 24 months, it's easy to make an expensive mistake. This guide breaks down every option clearly, so you can pick the right home internet plan in Germany from day one.

## What Types of Home Internet Are Available in Germany?

Germany uses several different technologies to deliver broadband to homes. Understanding the difference matters because **not every technology is available at every address** — your options depend entirely on the infrastructure in your building or street.

### DSL (Digital Subscriber Line)

DSL is the most widespread technology in Germany. It runs over the existing telephone copper network managed largely by Deutsche Telekom. Most apartments — especially in older buildings — are already connected to a DSL line.

- **Speed range:** typically 16 Mbit/s up to 100 Mbit/s (VDSL)
- **Most common providers:** Telekom, 1&1, Vodafone DSL, o2 Home
- **Average monthly cost:** €25–€45/month including a router
- **Contract length:** usually 24 months, with a 1-month cancellation notice before renewal

DSL is reliable for everyday use — streaming Netflix, video calls on Zoom, browsing — but it can struggle if multiple people in the same flat are working from home simultaneously at higher demands.

### Kabel (Cable Internet)

Kabel internet uses the old cable TV network. In Germany, Vodafone Kabel is by far the dominant provider after acquiring Unitymedia in 2019. If your building has a cable TV socket (Kabeldose), you can almost certainly get Kabel internet.

- **Speed range:** 50 Mbit/s up to 1,000 Mbit/s (1 Gbit/s)
- **Main provider:** Vodafone Kabel (plus some regional providers like M-net in Bavaria)
- **Average monthly cost:** €30–€50/month
- **Advantage:** Much faster download speeds than DSL at the same price point
- **Disadvantage:** Upload speeds are noticeably slower than download speeds, which matters if you do video conferencing or upload large files

Kabel is widely available in major cities like Cologne, Frankfurt, Munich, and Hamburg.

### Glasfaser (Fiber Optic)

Glasfaser is fiber optic internet — the fastest and most future-proof technology. Germany has been expanding its fiber network aggressively since 2020, but coverage is still uneven. Rural areas and smaller towns often lack it, while some urban districts are rapidly being connected.

- **Speed range:** 200 Mbit/s up to 10 Gbit/s (depending on the plan)
- **Providers:** Deutsche Telekom Glasfaser, Vodafone, 1&1 Glasfaser, Deutsche GigaNetz, NetCologne, EWE
- **Average monthly cost:** €40–€65/month
- **Key point:** If Glasfaser is available at your address, it's almost always worth choosing — speeds are symmetrical (equal upload and download), which is excellent for remote workers

To check if fiber is coming to your street, you can look up your address on [Breitbandatlas](https://gigabitgrundbuch.bund.de) — Germany's official broadband coverage map.

## How to Check Which Internet Is Available at Your Address

Before comparing prices, you need to know what's actually available at your specific address (not just your city). Here's how:

1. **Go to a comparison portal** — [Verivox](https://www.verivox.de) or [Check24](https://www.check24.de) are the two most used in Germany
2. **Enter your full address** including street (Straße), house number (Hausnummer), and postcode (Postleitzahl)
3. **The portal will show you all available technologies and providers** at that address with current prices
4. **Filter by speed** — for a single person, 50 Mbit/s is comfortable; for a family or shared flat (WG), aim for at least 100–250 Mbit/s
5. **Compare total costs** — look at the monthly fee AND any one-time setup fee (Einrichtungsgebühr), which can be €50–€80 but is often waived during promotions

## How Much Does Home Internet Cost in Germany?

Here's a realistic breakdown of what you can expect to pay in 2024/2025:

| Technology | Speed | Monthly Cost | Provider Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| DSL | 50 Mbit/s | ~€28–€35 | 1&1, o2 Home |
| DSL (VDSL) | 100 Mbit/s | ~€35–€45 | Telekom MagentaZuhause |
| Kabel | 250 Mbit/s | ~€35–€45 | Vodafone Kabel |
| Kabel | 500 Mbit/s | ~€40–€50 | Vodafone Kabel |
| Glasfaser | 200 Mbit/s | ~€40–€55 | Deutsche GigaNetz |
| Glasfaser | 1 Gbit/s | ~€55–€70 | Telekom Glasfaser |

Most contracts run **24 months**. Watch out for the **first-year discount** — many providers offer a reduced price for months 1–12, then raise it significantly in year two. Always read the full price listed for months 13–24.

## Signing a Contract as a Newcomer in Germany

You don't need German citizenship to sign an internet contract, but you do need a few things in place:

- **A registered German address** (Anmeldebescheinigung) — providers will deliver the router there and verify billing
- **A German bank account (IBAN)** — almost all providers require direct debit (SEPA-Lastschrift)
- **A valid ID or residence permit** — some providers run a credit check via Schufa; if you're new and have no Schufa score yet, this can occasionally cause a rejection (see pitfalls below)

Most providers allow you to sign contracts entirely online in German. If your German isn't strong yet, Check24 and Verivox have fairly clear interfaces — and many providers like 1&1 and o2 also have English customer support lines.

### Ordering the Router

In Germany, your internet provider will send you a router (called a Fritz!Box in many cases, made by AVM — a very popular German brand). This router is usually included in the monthly fee or rented for €5–€8/month. You can also use your own compatible router if you prefer.

## What About Internet in a Shared Flat (WG)?

If you're moving into a Wohngemeinschaft (shared flat), the internet contract is usually already in place and set up by the main tenant. You'll typically just contribute to the monthly cost split between flatmates — usually €8–€15 per person.

If you're setting up a new WG yourself, a Kabel or VDSL contract at 250 Mbit/s+ is usually the sweet spot for 3–5 people sharing.

## What People Get Wrong About Home Internet in Germany

### Assuming fiber is everywhere

Many newcomers assume Germany has widespread fiber — in reality, Germany ranks below the EU average in fiber penetration. In cities like Berlin or Munich, some neighborhoods still rely on DSL or Kabel. Always check your specific address first.

### Ignoring the contract renewal trap

German internet contracts automatically renew for another 12 months if you don't cancel within the notice period (Kündigungsfrist) — usually 1 month before the end of the 24-month term. Set a calendar reminder to cancel or renegotiate before your contract ends.

### Forgetting the setup fee

Many attractive advertised prices don't include the Einrichtungsgebühr (installation fee) of €50–€80. This is often waived in promotional offers, but not always. Check the fine print before ordering.

### Getting rejected due to no Schufa history

If you've just arrived in Germany, you have no Schufa credit history. Some providers will reject your application automatically. If this happens, try 1&1 or o2 — they tend to be more flexible with new residents. Alternatively, ask your employer to co-sign or use a prepaid home internet option (like Telekom's prepaid LTE home router) as a temporary solution.

### Not porting your number

If you previously had a German landline number (from a previous address), you can port it to your new contract. This is optional but worth knowing — you can request it during the order process.

## Conclusion

Choosing the right home internet in Germany — whether DSL, Kabel, or Glasfaser — comes down to what's available at your address, how many people are sharing the connection, and how long you plan to stay. Start with Check24 or Verivox, check your address, compare the 24-month total cost (not just the first-year promotional price), and go with fiber if it's available.

Getting settled in Germany involves dozens of decisions like this. If you want guidance on navigating German bureaucracy, writing your Anschreiben, or building a CV that lands you an Ausbildung, [book a free consultation and use our CV builder](/cv-builder) to move to Germany with confidence.

faqs.question: What is the best home internet provider in Germany for newcomers?
faqs.answer: There's no single best provider — it depends on what's available at your address. Use Check24 or Verivox to compare options. For flexibility and English support, 1&1 and o2 Home are good starting points, especially if you don't yet have a Schufa history.

faqs.question: Can I get home internet in Germany without a Schufa score?
faqs.answer: Yes, though some providers may reject applications without a Schufa history. Try 1&1 or o2 Home, which are generally more flexible with new residents. As a temporary solution, Telekom offers prepaid LTE home routers that require no credit check.

faqs.question: How long does it take to get internet set up after ordering in Germany?
faqs.answer: For DSL and Kabel, expect 2–4 weeks from the order date, as a technician may need to activate the line. Glasfaser can take longer if infrastructure work is needed. The provider will send you the router by post and confirm your activation date by email.

faqs.question: Is Glasfaser (fiber) available in all German cities?
faqs.answer: No. Germany's fiber rollout is ongoing and uneven. Major cities like Frankfurt, Hamburg, and Cologne have growing fiber coverage, but many streets — even in large cities — still rely on DSL or Kabel. Check your specific address on the official Breitbandatlas map at gigabitgrundbuch.bund.de.

faqs.question: What speed do I need for a shared flat in Germany?
faqs.answer: For a WG with 3–5 people — streaming, video calls, gaming, and working from home — aim for at least 100–250 Mbit/s. A Kabel 250 Mbit/s plan or a VDSL 100 Mbit/s plan from Vodafone or Telekom typically costs €35–€45/month and handles a full household comfortably.

rw-50.title: Rufnummermitnahme: How to Transfer Your Phone Number Between Carriers in Germany
rw-50.summary: Learn how to transfer your German phone number to a new carrier (Rufnummermitnahme) — step-by-step, with real costs, timelines, and mistakes to avoid.
rw-50.content:
Moving to a better mobile plan in Germany doesn't mean you have to give up the number your friends, family, and employer already know. The process of keeping your number when switching carriers is called **Rufnummermitnahme** — and while it sounds complicated, it's actually straightforward once you know the steps. Whether you're switching from Telekom to a budget MVNO or from one prepaid SIM to another, this guide walks you through everything.

## What Is Rufnummermitnahme and Why Does It Matter?

**Rufnummermitnahme** literally means "phone number portability" in German. It's the legal right — guaranteed under German telecommunications law (Telekommunikationsgesetz, TKG) — that allows you to keep your existing mobile number when you switch to a different carrier.

For Moroccans living in Germany, this matters a lot. Your phone number is often tied to:

- Your bank account (two-factor authentication via SMS)
- Your German employer or job applications
- Family and friends who already have your number
- Government or Ausländerbehörde correspondence

Losing your number means updating dozens of contacts and services. With Rufnummermitnahme, you avoid that headache entirely — and it costs you nothing extra in most cases.

## Which Carriers Support Number Portability in Germany?

Good news: **all German mobile carriers** are legally required to support Rufnummermitnahme. This includes:

- **Major networks:** Telekom, Vodafone, O2 (Telefónica)
- **Budget brands (MVNOs):** Aldi Talk, Lidl Connect, congstar, Blau, WinSIM, freenet, otelo, Klarmobil, simyo
- **Discount online carriers:** PremiumSIM, Sparhandy, handyvertrag.de

It doesn't matter whether you're on a postpaid contract (Vertrag) or a prepaid SIM — you can transfer your number in either direction.

### Important: Portability Only Works Within Germany

You can only port a German mobile number (starting with +49) between German carriers. If you came from Morocco and want to keep a Moroccan number, that's not possible within the German system. Rufnummermitnahme applies exclusively to numbers already registered in the German national numbering plan.

## Step-by-Step: How to Transfer Your Number in Germany

Here's how the process works in practice:

### Step 1 — Get Your Portability Code (Portierungskennung or KÜN)

Before you can move your number, you need a code from your **current carrier**. This is called the **Portierungskennung** (also known as the KÜN — Kundenkennungsnummer).

- Call your current carrier's customer service or log into your online account
- Request the portability code — they are legally required to provide it within 1 business day
- The code is usually valid for **30 days**
- Example: Aldi Talk gives you the code via their website under "Mein Konto"; congstar provides it by phone or chat

### Step 2 — Sign Up With Your New Carrier

Choose your new plan and sign up. During the registration process, you'll see a field asking whether you want to keep your existing number (usually labeled "Rufnummermitnahme" or "Bestehende Rufnummer mitnehmen").

- Select "Yes" and enter your old phone number
- Enter the portability code (KÜN) you received in Step 1
- Specify the date you want the transfer to happen (or request "as soon as possible")

### Step 3 — Cancellation Is Handled Automatically

Here's something many people get wrong: **you do not need to separately cancel your old contract**. When you initiate a number port, the new carrier sends a transfer request to your old carrier, which simultaneously cancels your old contract or SIM. This is handled automatically under German law.

Exception: If you're on a postpaid contract with a minimum term (Mindestvertragslaufzeit), you may still owe fees until the contract period ends — but the number transfer itself still goes through.

### Step 4 — Wait for the Transfer

The actual number transfer typically takes:

- **1–3 business days** for prepaid-to-prepaid transfers
- **Up to 7 business days** for postpaid contracts in some cases

You'll usually receive an SMS or email from both carriers confirming the transfer date. On that date, your old SIM stops working and your new SIM becomes active with your old number.

### Step 5 — Keep Your Old SIM Ready During Transition

Don't throw away your old SIM until the transfer is fully confirmed. On the handover day, there may be a window of 1–2 hours where neither SIM works. Keep your phone nearby and test the new SIM as soon as the switch is supposed to happen.

## Costs: How Much Does Rufnummermitnahme Actually Cost?

In most cases, **Rufnummermitnahme is free**. German law prohibits carriers from charging excessive fees for number portability. However, watch for these potential costs:

| Situation | Typical Cost |
|---|---|
| Portability code (KÜN) from current carrier | Free (legally required) |
| Prepaid-to-prepaid transfer | Free (most carriers) |
| Postpaid number transfer | Free at new carrier; early termination fees may apply at old carrier |
| Activation fee at new carrier | €0–€29.99 (varies by provider; often waived with online signup) |

For example, WinSIM and PremiumSIM frequently run promotions with 0€ activation and free number porting. Aldi Talk charges no porting fee. Even O2 and Telekom do not charge for receiving a ported number.

**Watch out for early termination fees (Vertragsstrafe):** If you're locked into a 24-month contract with, say, Vodafone, and you port out after 6 months, you may owe the remaining monthly fees. Always check your contract terms before initiating a port.

## Rufnummermitnahme for Prepaid SIMs: Special Notes

Many Moroccans in Germany start with a prepaid SIM (like an Aldi Talk or Lidl Connect card) before committing to a longer contract. Here's what you need to know for prepaid-to-prepaid transfers:

- **Remaining credit:** Any remaining balance on your old prepaid SIM is typically **lost** when you port out. Spend it down first or accept the loss.
- **Validity:** Make sure your old SIM is still active (not expired) when you request the port. An expired prepaid SIM cannot be ported.
- **Top-up not required:** You don't need to top up the old SIM just to initiate the port — as long as it's currently active.

## What People Get Wrong About Number Portability in Germany

This is where most confusion and frustration happens. Here are the most common mistakes:

- **Cancelling the old contract before porting:** Don't do this. Cancel after porting, or let the port cancel it automatically. If you cancel first, you may lose your number.
- **Letting the prepaid SIM expire:** Prepaid SIMs in Germany deactivate after a period of inactivity (often 12 months without a top-up). Once expired, the number is gone — you can't port it.
- **Missing the KÜN validity window:** The portability code is only valid for 30 days. If you get the code but wait too long to activate your new SIM, you'll need to request a new code.
- **Assuming the number transfers instantly:** It won't happen in real time. Plan the switch for a day when you can briefly be unreachable (e.g., a Sunday or day off).
- **Forgetting to update 2FA:** Once your number is on the new SIM, make sure any SMS-based two-factor authentication (banking apps, email accounts) still works correctly — the SMS will now arrive on the new SIM.
- **Not reading the new contract's minimum term:** Some cheap plans come with 24-month lock-in periods. If you want flexibility, look for monthly-cancellable (monatlich kündbar) plans.

## Conclusion: Keep Your Number, Switch to a Better Deal

Rufnummermitnahme is one of the most consumer-friendly rules in the German telecoms market, and it's something you should use without hesitation when a better plan comes along. The process takes just a few minutes of admin and a few days of waiting — and you walk away with a cheaper plan and the same number everyone already knows.

If you're still in the early stages of your move to Germany and want help navigating SIM cards, Ausbildung applications, or paperwork in general, **book a free consultation to learn German and move to Germany successfully**. Our team can help you with everything from your [CV builder](/cv-builder) to your [Anschreiben generator](/anschreiben-generator) so your German journey starts on the right foot.

faqs.question: How long does Rufnummermitnahme take in Germany?
faqs.answer: Most number transfers in Germany take 1–3 business days for prepaid SIMs. Postpaid contracts can take up to 7 business days. You'll receive confirmation from both carriers, and there may be a 1–2 hour window on the transfer day where your number is briefly unreachable.

faqs.question: Do I have to cancel my old contract before porting my number?
faqs.answer: No — and this is the most important thing to get right. When you initiate a number port with your new carrier, they notify your old carrier, which automatically cancels your old SIM. If you cancel the old contract first, you risk losing your number entirely.

faqs.question: Does Rufnummermitnahme cost money in Germany?
faqs.answer: In most cases, it's completely free. German law requires carriers to provide the portability code (KÜN) at no charge, and most carriers don't charge a porting fee. However, if you're mid-contract with a postpaid plan, you may still owe your remaining monthly fees as an early termination penalty.

faqs.question: What happens to my prepaid credit when I port my number?
faqs.answer: Any remaining balance on your old prepaid SIM is typically lost when you port out to a new carrier. It's best to use up your credit before initiating the transfer, or accept that small remaining balance as a switching cost.

faqs.question: Can I port a Moroccan number to a German carrier?
faqs.answer: No. Rufnummermitnahme only works within the German national numbering plan. You can only port numbers that already start with +49 (Germany). Moroccan numbers (+212) cannot be transferred into the German mobile network.

rw-51.title: Cheapest Ways to Call Morocco from Germany in 2025 (Real Costs + Apps)
rw-51.summary: Discover the cheapest ways to call Morocco from Germany in 2025, with real costs, app comparisons, and SIM card tips for Moroccans living abroad.
rw-51.content:
Staying connected with family back home in Morocco is one of the first practical challenges you face when you move to Germany — and phone bills can quietly drain your budget if you pick the wrong option. The good news is that in 2025, calling Morocco from Germany has never been cheaper, with several methods that cost virtually nothing compared to traditional phone plans. In this guide, you'll find a clear breakdown of every realistic option — apps, SIM cards, and calling cards — with real prices so you can choose what works best for your situation.

## Why Calling Morocco from Germany Gets Expensive (and How to Avoid It)

Standard German mobile contracts from providers like Telekom, Vodafone, or O2 typically charge between **€0.20 and €0.60 per minute** for international calls to Morocco. If you call home for 30 minutes a week, that's already €25–€75 per month disappearing from your pocket — money you need for rent, transport, or your Ausbildung costs.

The problem is that many newcomers simply use the SIM card they already have without checking international rates. A few simple changes to your setup can reduce this cost to near zero.

---

## The Cheapest Option: Internet-Based Calling Apps

If you and your family in Morocco have a smartphone and a decent internet connection, data-based calling is almost always the cheapest route — often completely free.

### WhatsApp Calls
WhatsApp is by far the most widely used option among Moroccan communities in Germany. As long as both sides have Wi-Fi or mobile data, calls are **free**, regardless of duration. Video calls are also free. The quality is generally good, though it can drop on weak connections. Most Moroccan families already use WhatsApp, making this the zero-setup solution.

**Tip:** Enable Wi-Fi calling in WhatsApp settings so calls go over your home broadband instead of your mobile data plan.

### Messenger and Instagram Calls
Facebook Messenger and Instagram also offer free voice and video calls over the internet. These work well if your relatives use Facebook, which remains popular in Morocco. Quality is comparable to WhatsApp.

### Google Meet and Zoom
Better for longer family catch-ups or group calls. Free on both sides, and available on any device — laptop, tablet, or phone.

### Viber
Viber deserves special mention because it also offers **Viber Out**, a paid feature that lets you call Moroccan landlines and non-Viber mobile numbers at very low rates — around **€0.015–€0.03 per minute** to Moroccan mobile numbers. This is useful when the person you're calling doesn't have a smartphone or data connection.

---

## Calling Cards and International Top-Up Services

When internet quality is unreliable — for example, in rural areas of Morocco — calling cards still offer excellent value.

### Lycamobile and Lebara Calling Cards
Both **Lycamobile** (lycamobile.de) and **Lebara** (lebara.de) sell prepaid credit in Germany that includes very cheap international minutes to Morocco. Rates are typically around **€0.01–€0.03 per minute** to Moroccan mobile numbers when you buy a bundle.

- Lebara's "World" SIM plans often include a set number of minutes to Morocco per month
- Lycamobile frequently runs promotions with bonus credit for international calls
- Both can be bought at supermarkets, kiosks, or online

### Boss Revolution
**Boss Revolution** (bossrevolution.com) is a dedicated international calling service used widely in the Moroccan diaspora. You load credit online or via their app and call Morocco at rates as low as **€0.006 per minute**. Calls go through a dial-in number, so no special app is needed on the Moroccan side.

---

## Best SIM Cards for Moroccans in Germany Who Call Home Often

If you want everything bundled — German data, calls within Germany, and cheap calls to Morocco — the following SIM options are worth considering.

### Lycamobile SIM (Recommended)
Lycamobile operates on Telefónica's network (same towers as O2) and is specifically designed for expat communities. Their plans start at around **€5–€10/month** and typically include:
- Flat rate calls within Germany
- Up to 5 GB of data
- Very cheap or included minutes to Morocco (varies by plan — check lycamobile.de for current offers)

### Lebara SIM
Similar positioning to Lycamobile, also on the Telefónica network. Plans from **€7.99/month** often include international minutes. Their website at lebara.de lets you compare which countries are included.

### congstar International Add-on
If you already have a congstar plan (popular with students and Azubi residents), you can add international calling bundles for **€2–€5/month** that reduce Morocco rates significantly.

---

## Using a Dual-SIM Phone: The Smart Expat Setup

Many Moroccans in Germany keep a Moroccan SIM alongside their German SIM by using a dual-SIM phone. This setup means:

- Your family in Morocco can call your Moroccan number at local rates (free or very cheap for them)
- You receive those calls on your German phone without paying anything extra
- You avoid international dialing entirely for incoming calls

Popular dual-SIM Android phones like Samsung Galaxy A-series or Xiaomi Redmi models start at around **€150–€200** and are widely available at MediaMarkt or Saturn in Germany.

The catch: your Moroccan SIM card will need to stay active. Maroc Telecom, Inwi, and Orange Maroc all allow you to keep a number active with minimal top-up (usually **50–100 MAD every 3–6 months**). Check each operator's policy before you leave.

---

## Step-by-Step: Setting Up the Cheapest Calling System

Here's a simple plan you can implement in your first week in Germany:

1. **Get a Lycamobile or Lebara SIM** — buy one at any supermarket (Rewe, Lidl, Penny) or online for free. Activation takes about 10 minutes with your ID.
2. **Download WhatsApp and connect to your home Wi-Fi** — tell your family to do the same in Morocco. This covers 90% of your calling needs at zero cost.
3. **Install Viber** and add €5 of Viber Out credit for calling Moroccan landlines when needed.
4. **Keep your Moroccan SIM in your phone's second slot** with a small top-up so family can reach you at local rates.
5. **Check lycamobile.de or lebara.de monthly** — both regularly offer promotional bundles with extra Morocco minutes.

Total monthly cost using this setup: **€0–€10**, depending on how often you call landlines.

---

## What People Get Wrong About Calling Morocco from Germany

**Mistake 1: Assuming your German contract includes international calls.**
Most standard contracts explicitly exclude international minutes unless you add a specific package. Always check your contract's "Ausland" (international) section.

**Mistake 2: Using roaming when visiting Morocco.**
If you travel back home and use your German SIM in Morocco, roaming charges apply and can be very high — often €0.50+ per minute. Switch to your Moroccan SIM the moment you land.

**Mistake 3: Ignoring Wi-Fi quality.**
WhatsApp calls break up badly on slow connections. If quality is poor, try switching to voice-only (disable video), or use Boss Revolution as a backup — it routes calls through regular phone lines, which are more stable.

**Mistake 4: Forgetting to recharge the Moroccan SIM.**
Many people lose their Moroccan number because they forget to top it up every few months. Set a calendar reminder and recharge remotely via the operator's app or through services like **MamaExpress** (mamaexpress.de) from Germany.

**Mistake 5: Paying for an expensive "international" plan you don't need.**
Some providers market "international" plans at €15–€20/month but the Morocco rates are barely better than standard. Compare actual per-minute rates before signing anything.

---

## Conclusion

Calling Morocco from Germany doesn't have to cost you anything significant. WhatsApp and similar apps handle most calls for free. For times when internet isn't reliable, Lycamobile, Lebara, or Boss Revolution bring costs down to less than a cent per minute. A dual-SIM setup is the smartest long-term configuration for staying connected without surprise bills.

If you're in the middle of planning your move to Germany — finding an Ausbildung, sorting your visa documents, or preparing your application — every euro saved on phone bills helps. [Book a free consultation to learn German and move to Germany successfully](/cv-builder) and get personalised advice on the practical side of relocating, from SIM cards to salary negotiation.

faqs.question: What is the cheapest app to call Morocco from Germany?
faqs.answer: WhatsApp is the cheapest option — calls are completely free over Wi-Fi or mobile data. For calling Moroccan landlines or non-smartphone users, Viber Out costs around €0.015–€0.03 per minute, and Boss Revolution can go as low as €0.006 per minute.

faqs.question: Which SIM card in Germany offers the best rates for calling Morocco?
faqs.answer: Lycamobile and Lebara are the top choices for Moroccans in Germany. Both offer prepaid plans from around €5–€10/month that include cheap or bundled international minutes to Morocco. Check lycamobile.de and lebara.de for current promotions, as rates and bundles change regularly.

faqs.question: Can I keep my Moroccan SIM card active while living in Germany?
faqs.answer: Yes. All three major Moroccan operators — Maroc Telecom, Inwi, and Orange Maroc — allow you to keep your number active with a small periodic top-up (around 50–100 MAD every few months). You can recharge remotely from Germany using services like MamaExpress (mamaexpress.de) or directly through each operator's app.

faqs.question: How does a dual-SIM phone help me call Morocco cheaply?
faqs.answer: With a dual-SIM phone, you keep your German SIM for local calls and data, and your Moroccan SIM in the second slot. Family in Morocco can call your Moroccan number at their local rate, meaning the call is free or very cheap for them and costs you nothing on the German side. Dual-SIM Android phones are available from MediaMarkt or Saturn starting at around €150–€200.

faqs.question: Are there calling cards I can buy in Germany to call Morocco?
faqs.answer: Yes. Lycamobile and Lebara both sell prepaid calling cards and SIMs at supermarkets like Rewe, Lidl, and Penny. Boss Revolution credit can be bought online at bossrevolution.com. These options are ideal when internet quality is poor and you need a reliable connection to Moroccan landlines.

rw-53.title: Roaming in Europe from Germany: Everything You Need to Know
rw-53.summary: Living in Germany and traveling Europe? Here's exactly how roaming works, what it costs, and which SIM cards save you the most money.
rw-53.content:
You've landed in Germany, you've got a German SIM card, and now you're planning a weekend trip to Amsterdam or a quick visit to family back in Morocco via a layover in Paris. The moment you cross the border, one question hits immediately: will your phone still work, and how much will it cost you? Roaming in Europe from Germany is actually one of the least complicated things about living here — if you know the rules. This guide breaks down everything from EU roaming regulations to the best SIM cards for travelers, with real numbers so you can plan without surprises.

## What Is Roaming and Why Does It Matter for People in Germany

Roaming simply means using your mobile phone's calls, texts, and data while connected to a foreign network outside your home country. When you're in Germany and travel to another European country, your German SIM card connects to a local network there — and depending on your contract, you either pay extra or you don't.

For Moroccans living in Germany, roaming matters in two very common situations:

- Traveling within Europe (France, Spain, Netherlands, Italy, etc.) for tourism or work
- Transiting through non-EU countries or visiting Morocco directly

Understanding the difference between **EU roaming** and **international roaming outside the EU** can save you anywhere from €10 to €200 on a single trip.

## EU Roaming Rules: The "Roam Like at Home" Regulation

Since June 2017, the European Union enforces a regulation called **"Roam Like at Home"** (RLAH). This rule means that if you have a German mobile contract or prepaid SIM, you can use your included minutes, texts, and data in any of the **27 EU member states plus Iceland, Liechtenstein, and Norway** — at no extra charge.

### Countries Covered Under EU Roaming

Here is the full list of countries where EU roaming applies from Germany:

- All 27 EU countries: France, Spain, Italy, Portugal, Netherlands, Belgium, Austria, Greece, Poland, Czech Republic, and more
- EEA countries: Norway, Iceland, Liechtenstein

**Switzerland is NOT included** — despite being surrounded by the EU. The same goes for the UK after Brexit, Turkey, and Morocco.

### How Much Data Can You Use Abroad?

This is where it gets slightly technical. EU law doesn't give you unlimited roaming data even if you have an unlimited German plan. Providers are allowed to set a **fair use cap** on data used abroad. The minimum is calculated by a formula, but in practice:

- **Telekom (Magenta Mobil):** Up to your full data allowance in the EU
- **Vodafone:** Full data allowance in the EU with fair use limits on unlimited plans (usually capped at 25–35 GB)
- **O2 (Telefónica):** Full data allowance included in EU roaming
- **Aldi Talk / Congstar / EDEKA:** EU roaming included, but data may be throttled to speeds like 384 kbps after a cap

Always check your specific plan's terms at the provider's website (e.g., [telekom.de](https://www.telekom.de), [vodafone.de](https://www.vodafone.de), [o2online.de](https://www.o2online.de)).

## Roaming Outside the EU: What Happens When You Go to Morocco or Turkey

This is where the costs can really add up. When you travel to Morocco — for example, to visit family in Casablanca, Rabat, or Marrakech — you are completely outside the EU roaming zone. Your German provider will charge international roaming rates, which can be brutal.

### Typical International Roaming Costs from German Providers (Non-EU)

| Provider | Data per MB (Morocco) | Call per minute | SMS |
|---|---|---|---|
| Telekom (without add-on) | €0.20–€0.60/MB | €1.50–€2.00 | €0.40 |
| Vodafone (without add-on) | €0.20–€0.99/MB | €1.50–€2.50 | €0.40 |
| O2 (without add-on) | €0.19–€0.59/MB | €1.00–€2.00 | €0.35 |

A single hour of casual smartphone use — checking maps, WhatsApp, Instagram — can consume 50–200 MB. At €0.50/MB, that's €25–€100 for one hour. Accidentally leaving roaming on overnight could mean a €300+ bill when you wake up.

### What to Do Instead When Visiting Morocco

- **Buy a local Moroccan SIM** from Maroc Telecom, Orange Maroc, or Inwi at the airport for around 30–50 MAD (€3–€5). You get a local number and affordable data.
- **Turn off mobile data before landing** and use Wi-Fi only. WhatsApp calls over Wi-Fi cost nothing.
- **Use a roaming add-on** from your German provider. Telekom, for example, offers a "Travel & Surf" day pass for €4.95/day that includes 500 MB in Morocco.
- **Get an eSIM** for Morocco before you travel. Services like Airalo or Holafly sell eSIMs for Morocco starting at around €4–€6 for 1 GB.

## Best SIM Cards for Roaming Across Europe from Germany

If you travel within Europe frequently, choosing the right German SIM from the start makes a big difference.

### Top Picks for Heavy EU Travelers

**1. Telekom (Magenta Mobil S) — from €19.95/month**
Best network coverage in Germany and strong roaming speeds across all EU countries. Includes full data allowance in EU. Ideal if you travel to Eastern Europe or rural France and Spain.

**2. O2 Basic — from €14.99/month**
Good value for moderate travelers. EU roaming included, reliable in major European cities.

**3. 1&1 Mobile — from €9.99/month**
Budget-friendly with EU roaming. Runs on Telefónica/O2 network. Good for city travel.

**4. Congstar (Telekom network) — from €10/month (prepaid)**
Solid option for Moroccan immigrants on a budget who still want reliable EU roaming. Uses Telekom's network. Available at [congstar.de](https://www.congstar.de).

**5. SMARTMOBIL.DE — from €6.99/month**
Ultra-cheap, EU roaming included, runs on Telekom or Vodafone network depending on plan.

### What About eSIMs for Europe-Wide Travel?

eSIM providers like **Airalo**, **Nomad**, or **Maya Mobile** let you buy regional data packages for all of Europe at flat rates. For example, Airalo sells a 3 GB Europe-wide eSIM for around €9–€12. This is a great secondary option if you want data without worrying about fair use limits on your German plan.

## Switzerland, UK, and Other "Tricky" Destinations

A common mistake is assuming all neighboring countries are covered under EU roaming. Here's what actually happens:

- **Switzerland:** Not in the EU. German providers charge extra. Expect €0.20–€0.50/MB without an add-on. Buy a Swiss SIM or a roaming day pass.
- **United Kingdom (post-Brexit):** No longer covered by EU rules. Many German providers now charge UK roaming fees. Vodafone Germany, however, still includes the UK for free in some plans — check before you go.
- **Turkey:** Outside EU. Same as Morocco — buy local or use an add-on.
- **Western Balkans (Serbia, Bosnia, Kosovo):** Not EU. Costs apply.
- **Albania, North Macedonia:** EU candidate countries but NOT covered by RLAH yet.

## Common Pitfalls: What People Get Wrong About Roaming in Europe

This section could save you a lot of money and frustration.

**1. Assuming Switzerland is in the EU roaming zone.**
It's one of the most common mistakes. People drive from Germany to Zurich and suddenly have a €80 data bill. Always check before crossing into Switzerland.

**2. Forgetting to check your fair use data cap.**
If you have an unlimited German plan, you may be capped at 25 GB when using it in the EU. Streaming Netflix on a two-week holiday in Spain could hit that limit fast.

**3. Leaving roaming on automatically when flying into Morocco or Turkey.**
Your phone connects to a local network the moment you land, even before you exit the plane. Turn off mobile data in airplane settings before you land if you're not using a roaming add-on.

**4. Not checking if your plan covers calls as well as data.**
Some budget plans include free EU data but still charge per minute for calls made abroad. Read the fine print.

**5. Relying on hotel Wi-Fi as your only backup.**
Hotel Wi-Fi in Southern Europe and Morocco can be unreliable. Having a local SIM or eSIM as backup is always worth the €3–€5 investment.

**6. Thinking prepaid cards don't include EU roaming.**
Most German prepaid SIMs — including Aldi Talk, Lidl Connect, and Congstar — do include EU roaming. You don't need a contract for this benefit.

## Conclusion: Roam Smart, Spend Less

Roaming in Europe from Germany is genuinely simple once you understand the rules. Within the EU, your German SIM works just like at home — no extra charges, no setup needed. The problems only appear when you step outside the EU zone, especially when visiting Morocco, Switzerland, or Turkey. In those cases, the solution is almost always the same: a local SIM, a day pass add-on, or a cheap eSIM.

Plan ahead, turn off auto-roaming before landing in non-EU countries, and pick a German provider with solid EU coverage. If you're still in the process of setting up your life in Germany — from your SIM card to your job application — [Book a free consultation to learn German and move to Germany successfully](/cv-builder) and get personalized guidance every step of the way.

faqs.question: Is roaming free in all European countries when I have a German SIM?
faqs.answer: No. EU roaming is free in the 27 EU countries plus Norway, Iceland, and Liechtenstein. Switzerland, the UK, Turkey, and Morocco are NOT covered — extra charges apply there.

faqs.question: Can I use my German unlimited data plan freely across Europe?
faqs.answer: Not always. EU law allows providers to cap roaming data even on unlimited plans. Vodafone Germany, for example, limits EU roaming data to around 25–35 GB. Check your specific plan at your provider's website.

faqs.question: What is the cheapest way to have internet access when visiting Morocco from Germany?
faqs.answer: Buy a local Moroccan SIM from Maroc Telecom, Orange Maroc, or Inwi at the airport for around 30–50 MAD (€3–€5). Alternatively, buy a Morocco eSIM from Airalo or Holafly before you travel, starting at around €4 for 1 GB.

faqs.question: Do German prepaid SIM cards include EU roaming?
faqs.answer: Yes, most do. Aldi Talk, Lidl Connect, Congstar, and EDEKA Mobil all include EU roaming on their prepaid plans. Data speeds may be limited on cheaper plans, but basic roaming works.

faqs.question: What should I do to avoid surprise roaming bills when traveling?
faqs.answer: Before landing in any non-EU country, turn off mobile data in your phone settings. Use Wi-Fi only, buy a local SIM, or activate a roaming day pass from your German provider. Never assume roaming is free outside the EU zone.

rw-55.title: Studienkolleg in Germany: The Complete Guide to the Preparatory Year for Moroccan Students
rw-55.summary: Everything Moroccan students need to know about Studienkolleg — what it is, how to apply, costs, and how to pass the Feststellungsprüfung.
rw-55.content:
If your Moroccan Baccalaureate isn't recognized as a direct university entry qualification in Germany, you're not stuck — you just need one extra year. The Studienkolleg, Germany's official preparatory year (السنة التحضيرية), bridges the gap between your high school diploma and full university admission. Understanding exactly how it works, where to apply, and what to expect can save you months of confusion and costly mistakes.

## What Is Studienkolleg and Who Needs It?

The Studienkolleg is a state-run preparatory college designed specifically for international students whose home-country school-leaving certificate doesn't meet German university entry standards. In Germany, it's treated as a structured academic year — not a language course, not a formality — but a serious qualification program that ends with a formal exam called the **Feststellungsprüfung (FSP)**.

As a Moroccan student, your Baccalauréat almost always places you in this category. The German university system requires what they call **Hochschulzugangsberechtigung** (university entrance qualification), and the Moroccan Bac alone doesn't fulfill this — at least not for most universities. You have two routes:

- **Complete the Studienkolleg** and pass the FSP
- **Study two years at a Moroccan university** in a recognized program, then apply directly (without Studienkolleg)

Most students who come straight after the Bac choose the Studienkolleg path.

### Who Is Exempt?

You may skip Studienkolleg if you have completed at least two years of a recognized degree program at a Moroccan university (like at Université Mohammed V or Université Hassan II) with a sufficient number of credit hours. Always verify this with the specific German university you're targeting, or use the **anabin database** (anabin.kmk.org) to check your qualification status.

## The Different Studienkolleg Courses (Schwerpunkte)

Not all Studienkolleg programs are the same. You apply to a specific **Schwerpunkt** (focus course) depending on your intended degree program in Germany. Choosing the wrong one is one of the most common and costly mistakes students make.

Here are the main types:

- **T-Kurs (Technik):** For students planning to study engineering, computer science, mathematics, or natural sciences. This is the most common track for Moroccan students.
- **W-Kurs (Wirtschaft):** For business, economics, and social sciences.
- **M-Kurs (Medizin):** For medicine, pharmacy, dentistry, and biology.
- **G-Kurs (Geisteswissenschaften):** For humanities, law, and language studies.
- **S-Kurs (Sprache):** For students aiming at language and literature degrees — rare for Moroccans but relevant for some.

Your Schwerpunkt determines which subjects you'll study and which exam you'll sit at the end. The T-Kurs, for example, includes mathematics, physics, chemistry, and German. The W-Kurs includes economics, mathematics, and German.

## Where Are Studienkollegs Located in Germany?

Every German federal state (Bundesland) has at least one Studienkolleg, and some have several. Here are well-known options:

- **Studienkolleg Berlin** (studienkolleg.berlin) — attached to public universities in Berlin
- **Studienkolleg Bayern** in Munich — one of the most competitive
- **Studienkolleg Hessen** in Kassel and Frankfurt area
- **Studienkolleg NRW** — serving universities in North Rhine-Westphalia
- **Studienkolleg Hamburg** — popular for its location and university connections

Some Studienkollegs are attached to specific universities (like TU München or Universität Stuttgart), meaning passing their FSP gives you priority admission to that institution. Others are state-wide and let you apply to multiple universities with the FSP result.

### Private Studienkollegs

There are also private Studienkollegs. These are easier to get into but cost significantly more — typically **€3,000–€8,000 per semester** compared to public ones which cost little to nothing (just the standard semester fee of around **€150–€350**). A private Studienkolleg FSP may not be accepted by all public universities, so always check in advance.

## The Application Process: Step by Step

Applying to a Studienkolleg requires careful planning. Deadlines vary by institution, but most follow the German academic calendar with **winter semester (October start)** and **summer semester (April start)** intakes.

### Required Documents

- Moroccan Baccalauréat certificate (original + certified German or English translation)
- Official transcripts from secondary school
- German language certificate — minimum **B2 level**, with many Studienkollegs requiring **C1** (TestDaF, DSH, or Goethe-Zertifikat)
- Passport copy
- Motivation letter / application form
- Proof of financial means (blocked account with at least **€11,208 per year** as of 2024)
- Passport-size photos
- APS certificate — this is **mandatory for Moroccan students**

### The APS Certificate

The **APS (Akademische Prüfstelle)** is a document verification process run by the German Embassy in Rabat. Moroccan students must have their academic documents verified and receive an APS certificate before any German university or Studienkolleg will accept their application. The process takes several weeks and costs around **€150–€200**. Book your appointment early at the German Embassy website (rabat.diplo.de).

### Application Platforms

- **uni-assist.de** — the central application portal used by most public universities and their Studienkollegs
- Direct application to the Studienkolleg's own portal (some institutions accept this)
- **Hochschulstart.de** — used for medicine-related programs

Application deadlines are typically:
- Winter semester: **May 15 – July 15**
- Summer semester: **November 15 – January 15**

These vary, so always check the specific institution's website.

## The Feststellungsprüfung (FSP): What You're Working Toward

The entire Studienkolleg year builds toward the **Feststellungsprüfung** — the final assessment exam that grants you university entry. This is not a small test. It's a formal examination in multiple subjects, conducted in German, and graded on a scale that contributes to your university application ranking.

### What the FSP Covers

For the T-Kurs, you'll be examined in:
- German (written and oral)
- Mathematics
- Physics or Chemistry (depending on your chosen subject)

The FSP result directly affects your university admission chances. A strong FSP grade (especially in maths-heavy Studienkollegs) can open doors to competitive programs like mechanical engineering at TU Berlin or computer science at KIT Karlsruhe.

### What Happens If You Fail?

You can resit the FSP once. If you fail twice, you are not allowed to take it again — meaning you cannot attend a German university through this route. This is why preparation is serious and consistent study throughout the year is non-negotiable.

## Costs and Living Expenses to Expect

Here's a realistic monthly budget for a student at Studienkolleg in Germany:

- **Tuition:** €0 at public institutions (semester fee ~€150–€350 total per semester)
- **Accommodation:** €300–€700/month (student dorms are cheaper; cities like Munich are more expensive)
- **Food & groceries:** €150–€250/month
- **Transport:** €30–€90/month (many student cards include public transport)
- **Health insurance:** ~€120/month (mandatory for students)
- **Total estimate:** €700–€1,200/month depending on city

Over one academic year, budget for roughly **€8,500–€14,000** in total living and administrative costs. Germany requires you to demonstrate you can cover this through a **blocked account (Sperrkonto)** before issuing your student visa.

## Common Pitfalls: What Moroccan Students Get Wrong

Many students go into the Studienkolleg process with avoidable misunderstandings. Here are the most frequent ones:

- **Applying to the wrong Schwerpunkt:** Choosing the W-Kurs when your goal is engineering wastes an entire year. Match your Kurs to your intended degree before applying.
- **Underestimating the German language requirement:** Many applicants arrive with B1 German and get rejected or placed in language courses first. Reach B2 minimum — ideally C1 — before applying.
- **Forgetting the APS certificate:** This step is unique to Moroccan (and Chinese and Vietnamese) students. Skipping it means immediate rejection.
- **Assuming any FSP is accepted everywhere:** A private Studienkolleg FSP may not be recognized by the university you actually want to attend. Confirm compatibility before enrolling.
- **Missing application windows:** The German system is strict about deadlines. Missing a window by even a day means waiting another semester — six months lost.
- **Not preparing for the Aufnahmeprüfung:** Most Studienkollegs require an entrance exam (Aufnahmeprüfung) to even get a place. This typically tests German and basic subject knowledge. Don't assume acceptance is automatic.

## Conclusion: Your Studienkolleg Year Is an Investment, Not a Detour

The Studienkolleg preparatory year is not a consolation prize — it's a structured, respected pathway that tens of thousands of international students use every year to enter German universities. For Moroccan students in particular, it's often the most realistic and direct route to studying engineering, medicine, business, or any other field at a top German university.

Prepare your language skills early, get your APS certificate sorted, choose the right Schwerpunkt, and treat the FSP like the important exam it is. One focused year can open up a degree, a career, and a life in Germany.

If you're not sure where to start — whether it's writing a strong motivation letter or building a competitive CV — [book a free consultation to learn German and move to Germany successfully](/cv-builder). Getting the right guidance early makes everything else easier.

faqs.question: Do all Moroccan students need to attend Studienkolleg before studying in Germany?
faqs.answer: Not necessarily. If you've completed at least two years of a recognized university degree in Morocco (with enough credit hours), you may apply directly to German universities without Studienkolleg. Check your qualification on the anabin database at anabin.kmk.org. If you come straight after the Baccalauréat, you almost certainly need Studienkolleg.

faqs.question: What German language level do I need to apply for Studienkolleg?
faqs.answer: Most public Studienkollegs require at least B2 level German, and many competitive ones expect C1. You'll need to prove this with a recognized certificate such as TestDaF (score of 4 in each section), DSH-2, or Goethe-Zertifikat C1. Starting German early — ideally 12–18 months before you plan to apply — gives you the best chance.

faqs.question: What is the APS certificate and how do Moroccan students get it?
faqs.answer: The APS (Akademische Prüfstelle) is a document verification service run by the German Embassy. Moroccan students must submit their school and university documents for authentication before any German institution will process their application. The process costs approximately €150–€200 and takes several weeks. Book your appointment through the German Embassy in Rabat at rabat.diplo.de well in advance.

faqs.question: Can I fail the Studienkolleg and reapply?
faqs.answer: You can retake the Feststellungsprüfung (FSP) once if you fail the first time. However, if you fail both attempts, you are permanently barred from taking it again, which closes the Studienkolleg route to German universities. This makes consistent preparation throughout the year critically important — treat every subject seriously from day one.

faqs.question: How long does the entire process take from Morocco to starting university in Germany?
faqs.answer: Realistically, plan for 18–24 months from the time you start preparing. This includes 6–12 months to reach the required German language level, 1–3 months for APS verification and application processing, and then one full academic year (10 months) at Studienkolleg before you can begin your actual university degree. Starting early and staying organized is the biggest advantage you can give yourself.

rw-57.title: Student Housing in Germany: Wohnheim vs WG — What Moroccan Students Need to Know
rw-57.summary: Choosing between a Wohnheim and a WG in Germany? This guide breaks down costs, pros, cons, and how to find student housing fast.
rw-57.content:
Finding a place to live in Germany before your studies begin is one of the most stressful parts of the whole process — and for many Moroccan students, it's also the least understood. The two main options you'll hear about are the **Wohnheim** (student dormitory) and the **WG** (shared apartment, or *Wohngemeinschaft*), and picking the wrong one for your situation can cost you time, money, and a lot of unnecessary headaches. This guide walks you through exactly how both options work, what they realistically cost in 2024, and how to land a room before you even board your flight.

## Understanding Student Housing in Germany: The Two Main Paths

Germany doesn't have the sprawling university campuses you might picture from American movies. Most German universities are spread across a city, and students live in regular neighborhoods — not in on-campus residences. That said, there is a strong infrastructure for affordable student housing, managed largely by the **Studentenwerk** (student services organization) in each city.

Your two main options are:

- **Wohnheim** — a student dormitory run by the Studentenwerk or a private provider
- **WG (Wohngemeinschaft)** — a shared private apartment where you rent one room and share common spaces with flatmates

Both have real advantages. The right choice depends on your budget, your German level, and how quickly you need to secure a place.

## What Is a Wohnheim and How Does It Work?

A Wohnheim is a purpose-built student residence, usually managed by the local Studentenwerk. Think of it as a building filled entirely with students, with shared kitchens, bathrooms (in some cases), and communal areas.

### Types of Wohnheim rooms

- **Single room with shared kitchen and bathroom** — the most common and cheapest option
- **Single room with private bathroom (en suite)** — slightly more expensive, more privacy
- **Studio apartment** — your own kitchen, bathroom, and living space within the dorm building
- **Couple or double rooms** — available in some cities if you're moving with a partner

### Costs

Wohnheim rent is subsidized and genuinely affordable by German standards:

- Munich (München): €280–€420/month
- Berlin: €220–€380/month
- Leipzig or Chemnitz: €150–€250/month
- Frankfurt: €250–€400/month
- Hamburg: €230–€370/month

These prices include utilities (water, heating, internet) in most cases — which is a big deal compared to the private market.

### How to apply

You apply through your local **Studentenwerk** website. Every city has one. For example:
- Berlin: [studentenwerk-berlin.de](https://www.studentenwerk-berlin.de)
- Munich: [studierendenwerk-muenchen.de](https://www.studierendenwerk-muenchen.de)
- Hamburg: [studierendenwerk-hamburg.de](https://www.studierendenwerk-hamburg.de)

**The critical point: waiting lists can be 6–18 months long**, especially in Munich and Berlin. Apply the moment you receive your university admission letter — or even earlier if the Studentenwerk allows pre-applications.

### Who should choose a Wohnheim?

- Students arriving in Germany for the first time
- Those with a tight budget
- Students who want everything handled (no landlord negotiations, no utility contracts)
- People who want a ready-made community of other students

## What Is a WG and How Does It Work?

A WG (*Wohngemeinschaft*) is a shared private apartment. You rent one room, and you share the kitchen, living room, and bathroom with 2–5 other people (sometimes more). Your flatmates might be students, young professionals, or a mix.

### Costs

WG rooms are priced on the open market and vary widely:

- Munich: €600–€900/month (warm, meaning utilities included)
- Berlin: €500–€750/month
- Cologne: €450–€650/month
- Leipzig: €300–€500/month
- Heidelberg: €500–€700/month

Note: "warm" rent (*Warmmiete*) includes utilities. "Cold" rent (*Kaltmiete*) does not — always ask which one is being quoted.

### Where to find WG rooms

- **WG-Gesucht.de** — the biggest platform in Germany for shared apartments, essential
- **Immoscout24.de** — broader real estate platform, has WG listings too
- **Studenten-WG.de** — student-focused listings
- **Facebook groups** — search "[city name] WG" or "Wohnung [city name]"
- University notice boards and international student forums

### What landlords and current flatmates want to see

Most WG listings require you to write a short introduction about yourself (*Vorstellungsschreiben*). This is basically a cover letter for an apartment — you explain who you are, what you study, your habits, and why you'd be a good flatmate. A well-written intro dramatically increases your chances of getting a viewing.

You'll also typically need:
- Passport copy
- Enrollment confirmation (*Immatrikulationsbescheinigung*)
- Sometimes a **Schufa** credit report (less common for students)
- Proof of income or a financial guarantee (blocked account statement works)

### Who should choose a WG?

- Students who already have some German language skills
- Those who want more independence and a normal apartment feel
- Students who couldn't get a Wohnheim spot in time
- People who want to integrate faster into German daily life

## Wohnheim vs WG: A Side-by-Side Comparison

| Factor | Wohnheim | WG |
|---|---|---|
| Average monthly cost | €180–€420 | €350–€900 |
| Utilities included | Usually yes | Sometimes |
| Waiting time | 6–18 months | Days to weeks |
| Flexibility | Fixed contract terms | More flexible |
| Social life | Built-in student community | Depends on flatmates |
| German skills needed | Low | Medium–High |
| Application difficulty | Straightforward | Competitive |

## Private and University-Linked Alternatives

Beyond the classic Wohnheim and WG, a few other options are worth knowing about:

### Private dormitories
Companies like **The Fizz**, **YOUNIQ**, and **International Campus** run private student residences in major cities. Costs range from €500–€900/month but everything is included (furniture, wifi, cleaning of common areas) and the waiting lists are shorter. Good as a backup.

### Temporary housing (for your first weeks)
If you arrive without permanent housing confirmed, use:
- **Airbnb** or **Booking.com** for the first 1–2 weeks
- Youth hostels (around €25–€50/night)
- University international offices sometimes have short-term housing lists

Never arrive in Germany without at least 2–3 weeks of confirmed temporary accommodation.

## Common Pitfalls — What People Get Wrong

**Applying too late for a Wohnheim.** The single biggest mistake. Students apply after arriving in Germany and then wait a year. Apply the same week you get your admission.

**Not reading the WG listing carefully.** Some listings say *Kaltmiete* but add €150–€200 in utilities on top. Do the math before you message the landlord.

**Sending a generic WG introduction.** Dozens of people apply for the same room. A copy-paste message gets ignored. Write something specific — mention the city, the neighborhood, or something from the listing itself.

**Forgetting that you need a registered address for your visa.** In Germany, you must register your address (*Anmeldung*) at the local residents' office within 14 days of moving in. You can only do this once you have a real lease or sublease agreement — not an Airbnb booking. Plan for this from day one.

**Assuming every city is the same.** Leipzig and Dresden have dramatically more affordable housing than Munich or Frankfurt. If you have flexibility in your university choice, factor housing costs into your decision.

**Falling for rental scams.** On platforms like WG-Gesucht, scammers post fake rooms and ask for deposits via wire transfer before you've seen the place. Never send money without a verified viewing, in person or via video call.

## Practical Timeline: When to Do What

- **6–12 months before arrival**: Apply to Studentenwerk Wohnheim in your target city
- **3–6 months before**: Start browsing WG-Gesucht and send applications
- **2–3 months before**: Confirm temporary housing for your first weeks if permanent housing isn't secured
- **Before departure**: Have a lease or sublease agreement ready so you can do your Anmeldung on arrival

## Conclusion

Student housing in Germany is manageable — but only if you start early and understand how the system works. A Wohnheim gives you security, low costs, and community, but the waiting list is real. A WG gives you freedom and faster availability, but it takes effort to land a room in a competitive market. Most successful Moroccan students apply to both simultaneously and take whichever comes through first.

If you're still building your application documents — like your motivation letter or CV for university admission — or if you need guidance on the German language requirements to write a convincing WG introduction, **book a free consultation to learn German and move to Germany successfully**. Our team has helped hundreds of Moroccan students navigate exactly this process.

👉 [Build your CV and documents here](/cv-builder)

faqs.question: How long is the waiting list for a Wohnheim in Germany?
faqs.answer: It depends on the city. In Munich and Berlin, waiting lists are typically 6–18 months. In smaller cities like Leipzig or Erfurt, you might get a room in 2–4 months. Apply immediately after receiving your admission letter — don't wait until you arrive.

faqs.question: Can I find a WG room in Germany without speaking German?
faqs.answer: Yes, especially in large university cities where many flatmates are international students. However, writing your WG introduction (*Vorstellungsschreiben*) in German — even basic German — significantly increases your response rate. Most listings on WG-Gesucht.de accept English introductions in cities like Berlin, Munich, and Hamburg.

faqs.question: How much money should I budget for student housing in Germany per month?
faqs.answer: For a Wohnheim, budget €180–€420/month depending on the city. For a WG room, budget €350–€900/month. Smaller eastern German cities like Leipzig or Chemnitz are the most affordable. Munich and Frankfurt are the most expensive. Always check whether utilities are included in the quoted rent.

faqs.question: Is it safe to pay a deposit for a WG room before arriving in Germany?
faqs.answer: Be very cautious. Rental scams are common on platforms like WG-Gesucht.de. Never transfer money to someone you haven't met via a verified video call or in-person viewing. Legitimate landlords understand this concern. If someone pressures you to pay immediately without a viewing, it's almost certainly a scam.

faqs.question: What documents do I need to rent a WG room in Germany as a Moroccan student?
faqs.answer: Typically: your passport, university enrollment confirmation (*Immatrikulationsbescheinigung*), proof of financial means (your blocked account statement works well), and a well-written personal introduction. Some landlords ask for a Schufa credit report, but this is less common for international students who are new to Germany.

rw-59.title: Living in Germany's Cheapest Student Cities: A Complete Guide for Moroccan Students
rw-59.summary: Discover the most affordable student cities in Germany, with real costs, city comparisons, and practical tips for Moroccan students planning their move.
rw-59.content:
Moving to Germany as a student is one of the smartest decisions you can make for your future — but the cost of living can vary dramatically depending on where you study. While Munich and Frankfurt often steal the headlines, several German cities offer excellent universities, vibrant student life, and monthly budgets that won't leave you counting coins by the end of the semester. This guide breaks down the cheapest student cities in Germany with real numbers, honest comparisons, and actionable advice for Moroccan students planning their move.

## Why Choosing the Right City Matters as Much as Choosing the Right University

Most students focus entirely on university rankings when applying to study in Germany. That's understandable, but your quality of life — and your ability to actually finish your degree without financial panic — depends just as much on where you live as on where you study.

The difference between living in Munich and living in Chemnitz, for example, can be over €500 per month. Over a five-year degree, that's €30,000 — money that could fund a master's degree, a business, or a comfortable life back in Morocco if you return.

Germany has excellent universities in almost every major city. You don't have to sacrifice academic quality to save money. You just need to know which cities offer the best balance.

## The Cheapest Student Cities in Germany: City-by-City Breakdown

Here are the most affordable cities for students in Germany, based on average monthly living costs including rent, food, transport, and basic lifestyle:

### Chemnitz — The Most Affordable Option

Chemnitz in Saxony consistently ranks as one of the cheapest cities in Germany for students. The Technische Universität Chemnitz is a solid engineering and technology university with programs in English.

- **Average monthly rent (student room):** €200–€320
- **Monthly living costs (all-in):** €600–€800
- **Semester ticket (local transport):** ~€100 per semester
- **Main university:** TU Chemnitz

If you're studying engineering, computer science, or business, Chemnitz is worth serious consideration.

### Leipzig — Affordable with a Thriving Cultural Scene

Leipzig is one of Germany's fastest-growing cities and has a strong student population. It's significantly cheaper than Berlin, despite being just 1.5 hours away by train.

- **Average monthly rent:** €300–€450
- **Monthly living costs:** €750–€1,000
- **Main universities:** Universität Leipzig, HTWK Leipzig
- **Known for:** Music, arts, strong startup scene

Leipzig offers a quality of life that punches well above its price tag.

### Halle (Saale) — Budget Living Near Leipzig

Right next to Leipzig, Halle is even cheaper and shares strong academic ties through the Martin Luther University Halle-Wittenberg.

- **Average monthly rent:** €220–€350
- **Monthly living costs:** €600–€850
- **Notable fact:** One of the oldest universities in Germany, founded in 1694

Many students live in Halle and commute to Leipzig for social life — the train takes about 30 minutes and costs very little with a semester ticket.

### Magdeburg — Tech and Engineering on a Budget

Magdeburg is home to Otto von Guericke University, which has a particularly strong reputation in engineering and life sciences. The city is affordable and manageable in size.

- **Average monthly rent:** €250–€380
- **Monthly living costs:** €650–€900
- **Strong programs:** Mechanical engineering, medical engineering, computer science

### Jena — Small City, Strong Science

Jena in Thuringia is home to Friedrich Schiller University and is famous for its optics and science industries (Zeiss, Jenoptik). It's small, safe, and affordable.

- **Average monthly rent:** €280–€400
- **Monthly living costs:** €700–€950
- **Bonus:** Strong industry connections for internships and graduate jobs

### Dortmund and Bochum — Affordable Ruhr Area Cities

The Ruhr area in western Germany includes Dortmund, Bochum, and Essen — all affordable cities with large universities and excellent transport connections.

- **Average monthly rent (Dortmund/Bochum):** €300–€480
- **Monthly living costs:** €800–€1,050
- **Main universities:** TU Dortmund, Ruhr-Universität Bochum
- **Advantage:** One semester ticket covers the entire Ruhr transport network

The Ruhr area is ideal if you want affordable living without being in a small or isolated city.

## What Does a Realistic Monthly Budget Look Like?

Let's build a concrete monthly budget for a Moroccan student living in Leipzig — one of the best mid-range options:

| Expense | Cost |
|---|---|
| Rent (student dormitory) | €280 |
| Food and groceries | €200 |
