faqs.answer: Qualified nurses in Germany typically earn €2,500 to €3,200 gross per month in entry-level positions. With specializations such as intensive care or anaesthesia nursing, experienced professionals regularly earn €3,500 to €4,500+ per month, plus supplements for nights and weekends.

faqs.question: Which German cities have the most nursing Ausbildung opportunities for international applicants?
faqs.answer: Berlin, Hamburg, Munich, Frankfurt, and Cologne have the highest number of open positions. However, cities in eastern Germany such as Leipzig, Dresden, and Magdeburg also have strong demand with lower living costs, which can result in a better quality of life on a trainee salary.

rw-70.title: Ausbildung in Germany Over 25: Is It Still Possible for Moroccans?
rw-70.summary: Wondering if you can start an Ausbildung in Germany after 25 as a Moroccan? Yes, you can — here's exactly how to make it work.
rw-70.content:
Starting a vocational training program in Germany might feel like a young person's game, but the reality is far more encouraging than most Moroccans believe. Thousands of adults over 25 — including many from Morocco — successfully complete an Ausbildung every year and go on to build stable, well-paying careers in Germany. If you're in your late twenties, thirties, or even forties and wondering whether this door is still open for you, the short answer is yes — and this guide will show you exactly how to walk through it.

## What Is an Ausbildung and Why Age Matters Less Than You Think

An Ausbildung is Germany's dual vocational training system, combining practical work at a company with part-time classes at a vocational school (Berufsschule). It typically lasts between two and three and a half years, depending on the profession, and ends with a nationally recognized qualification.

Legally, there is **no upper age limit** for starting an Ausbildung in Germany. The law does not bar anyone from signing a training contract based on their age. What does matter is your German language level, your residency status, and — most importantly — finding an employer willing to hire you as a trainee.

The misconception that Ausbildung is only for teenagers comes from the fact that the German school system traditionally funnels 16–18-year-olds into these programs. But the labor market reality is different: Germany has over 70,000 unfilled Ausbildung positions every year, and employers are actively looking beyond the traditional age group.

## Which Professions Are Most Open to Applicants Over 25

Not every sector is equally welcoming to older applicants, but several high-demand fields actively recruit adults:

- **Healthcare and nursing (Pflege):** Germany is facing a severe nursing shortage. Hospitals, care homes, and clinics in cities like Munich, Frankfurt, and Hamburg regularly hire adult trainees. Nursing assistants can earn €800–€1,100/month during training.
- **IT and digital professions:** Fachinformatiker (IT specialist) programs value real-world thinking. If you have any background in tech, this is a strong option.
- **Logistics and warehouse management:** Companies like Amazon, DHL, and DB Schenker run structured Ausbildung programs and often prefer mature, reliable workers.
- **Trades (Handwerk):** Electricians, plumbers, and HVAC technicians are desperately needed. Many master craftsmen (Meister) specifically seek adult apprentices who take the work seriously.
- **Retail and commerce (Kaufmann/Kauffrau):** Office-based commercial training is abundant and beginner-friendly for older applicants.

### Why Employers Sometimes Prefer Older Applicants

Here is something the career guides rarely say out loud: many German employers find adult trainees more dependable. You show up on time, you don't call in sick every Friday, and you understand that this opportunity matters. Lean into that. Mention your life experience, your motivation, and your reliability in your cover letter and interview.

## Visa and Residency Requirements for Moroccans Over 25

Your immigration path determines which type of Ausbildung you can access.

### If You Are Already in Germany

If you hold a residence permit (Aufenthaltserlaubnis) for study, work, or family reasons, you can typically apply for an Ausbildung without changing your visa. Once you have a signed training contract, you can apply to convert your permit to an **Ausbildung visa** at your local Ausländerbehörde.

### If You Are Still in Morocco

You need to apply for a **German Ausbildung visa (§16a AufenthG)** at the German consulate in Rabat or Casablanca. To get this visa, you need:

- A signed Ausbildungsvertrag (training contract) from a German company
- Proof of German language skills (usually B1 minimum, B2 preferred)
- A valid Moroccan passport
- Proof of recognized educational qualifications (your Bac diploma may need to be evaluated — check anabin.kmk.org)
- Health insurance coverage
- Proof of accommodation in Germany

Processing times at the German consulate in Morocco currently range from **8 to 16 weeks**, so plan ahead.

## How to Find an Ausbildung Position as a Moroccan Over 25

This is where most people get stuck. Here is a practical, step-by-step approach:

1. **Set your German level as priority one.** Almost every employer requires at least B1. B2 opens significantly more doors. Reach this level before you apply.
2. **Search on the right platforms.** Use [Jobbörse der Bundesagentur für Arbeit](https://www.arbeitsagentur.de/jobsuche/), [Ausbildung.de](https://www.ausbildung.de), and [Indeed.de](https://de.indeed.com). Filter by profession and city.
3. **Target smaller companies.** Large corporations often have rigid HR systems that filter out older applicants automatically. Small and medium-sized businesses (Mittelstand) are far more flexible.
4. **Write a strong, honest cover letter (Anschreiben).** Explain your motivation clearly. Don't apologize for your age — frame your experience as an asset.
5. **Apply to at least 20–30 positions.** Response rates can be low. Volume matters.
6. **Contact your local IHK or HWK.** The Chamber of Commerce (IHK) and Chamber of Crafts (HWK) in every German city maintain lists of companies seeking trainees and can connect you directly.
7. **Use the Make it in Germany portal.** [Make it in Germany](https://www.make-it-in-germany.com) is a federal government platform specifically designed to help international candidates find Ausbildung and work placements.

### What About the Recognition of Your Moroccan Qualifications?

If your field requires prior education (for example, nursing often requires proof of secondary schooling), your Moroccan diploma may need official recognition. Use the [Anabin database](https://anabin.kmk.org) to check the status of your institution, and contact the relevant recognition authority (Anerkennungsstelle) in your target German state. The [BIBB portal](https://www.anerkennung-in-deutschland.de) offers a free recognition advisory tool in multiple languages.

## Money: What You Earn and What It Costs During an Ausbildung

As of 2024, Germany's minimum Ausbildung salary is:
- **Year 1:** €649/month
- **Year 2:** €766/month
- **Year 3:** €876/month

Many employers pay significantly more — especially in healthcare and IT, where salaries of €900–€1,300/month during training are common.

Living costs in Germany vary by city. As a rough guide:
- Berlin: ~€900–€1,100/month (rent + food + transport)
- Munich: ~€1,200–€1,500/month
- Leipzig or Nuremberg: ~€700–€900/month

This means your training salary may not fully cover your costs, especially in expensive cities. Many trainees work mini-jobs on weekends, and some states offer financial support through BAB (Berufsausbildungsbeihilfe), a federal grant you can apply for through the Bundesagentur für Arbeit.

## What People Get Wrong About Ausbildung Over 25

**"I'm too old to learn fast enough."** Learning speed is not the barrier — language is. If your German is solid, you can absolutely keep up with younger classmates in Berufsschule. Many older students perform better because they are more focused.

**"No company will take me."** Wrong. Sectors like nursing, logistics, and trades have shortages so severe that employers actively welcome anyone who is motivated and reliable. Age is rarely the reason applications are rejected — weak German or a poorly written cover letter usually is.

**"I need to have a German school leaving certificate."** Not always true. Many Ausbildung programs accept equivalent foreign qualifications. Use the Anabin database to check yours.

**"I'll be finished training at 30 — that's too late."** Finishing at 30 with a German vocational qualification means you have potentially 35 years of career ahead of you in one of Europe's strongest economies. That is not too late — that is a solid foundation.

**"My Moroccan German teacher said B1 is enough."** B1 gets you through the visa application. But at B2–C1, you will understand your trainer, follow class lectures, and communicate with patients or customers without constant strain. Invest in your German.

## Conclusion

Starting an Ausbildung in Germany after 25 as a Moroccan is not only possible — it is a smart, structured path to long-term stability in Europe. The legal framework supports you, the labor market needs you, and employers in healthcare, trades, and logistics are actively looking for adults like you. Your biggest tasks right now are improving your German, writing a compelling application, and targeting the right sectors.

Take the first step today. Whether you need help building a strong Ausbildung application or crafting the perfect Anschreiben, [book a free consultation](/anschreiben-generator) and get expert support to move to Germany successfully.

faqs.question: Is there an official age limit for starting an Ausbildung in Germany?
faqs.answer: No. German law sets no upper age limit for Ausbildung. You can sign a training contract at 27, 35, or even 45. What matters is finding an employer willing to hire you and meeting language and visa requirements.

faqs.question: What German level do I need to start an Ausbildung as a Moroccan applicant?
faqs.answer: Most employers and visa authorities require at least B1, but B2 is strongly recommended. At B2, you can follow lessons at the Berufsschule, understand workplace instructions, and communicate with customers or patients — all of which directly affect your performance and your chances of being hired.

faqs.question: How much money will I earn during an Ausbildung in Germany?
faqs.answer: As of 2024, the legal minimum is €649/month in the first year, rising to €876/month by the third year. In high-demand fields like healthcare or IT, trainees often earn €900–€1,300/month. You may also qualify for BAB financial assistance through the Bundesagentur für Arbeit if your income doesn't cover living costs.

faqs.question: Do I need to have my Moroccan diplomas officially recognized before applying?
faqs.answer: It depends on the profession. For regulated fields like nursing, formal recognition of your secondary education is usually required. For many commercial or trade-based programs, it is not mandatory. Use the free tool at anerkennung-in-deutschland.de to check exactly what applies to your situation and target profession.

faqs.question: Which German cities are best for Moroccans looking for an Ausbildung over 25?
faqs.answer: Cities with large healthcare, logistics, and trade sectors are your best bet. Frankfurt, Hamburg, Munich, Cologne, and Nuremberg all have high numbers of unfilled Ausbildung positions. Smaller cities like Leipzig, Dresden, and Mannheim also offer strong opportunities with lower competition and lower living costs — making your training salary stretch further.

rw-32.title: Steuererklärung: How to Get Your German Tax Refund Every Year
rw-32.summary: Learn how to file a Steuererklärung in Germany and get hundreds of euros back every year — a practical guide for Moroccans working in Germany.
rw-32.content:
Every year, thousands of workers in Germany leave hundreds — sometimes thousands — of euros on the table simply because they never file a tax return. If you moved from Morocco to work or do an Ausbildung in Germany, the Steuererklärung (German tax return) is one of the most powerful financial tools available to you. Filing it correctly could put €500, €1,000, or even more back in your pocket — legally and every single year.

## What Is a Steuererklärung and Why Should You File One?

A Steuererklärung is the annual tax declaration you submit to the German tax office (Finanzamt). Your employer already deducts income tax (Lohnsteuer) from your salary every month. But that automatic deduction is based on rough estimates — it doesn't account for your actual expenses, your personal situation, or any deductions you're entitled to claim.

When you file a tax return, the Finanzamt recalculates what you actually owe. In most cases, especially for employees, Azubis (apprentices), and newly arrived immigrants, **you get money back**.

### Who Has to File — and Who Should File Voluntarily?

**Mandatory filing** applies if you:
- Have income from two or more sources (e.g., a side job alongside your main job)
- Received more than €410 in wage replacement benefits like Kurzarbeitergeld or Elterngeld
- Were married and you or your spouse chose tax class combinations III/V

**Voluntary filing** is open to almost everyone else — and this is where most Moroccan workers and Azubis in Germany benefit the most. You have **4 years** to file voluntarily. That means in 2025 you can still file returns for 2021, 2022, 2023, and 2024.

## How Much Money Can You Actually Get Back?

The average tax refund in Germany is around **€1,095 per year**, according to the German Taxpayers Association (Bund der Steuerzahler). Of course, your refund depends on your personal situation, but here are realistic examples:

- **Azubi earning €800/month** in Dortmund: Paid ~€600 in Lohnsteuer over the year, gets back ~€400–€500 after deducting work-related expenses and commuting costs.
- **Skilled worker earning €2,500/month** in Munich: Paid ~€4,800 in taxes; after deducting rent for a second home near work, professional training costs, and union fees, gets back €800–€1,400.
- **First-year worker who moved from Morocco**: Moving expenses, German language course fees, and travel home for family visits may all count as deductible — refund potential is often higher in the first year.

The math is simple: the more legitimate deductions you can document, the larger your refund.

## What Can You Deduct? The Key Categories

This is where most people miss out. You don't need to be a tax expert — you just need to know what costs are deductible.

### Werbungskosten — Work-Related Expenses

Germany automatically grants everyone a **flat deduction of €1,230** (as of 2023) for work-related expenses. But if your actual costs exceed this, you should list them:

- **Commuting costs (Pendlerpauschale):** €0.30 per km for the first 20 km, €0.38/km beyond that, for every working day. Example: 25 km commute × 220 working days × blended rate = roughly **€1,700** in deductions.
- **Work clothing and tools:** Costs for uniforms, safety shoes, or professional tools not provided by your employer.
- **Professional training and certifications:** Language courses related to your job, professional development seminars.
- **Union membership fees (Gewerkschaftsbeiträge):** Fully deductible if you're a member of IG Metall, Ver.di, or another union.
- **Home office costs:** If you worked from home, you can deduct €6 per day, up to €1,260/year (2023 rules).

### Sonderausgaben — Special Expenses

- **Health insurance contributions** you pay yourself (relevant if you switched providers)
- **Church tax (Kirchensteuer):** Fully deductible
- **Donations** to registered charities
- **Riester pension contributions** (up to €2,100/year)

### Außergewöhnliche Belastungen — Extraordinary Expenses

Medical bills, dental costs, or costs of supporting family members in Morocco can sometimes qualify here — this requires documentation, but it's worth exploring.

### Moving Costs (Umzugskosten)

If you moved to Germany for work or relocated within Germany for a new job, a significant portion of your moving costs is deductible. The flat rate (Umzugskostenpauschale) for a single person in 2024 is **€964**. Receipts for transport, temporary housing, and re-registration costs can push this higher.

## How to Actually File Your Steuererklärung

You have several options, ranging from free to professional:

### Option 1: ELSTER (Free, Official)

**ELSTER** (www.elster.de) is the official German tax portal. It's free, secure, and directly connected to the Finanzamt. The interface is in German, which can be a barrier — but if your German is at B1 level or above, it's manageable. You'll need to register first with your tax ID (Steuer-ID), which you receive by post when you register your address in Germany.

### Option 2: Tax Apps (Easy and Affordable)

Several apps make filing much simpler, with English-language support and guided questionnaires:

- **Taxfix** (taxfix.de): ~€39.99 per return, English available, average refund claim: €1,063
- **Wundertax** (wundertax.de): ~€29.95, simple interview-style questions
- **SteuerGo** (steuergo.de): Free to calculate, pay only to submit (~€29.95)
- **WISO Steuer** (buhl.de): ~€34.99, more powerful for complex situations

### Option 3: Lohnsteuerhilfeverein (Tax Assistance Club)

For a small annual membership fee (usually €50–€150 depending on your income), you get personalized help from a certified tax advisor. Search for clubs like **Lohnsteuerhilfe Bayern e.V.** or **VLH** (vlh.de). This is a great option if your situation is slightly complex — for example, if you support family in Morocco or have income from multiple sources.

### Option 4: Steuerberater (Tax Consultant)

A professional tax consultant (Steuerberater) costs €150–€500+ per return but handles everything for you. Worth it if you're self-employed or have a complicated tax situation.

## Step-by-Step: What You Need to Gather

Before you start, collect these documents:

- **Lohnsteuerbescheinigung** — your annual wage and tax statement from your employer (usually provided in January/February)
- **Steuer-ID** — your personal tax identification number (11 digits)
- **Bank IBAN** — for the refund transfer
- Receipts or records for commuting distances
- Receipts for any deductible expenses (training, tools, work clothing)
- Health insurance premium statements
- Any other relevant certificates (Riester, church tax, donations)

## Deadlines You Need to Know

- **Mandatory filers:** July 31 of the following year (e.g., July 31, 2025 for the 2024 tax year). With a tax advisor, you get until the end of February the year after that.
- **Voluntary filers:** 4 years from the end of the tax year. For 2020, the deadline was December 31, 2024 — so don't delay for more recent years.

Missing deadlines for mandatory returns results in late-filing penalties (Verspätungszuschlag) of at least €25 per month.

## What People Get Wrong About the Steuererklärung

- **"I don't earn enough to file."** Even if you earned below the basic tax-free allowance (Grundfreibetrag — €11,604 in 2024), you may still have had tax deducted and should file to get it back.
- **"It's too complicated."** Tax apps like Taxfix make it a 20-minute process for most employees.
- **"I already left Germany, so it's too late."** False. You can file from abroad, and the 4-year window still applies.
- **"My employer already does it."** No employer files your Steuererklärung. They submit your wage data to the Finanzamt, but the actual return is your responsibility.
- **"I'll owe money if I file."** If you were a regular salaried employee the whole year, it's very rare to owe money after filing. The risk is real only in specific situations (e.g., you had two jobs simultaneously at a combined unfavorable tax class).
- **"I can't claim anything — I just arrived."** First-year filers often have the highest refunds because of moving costs, language course fees, and the fact that the tax office didn't know your full situation yet.

## Conclusion

Filing your Steuererklärung is one of the smartest financial moves you can make as a Moroccan worker or Azubi in Germany. It takes a few hours, costs little or nothing, and the average return is over €1,000. The longer you wait, the more unclaimed money you're leaving behind.

Start with a free calculation on **Taxfix** or **SteuerGo** — you'll see your estimated refund before paying anything. If you want help understanding the German system, your rights as a worker, and how to build a strong professional foundation in Germany, [book a free consultation and start your journey today](/cv-builder).

faqs.question: Do I have to file a Steuererklärung in Germany if I work as an Azubi?
faqs.answer: You are not usually required to file as an Azubi, but you almost certainly should — voluntarily. Most apprentices have taxes deducted automatically and get a significant portion back after filing, often €300–€700 or more depending on commuting distance and other deductions.

faqs.question: What is my Steuer-ID and how do I get it?
faqs.answer: Your Steuer-ID (Steueridentifikationsnummer) is an 11-digit personal tax number issued to everyone who registers an address in Germany. It arrives by post from the Bundeszentralamt für Steuern within a few weeks of registration. If you lost it, you can request it again at www.bzst.de.

faqs.question: Can I file my German tax return in English?
faqs.answer: The official ELSTER portal is only in German. However, apps like Taxfix and Wundertax offer English-language interfaces and guide you through the entire process with simple questions. These are the best options if your German is still at a beginner level.

faqs.question: How long does it take to receive the tax refund after filing?
faqs.answer: It typically takes 6 to 12 weeks after the Finanzamt receives your return. During busy periods (March–May), it can take a bit longer. You'll receive a written notice (Steuerbescheid) by post before the money arrives in your bank account.

faqs.question: Can I deduct the cost of German language courses on my tax return?
faqs.answer: Yes, in many cases. If the language course is directly related to your job or was required by your employer, it qualifies as a Werbungskosten (work-related expense). Even integration courses can sometimes be partially deductible. Keep your receipts and enrollment confirmation as proof.

rw-37.title: Girocard vs Mastercard/Visa in Germany: Which Card Should You Use and When?
rw-37.summary: Learn the real difference between Girocard and Mastercard/Visa in Germany — when to use each, what they cost, and how to avoid common payment mistakes.
rw-37.content:
When you first open a German bank account, you might be surprised to receive two cards instead of one — or to find that your shiny new card doesn't work at certain shops. Germany's payment system has its own quirks, and understanding the difference between Girocard and Mastercard/Visa can save you real money and a lot of embarrassment at the checkout counter.

This guide breaks down exactly what each card does, where each one works, what fees are involved, and how to build a smart card strategy as someone new to Germany — whether you're starting an Ausbildung in Munich, working in Frankfurt, or studying in Berlin.

## What Is a Girocard (and Why Does Germany Still Love It)?

The Girocard is Germany's domestic debit card system. It was previously known as the EC-Karte (electronic cash card), and you'll still hear Germans call it that. Almost every German bank account — from Deutsche Bank to Sparkasse to ING — comes with a Girocard by default.

It works through a German-only network called "girocard" (formerly known as the ZKA system) and is accepted at the vast majority of physical shops across Germany. Think of it as the backbone of German in-store payments.

### Where Girocard Works Well

- Supermarkets: REWE, EDEKA, Lidl, Aldi, Penny — all accept Girocard
- Drugstores: dm, Rossmann, Müller
- Gas stations, hardware stores, most German retail chains
- Public transport ticket machines in many cities
- ATMs across Germany (usually free at your own bank's machines)

The reason Germans trust it so much? It's fast, reliable, and almost always fee-free within Germany. Transactions are debited directly from your current account (Girokonto), so there's no risk of overspending beyond your balance.

## What Is Mastercard/Visa in the German Banking Context?

Mastercard and Visa are international card networks. In Germany, these come in two forms:

- **Credit cards** (Kreditkarte): You spend up to a set limit, and the bill arrives at the end of the month
- **Debit cards** with Mastercard/Visa branding: Increasingly common at online banks like N26, Revolut, and DKB — these debit directly from your account like a Girocard, but run on the Mastercard or Visa network

The key difference is **global acceptance**. While Girocard rarely works outside Germany (and sometimes not even in Austria or Switzerland), a Mastercard or Visa works in 190+ countries and on virtually every international website.

### Common Banks and What They Give You

| Bank | Girocard | Mastercard/Visa |
|---|---|---|
| Sparkasse | ✅ Yes | Optional (fee-based credit card) |
| Deutsche Bank | ✅ Yes | Optional credit card |
| DKB | ✅ Yes | ✅ Free Visa debit card |
| N26 | ❌ No | ✅ Mastercard debit |
| Revolut | ❌ No | ✅ Visa debit |
| ING | ✅ Yes | Optional Visa credit card |

If you're opening your first account as a newcomer to Germany, DKB or N26 are often the easiest options — both are available without a German address requirement and offer English-language support.

## Fees: What Each Card Actually Costs You

### Girocard Fees

- **Within Germany**: Almost always free — no transaction fee, no currency conversion
- **Abroad**: Most banks charge €1–5 per transaction plus a 1–2% foreign transaction fee
- **ATM withdrawals in Germany**: Free at your own bank's ATMs; €4–6 at other banks' machines

### Mastercard/Visa Fees

- **Standard credit cards in Germany**: Often €30–60/year in annual fees; foreign transactions may be free or have a 1–2% fee
- **DKB Visa debit**: Free account + free card; free ATM withdrawals worldwide (as long as you're an "active customer" — meaning at least one transaction per month)
- **N26 Mastercard debit**: Free card; €2 fee per ATM withdrawal in Germany (free withdrawals abroad at partner ATMs)
- **Revolut Visa**: Free plan available; ATM withdrawals free up to €200/month, then 2% fee

**Practical example**: If you're sending €300/month to Morocco from Germany, a Revolut or Wise account linked to a Visa gives you better exchange rates than using your Sparkasse Girocard to withdraw and transfer manually. The savings can be €10–20 per transaction.

## When to Use Girocard vs Mastercard/Visa

Here's a simple decision framework:

### Use Your Girocard When:
- Paying at German supermarkets, pharmacies, or retail stores in person
- Withdrawing cash from ATMs inside Germany
- Making everyday purchases in cities and towns — it's faster and always free
- Shopping at weekly markets or smaller German businesses (many only accept Girocard or cash)

### Use Mastercard/Visa When:
- Shopping online — almost no German e-commerce site accepts Girocard directly (though PayPal is a workaround)
- Traveling outside Germany — Girocard barely works abroad
- Booking hotels, flights, rental cars — these almost always require an international card
- Paying in restaurants in other European cities
- Subscriptions like Netflix, Spotify, or Amazon — these require an international card

### The Cash Reality in Germany

Germany remains unusually cash-heavy compared to Morocco's card-forward urban culture or France's near-universal card acceptance. Many small restaurants, bakeries, and kiosks in Germany still only accept cash (Bargeld). Always keep €20–50 in cash as backup. Some markets and small shops won't take any card at all — Girocard or otherwise.

## How to Build a Smart Card Setup as a Newcomer

The ideal setup for a Moroccan moving to Germany for Ausbildung or work looks like this:

1. **Open a free German bank account** with a Girocard — Sparkasse or Volksbank work great if you have a local branch; ING or DKB work well online
2. **Get a free Visa or Mastercard** — DKB's Visa is the gold standard for newcomers: free, worldwide ATM withdrawals, and accepted everywhere
3. **Keep Revolut or Wise** as a third option for sending money to Morocco and managing currency exchange at good rates
4. **Always carry some cash** — €20–30 minimum for daily situations in smaller towns

This three-layer approach covers you for every scenario: daily German shopping (Girocard), online purchases and travel (Visa/Mastercard), and family transfers back home (Revolut/Wise).

## What People Get Wrong About Cards in Germany

**Mistake 1: Assuming Mastercard/Visa works everywhere in Germany**
Many newcomers cancel their Girocard thinking an international card is superior. It's not — hundreds of German stores and markets don't accept Mastercard/Visa at all.

**Mistake 2: Using a Girocard abroad**
If you visit Morocco or travel to France for the weekend, your Girocard likely won't work in ATMs or shops. You'll be stuck without cash or access to your account. Always carry your Visa/Mastercard when leaving Germany.

**Mistake 3: Ignoring ATM fees**
Withdrawing cash with a Mastercard from a random German ATM can cost you €5–6 per transaction. Using your Girocard at your own bank's ATM is always free.

**Mistake 4: Trying to pay online with Girocard**
Girocard doesn't have a standard CVV number or the 3D Secure protocol in the way international cards do. Most online checkouts will reject it. Use your Visa or Mastercard for all internet purchases.

**Mistake 5: Thinking a credit card is required**
You don't need a credit card in Germany. A Visa or Mastercard *debit* card (like DKB's or N26's) works for hotels, car rentals, and online shopping. Some car rental companies do block a security deposit — check in advance.

## Conclusion: Use Both Cards, Know When to Reach for Each

Germany's payment landscape is unique. The Girocard dominates in-store payments, while Mastercard and Visa are essential for online shopping, travel, and anything outside Germany's borders. As a newcomer, you don't have to choose — you need both, and ideally a low-cost option like DKB's free Visa debit to keep fees as low as possible.

Setting up your banking correctly from day one makes life much easier during your Ausbildung or first months of work. If you're still navigating the paperwork side of your move — from writing your application to building a German-standard CV — book a free consultation to learn German and move to Germany successfully, and explore our [CV builder](/cv-builder) to put your best foot forward with German employers.

faqs.question: Can I use my Girocard outside of Germany?
faqs.answer: In most cases, no. Girocard works on a German-only network and is rarely accepted abroad — including in Morocco, France, or most other countries. Always bring a Mastercard or Visa when you travel outside Germany.

faqs.question: Does N26 give you a Girocard?
faqs.answer: No. N26 only issues a Mastercard debit card. This means it works great online and abroad, but a handful of German shops that only accept Girocard won't take it. Consider opening a secondary account with Sparkasse or ING if you live in a smaller German town.

faqs.question: Which card is best for sending money to Morocco from Germany?
faqs.answer: Neither Girocard nor standard credit cards offer good exchange rates for international transfers. Use Revolut or Wise instead — both are linked to a Visa or Mastercard and offer near-market exchange rates with much lower fees than traditional German banks.

faqs.question: Is DKB's free Visa card really free for ATM withdrawals?
faqs.answer: Yes, as long as you qualify as an "active customer" — meaning you make at least one card transaction per month. DKB then waives ATM fees globally. If you don't meet that threshold, fees apply. It's the most generous free card option for newcomers in Germany.

faqs.question: Do German online shops accept Girocard?
faqs.answer: Rarely. Most German e-commerce platforms like Zalando, Otto, or Amazon.de don't directly accept Girocard. You can sometimes use PayPal as a workaround (linked to your German bank account), but for direct card payments online, you need a Mastercard or Visa.

rw-45.title: Wise vs Revolut: The Best Way to Send Money to Morocco from Germany
rw-45.summary: Sending money from Germany to Morocco? Compare Wise and Revolut on fees, exchange rates, and speed to find the best transfer option for you.
rw-45.content:
Every month, thousands of Moroccans living in Germany send money home — to support family, pay rent, or save in dirhams. But the wrong transfer method can silently eat 5–8% of your money before it even arrives. Wise and Revolut have changed the game for international transfers, offering real exchange rates and transparent fees that traditional banks simply cannot match. This guide breaks down exactly how both services work, how much they cost, and which one is better for sending money from Germany to Morocco.

## Why Sending Money from Germany to Morocco Is Expensive the Old Way

German banks like Deutsche Bank, Sparkasse, and Commerzbank all offer international wire transfers — but they come at a price. A typical SWIFT transfer to a Moroccan bank account (in MAD or EUR) can cost:

- **€15–€35 in flat transfer fees**
- **2–4% hidden margin** baked into the exchange rate they offer you
- **1–5 business days** for the money to arrive

If you're sending €500 home every month and your bank charges a 4% total markup, you're losing around **€240 per year** without realising it. Over five years, that's over **€1,200 gone in fees**.

This is why fintech apps like Wise and Revolut have become so popular among Moroccan expats in Berlin, Munich, Frankfurt, and Cologne.

---

## How Wise Works for Germany–Morocco Transfers

Wise (formerly TransferWise) was built specifically to solve the hidden-fee problem in international transfers. It uses the **mid-market exchange rate** — the one you see on Google — and charges a small, transparent fee on top.

### What Wise Charges to Send Money to Morocco

For a transfer from EUR (Germany) to MAD (Morocco), Wise typically charges:

- A **fixed fee of around €0.60–€1.20**
- A **variable fee of 0.5–1.0%** of the transfer amount

So if you send **€500 to Morocco**, your total fee is roughly **€3–€6**. Compare that to €25+ at a bank with a worse exchange rate, and the savings are obvious.

### How to Use Wise

1. Go to [wise.com](https://wise.com) and create a free account
2. Verify your identity (passport or German residence permit works fine)
3. Enter how much you want to send (EUR → MAD)
4. Add your recipient's Moroccan bank account details (IBAN or account number + bank name like Attijariwafa, CIH Bank, Banque Populaire)
5. Pay from your German bank account or debit card
6. Your recipient gets MAD in their Moroccan account within **1–2 business days**

### Does Wise Support Morocco Directly?

Yes. Wise supports transfers to Morocco in **Moroccan Dirham (MAD)**. The recipient does not need a Wise account — just a regular Moroccan bank account. Moroccan banks that work well with incoming Wise transfers include **Attijariwafa Bank**, **CIH Bank**, **BMCE Bank**, and **Banque Populaire**.

---

## How Revolut Works for Germany–Morocco Transfers

Revolut is a digital bank and money app based in the UK and EU. It's very popular in Germany as a day-to-day banking app, and it also allows international transfers.

### What Revolut Charges to Send Money to Morocco

Revolut's pricing depends heavily on which plan you're on:

| Plan | Monthly Cost | Currency Conversion Limit | Fee Above Limit |
|---|---|---|---|
| Standard (free) | €0 | €1,000/month at interbank rate | 0.5% |
| Plus | €3.99 | €1,000/month | 0.5% |
| Premium | €9.99 | Unlimited | 0% |
| Metal | €15.99 | Unlimited | 0% |

On the free plan, if you send **€500 to Morocco**, you'll likely stay within the limit and pay **no conversion fee** — but Revolut adds a **weekend markup of 1%** if you transfer on Saturday or Sunday. Always transfer on weekdays.

### How to Use Revolut for Morocco Transfers

1. Download the Revolut app and create an account
2. Verify your identity (German ID, passport, or residence permit)
3. Go to "Send Money" → choose international transfer
4. Enter the recipient's Moroccan bank details
5. Choose MAD as the destination currency
6. Confirm and send

Revolut also lets you send money to recipients who don't have Revolut — they just need a bank account number.

---

## Wise vs Revolut: Head-to-Head Comparison

Here's a practical comparison if you're sending **€300 from Germany to Morocco**:

| Feature | Wise | Revolut (Free Plan) |
|---|---|---|
| Exchange rate | Mid-market rate | Mid-market rate (on weekdays) |
| Fee | ~€2.50–€4 | €0 (within monthly limit) |
| Transfer speed | 1–2 business days | 1–3 business days |
| Recipient needs account? | No (bank account only) | No (bank account only) |
| App quality | Excellent | Excellent |
| Cash pickup option | No | No |

**Winner for low-frequency senders:** Revolut free plan (if you stay under €1,000/month)
**Winner for high-volume or regular senders:** Wise (transparent, predictable fees every time)

---

## Other Options Worth Knowing

Wise and Revolut are the top choices, but they're not the only options. Here are a few others Moroccan expats use:

### Western Union and MoneyGram
These are old-school services with physical locations in Morocco. Useful if your recipient doesn't have a bank account, or if they need cash immediately. However, fees are high — often **3–6%** of the transfer, plus a poor exchange rate. Only use these for emergencies.

### Sendwave
A newer app specifically designed for remittances to Africa and Asia. Sendwave sometimes offers **zero fees** for Morocco transfers, but the exchange rate spread may be slightly less favourable than Wise. Worth checking as a third comparison.

### Your German Bank's Online Transfer
Deutsche Bank and Sparkasse do offer international SWIFT transfers online, but as mentioned, these typically cost **€15–€30 flat** plus a hidden exchange rate margin. Use this only if you have no other option.

---

## What People Get Wrong When Transferring Money to Morocco

**1. Transferring on weekends with Revolut**
Revolut applies a 1% weekend surcharge on currency conversion. On a €1,000 transfer, that's €10 extra. Simply wait until Monday morning.

**2. Using the bank by default**
Many people stick with their German bank out of habit. If you're sending €500/month and your bank charges €25 per transfer, you're losing €300 per year. Switching to Wise takes 15 minutes.

**3. Not checking the exchange rate before sending**
Exchange rates fluctuate daily. Apps like Wise and Revolut show you exactly how many MAD your recipient will receive before you confirm. Always check this number — don't just send blind.

**4. Entering the wrong bank details**
Moroccan bank accounts use a **24-digit RIB number** (Relevé d'Identité Bancaire), not a standard IBAN. Double-check the account number with your recipient before sending, especially for the first transfer.

**5. Expecting instant transfers**
Even Wise usually takes 1–2 business days. If a family member needs money urgently, plan ahead — don't wait until the last minute.

**6. Forgetting Moroccan currency regulations**
Morocco has capital controls. Large incoming transfers (above the equivalent of around €10,000 per year) may be questioned by Moroccan banks. For normal monthly remittances of a few hundred euros, this is not an issue.

---

## Setting Up Your Transfers: Practical Tips

- **Create a Wise account before you need it.** Verification can take a day or two if they need more ID documents.
- **Save your recipient's details.** Both Wise and Revolut let you save bank details so you can repeat transfers with one tap.
- **Set a recurring transfer on Wise.** If you send the same amount every month, Wise lets you automate this — great for supporting family consistently.
- **Compare both before each transfer.** Use [wise.com/compare](https://wise.com) and check Revolut's current rate to see who's offering more MAD that day.

---

## Conclusion

For most Moroccans in Germany, **Wise is the most reliable and transparent option** for sending money home. Its fees are low, the exchange rate is honest, and the process is simple even if your recipient has never heard of Wise. Revolut is an excellent alternative — especially on its free plan for smaller monthly amounts — but watch out for the weekend surcharge.

Either way, stop using your German bank for international transfers. The savings are real, they add up fast, and switching takes less than 20 minutes.

If you're still getting settled in Germany — figuring out your Ausbildung, your registration, or your residency paperwork — book a free consultation to learn German and move to Germany successfully. Our team helps Moroccans navigate every step of the process, from language learning to [building a strong CV](/cv-builder) and [writing a compelling cover letter](/anschreiben-generator) for your applications.

faqs.question: Can I use Wise to send money directly to a Moroccan bank account?
faqs.answer: Yes. Wise supports transfers to Morocco in Moroccan Dirham (MAD). Your recipient just needs a regular Moroccan bank account — they don't need a Wise account. Popular banks like Attijariwafa, CIH, BMCE, and Banque Populaire all work fine.

faqs.question: Is Revolut free to use for sending money to Morocco?
faqs.answer: Revolut's Standard plan is free and lets you convert up to €1,000/month at the mid-market rate with no fee. Above that limit, a 0.5% fee applies. Avoid transferring on weekends — Revolut adds a 1% surcharge on Saturday and Sunday.

faqs.question: How long does a Wise transfer from Germany to Morocco take?
faqs.answer: Most Wise transfers to Morocco arrive within 1–2 business days. The exact time depends on when you send and how quickly your German bank processes the payment. Wise shows you an estimated arrival time before you confirm the transfer.

faqs.question: What bank details do I need to send money to a Moroccan bank account?
faqs.answer: You need your recipient's 24-digit RIB number (Relevé d'Identité Bancaire), which is the Moroccan equivalent of an IBAN. Ask your recipient to get this from their bank statement or online banking app before your first transfer.

faqs.question: How much money can I send to Morocco per year without problems?
faqs.answer: For regular remittances of a few hundred euros per month, there are no issues. Morocco does have currency controls, and very large incoming transfers (roughly above €10,000 per year) may attract scrutiny from Moroccan banks. For normal family support transfers, this is not a concern.

rw-5.title: What Is Ausbildung and How Does It Work? A Complete Guide for Moroccans
rw-5.summary: Learn what Ausbildung is, how Germany's dual vocational training system works, and how Moroccans can use it to build a career in Germany.
rw-5.content:
Germany's Ausbildung system is one of the best-kept secrets in international career planning — and for Moroccans looking to build a real future in Europe, it could be the most practical path available. Unlike a university degree that takes four or five years and costs tens of thousands of euros, an Ausbildung gets you trained, paid, and employed in two to three years. If you've ever wondered what Ausbildung actually is and how the whole system works, this guide breaks it down in plain language.

## What Is Ausbildung?

Ausbildung (pronounced *ows-beel-doong*) is the German word for vocational training or apprenticeship. It's a structured program that lets you learn a trade or profession while working at a real company — and getting paid for it at the same time.

Germany has offered this system for over a century, and it's the main reason the country has one of the lowest youth unemployment rates in Europe. More than 325 officially recognized training occupations fall under the Ausbildung umbrella, covering everything from nursing and IT to electrical engineering, logistics, banking, and baking.

### The Two Types of Ausbildung

There are two main formats:

- **Dual Ausbildung (duale Ausbildung):** The most common type. You split your time between a company (3–4 days per week) and a vocational school called a *Berufsschule* (1–2 days per week). Both sides work together to teach you theory and practice.
- **School-based Ausbildung (schulische Ausbildung):** Done entirely at a vocational school, sometimes with internship phases. Common in healthcare fields like nursing assistants or physiotherapy.

For most Moroccans moving to Germany, the dual Ausbildung is the primary target — it pays a monthly training allowance and leads directly to employment.

## How the Dual System Actually Works

The dual system is built around a simple idea: you learn by doing. Here's how the structure looks in practice:

- **Duration:** 2 to 3.5 years, depending on the occupation
- **Company days:** You work at a real employer — a hospital, a workshop, an IT firm, a hotel — and receive hands-on training
- **School days:** You attend a *Berufsschule* in your city and learn the academic side of your field
- **Exams:** There are usually two main exams — an intermediate exam (Zwischenprüfung) midway through, and a final exam (Abschlussprüfung) at the end
- **Certificate:** Once you pass, you receive a nationally recognized qualification

The employer and the vocational school coordinate their content. So if you're training as an IT specialist (Fachinformatiker), the company teaches you real systems and workflows, while the school teaches you networking theory and programming concepts. The two sides reinforce each other.

### What Sectors Are Most Open to Moroccans?

Germany currently has shortages in dozens of fields. The sectors most actively recruiting international trainees include:

- **Healthcare and elder care** (Pflegefachmann/Pflegefachfrau)
- **IT and digitalization** (Fachinformatiker)
- **Electrical trades** (Elektroniker)
- **Logistics and warehousing** (Fachkraft für Lagerlogistik)
- **Hospitality and tourism** (Hotelfachmann/Hotelfachfrau)
- **Mechatronics** (Mechatroniker)
- **Commercial occupations** (Kaufmann im Einzelhandel, Kaufmann für Büromanagement)

Cities like Berlin, Munich, Hamburg, Frankfurt, and Stuttgart have the highest number of open Ausbildung positions, but smaller cities often have less competition and easier access for applicants.

## How Much Do You Get Paid During Ausbildung?

One of the most important things to understand: Ausbildung is not free labor, and it's not unpaid studying. You receive a monthly training allowance (Ausbildungsvergütung) from your employer.

Since 2020, Germany has a minimum training allowance set by law. The amounts increase each year of training:

- **Year 1:** €649/month (minimum, as of 2024)
- **Year 2:** €766/month
- **Year 3:** €876/month

In practice, many companies — especially in metal, electrical, or IT sectors — pay significantly more. Trainees in the metal industry in Bavaria, for example, can earn €900–€1,100/month in year one. Healthcare trainees in large hospital networks often earn €1,000–€1,200/month.

This allowance is enough to cover basic living costs in smaller German cities, especially if you find shared housing (WG). Rent in cities like Leipzig or Dortmund for a room in a shared flat runs roughly €400–€600/month.

## What Are the Requirements for Moroccans to Apply?

You don't need to be a German citizen or an EU national to do an Ausbildung. As a Moroccan, you can apply through Germany's skilled immigration pathway. Here are the key requirements:

### Language Level
German is essential. Most employers require at least **B1 level**, and many prefer **B2**. Healthcare positions often require B2 as a minimum. You'll need to show a language certificate — the most accepted ones are Goethe-Institut certificates or TestDaF.

### Educational Qualification
Your Moroccan school-leaving certificate (Baccalauréat) generally needs to be recognized. You can check your qualifications on [anabin.kmk.org](https://anabin.kmk.org), the official German database for foreign qualifications. Some occupations have no strict educational requirement beyond a basic secondary school diploma.

### Visa
You'll apply for a **Visa for Seeking Vocational Training (Visum zur Suche eines Ausbildungsplatzes)** — valid for 6 months — or directly for a **vocational training visa** once you have a signed training contract. The German embassy in Rabat or Casablanca handles these applications.

### Other Documents Typically Required
- Valid passport
- Moroccan Baccalauréat (with certified German translation)
- German language certificate (B1 or B2)
- Motivationsschreiben (cover letter)
- Lebenslauf (CV in Europass or German format)
- Signed Ausbildungsvertrag (training contract from the employer)

## How to Find an Ausbildung Place as a Moroccan

The job market exists — you just need to know where to look:

- **[Make it in Germany](https://www.make-it-in-germany.com):** The official German government portal for international applicants. Lists Ausbildung vacancies and explains the process.
- **[Bundesagentur für Arbeit (BA)](https://www.arbeitsagentur.de):** Germany's Federal Employment Agency. Their JOBBÖRSE database lists thousands of open training positions.
- **[Ausbildung.de](https://www.ausbildung.de):** A private platform with a large database of vacancies and company contacts.
- **Direct applications:** Many German companies — especially SMEs (Mittelstand) — prefer direct applications. Research companies in your target city and send a tailored cover letter and CV.

Applying between September and February gives you the best chance, since many companies select trainees 6–12 months before the training start date (usually August or September).

## What People Get Wrong About Ausbildung

A lot of Moroccans arrive at this topic with misconceptions that cost them time and money. Here are the most common ones:

- **"I need a university degree to do Ausbildung."** No. Ausbildung is designed as an alternative to university, not a step after it. Your Baccalauréat is usually enough.
- **"The language requirement is flexible."** It's not. If your German isn't at B1 minimum — preferably B2 — most employers will reject your application before reading further. Invest in language learning first.
- **"I can find a company after I arrive in Germany."** Technically possible on a job-seeking visa, but risky. It's much better to secure a signed training contract before applying for your visa.
- **"All Ausbildung positions pay the same."** Wrong. Pay varies hugely by sector and region. Research the Tarifvertrag (collective agreement) for your target industry.
- **"Ausbildung is only for young people."** There is no upper age limit. Germany actively welcomes adult applicants, including people in their late 20s and 30s.
- **"A school-based Ausbildung is the same as dual."** Not quite — school-based programs often don't include a regular training allowance, so financial planning differs.

## After Ausbildung: What Comes Next?

Finishing your Ausbildung is not the end — it's the beginning. Here's what typically follows:

- **Job offer from your training company:** Most employers offer a permanent contract to successful trainees. Legally, they're required to employ you for at least 6 months after the training ends if they want to keep you.
- **Skilled worker visa:** After completing your training in Germany, you can transition to a skilled worker residence permit (Fachkräfte-Einwanderungsgesetz), putting you on a path to permanent residency.
- **Upskilling (Weiterbildung):** Many Ausbildung graduates go on to do a *Meister* qualification (master craftsman) or a part-time degree to advance their careers. A Meisterbrief in Germany is equivalent in legal standing to a bachelor's degree.
- **Salary jump:** A qualified nurse in Germany earns €2,800–€3,500/month gross. A qualified mechatronics technician earns €2,500–€3,200/month. The training allowance is just the starting point.

## Conclusion

Ausbildung is one of the most structured, well-funded, and internationally respected vocational training systems in the world — and it's open to Moroccans who prepare correctly. The combination of real work experience, a monthly salary, and a recognized German qualification makes it far more accessible than a university route for many people. The key ingredients are solid German language skills, the right documents, and a targeted job search strategy.

If you're ready to take the next step, [book a free consultation](/anschreiben-generator) to get help writing your cover letter and CV, and start your journey toward a career in Germany today.

faqs.question: What is Ausbildung in simple terms?
faqs.answer: Ausbildung is Germany's vocational training system. You work at a real company 3–4 days a week, attend a vocational school 1–2 days a week, and earn a monthly salary — all while training for a recognized profession. It lasts 2 to 3.5 years depending on the field.

faqs.question: How much do you get paid during Ausbildung in Germany?
faqs.answer: The legal minimum training allowance in Germany starts at €649/month in year one (2024), rising to €876/month by year three. In well-paying sectors like IT or metalworking, trainees often earn €900–€1,200/month, which is enough to cover basic living costs in most German cities.

faqs.question: What German level do I need to apply for Ausbildung as a Moroccan?
faqs.answer: Most employers require at least B1 German, and many — especially in healthcare — require B2. You'll need a certificate from a recognized institution like the Goethe-Institut. Investing in language training before applying is the single most important step you can take.

faqs.question: Can Moroccans do Ausbildung in Germany without an EU passport?
faqs.answer: Yes. Germany has a dedicated visa for vocational training that allows non-EU nationals, including Moroccans, to train and work in Germany legally. You need a signed training contract, a recognized school certificate, and a B1/B2 German language certificate to apply at the German embassy in Rabat or Casablanca.

faqs.question: What happens after you finish Ausbildung in Germany?
faqs.answer: After completing your Ausbildung, most training companies offer you a permanent job contract. You also become eligible for a skilled worker residence permit under Germany's Fachkräfte-Einwanderungsgesetz, which puts you on a clear path to long-term residency. Many graduates also continue their education through a Meister qualification or part-time degree.

rw-8.title: Top 10 Most In-Demand Ausbildung Professions in Germany (2025 Guide)
rw-8.summary: Discover the 10 most in-demand Ausbildung professions in Germany, with real salary figures and tips to help Moroccans land the right training place.
rw-8.content:
Germany has over 300 recognized Ausbildung (vocational training) programs — but not all of them are created equal when it comes to job security, salary, and visa sponsorship. If you are a Moroccan planning to move to Germany through an Ausbildung program, choosing the right profession is the single most important decision you will make. This guide breaks down the 10 most in-demand Ausbildung professions in 2025, with real numbers, honest expectations, and practical steps to help you pick the right path.

## Why the Right Ausbildung Profession Changes Everything

Germany is facing a structural labor shortage. According to the German Federal Employment Agency (Bundesagentur für Arbeit), over 570,000 training places went unfilled in 2023. That number is rising. This means you have real leverage — but only in sectors where demand is genuinely high.

Choosing a profession in a high-demand sector means:

- Faster visa approval through the Ausbildungsvisum pathway
- Higher training allowances (Ausbildungsvergütung) from day one
- Near-guaranteed job offers after graduation
- Better chances of permanent residency through the skilled worker route

Choosing a low-demand field, on the other hand, means competing with hundreds of local applicants for very few spots.

## The Top 10 Most In-Demand Ausbildung Professions in Germany

### 1. Nurse / Healthcare Assistant (Pflegefachmann/-frau)

Germany's healthcare sector is in crisis-level shortage. The country needs an estimated 500,000 additional nursing professionals by 2030. Training lasts 3 years and is one of the few Ausbildung programs where your tuition is fully paid and you receive a monthly allowance of €1,100–€1,400 depending on the state and employer.

After graduation, average gross salary: **€2,800–€3,400/month**.

Employers like Caritas, Diakonie, and Helios Kliniken actively recruit internationally and many offer German language support before you arrive.

### 2. Electrician (Elektroniker/in)

Electrical tradespeople are among the most consistently sought-after professionals in Germany. With the energy transition (Energiewende) driving massive solar, wind, and grid infrastructure projects, demand is exploding. Training lasts 3.5 years.

Training allowance: **€800–€1,100/month**
Post-graduation salary: **€3,000–€3,800/month**

This profession also opens the door to self-employment and later promotion to Meister (master craftsman) status.

### 3. IT Specialist (Fachinformatiker/in)

One of the most popular Ausbildung tracks in Germany right now. You can specialize in application development (Anwendungsentwicklung) or systems integration (Systemintegration). Training takes 3 years.

Training allowance: **€900–€1,200/month**
Post-graduation salary: **€3,200–€4,500/month**

Companies like SAP, Deutsche Telekom, and thousands of mid-sized (Mittelstand) firms offer these positions. English proficiency is highly valued here, which is an advantage for many Moroccans already working in international environments.

### 4. Mechatronics Technician (Mechatroniker/in)

This profession combines mechanical and electronic engineering — essential for the automotive, robotics, and manufacturing sectors. BMW, Mercedes-Benz, and countless suppliers run Ausbildung programs for this role.

Training duration: 3.5 years
Training allowance: **€900–€1,200/month**
Post-graduation salary: **€3,000–€4,000/month**

### 5. Warehouse Logistics Specialist (Fachlagerist/in or Fachkraft für Lagerlogistik)

Germany is a logistics hub for all of Europe. Amazon, DHL, DB Schenker, and Lidl all offer Ausbildung positions in logistics. The Fachlagerist is a 2-year program; the Fachkraft für Lagerlogistik is 3 years and more specialized.

Training allowance: **€700–€1,000/month**
Post-graduation salary: **€2,400–€3,000/month**

Entry requirements are lower than technical fields, making this a realistic option if your German is at B1 level.

### 6. Cook (Koch/Köchin)

Germany's hospitality sector is severely understaffed. Training lasts 3 years and covers professional kitchen management, food costing, and international cuisine. Cities like Munich, Hamburg, and Berlin offer the highest number of positions.

Training allowance: **€700–€950/month**
Post-graduation salary: **€2,200–€3,000/month** (higher in hotel restaurants)

### 7. Social Care Worker (Erzieher/in or Sozialassistent/in)

With Germany's childcare expansion (Kita-Ausbau) ongoing, the demand for trained educators and social care workers is massive. This Ausbildung varies by state (Bundesland) but typically runs 2–3 years.

Training allowance: **€1,000–€1,300/month**
Post-graduation salary: **€2,600–€3,300/month**

This profession requires strong German (B2 is the realistic minimum) due to the nature of working with children and families.

### 8. Dental Assistant (Zahnmedizinische/r Fachangestellte/r – ZFA)

Dental clinics across Germany are struggling to find trained assistants. The training lasts 3 years and combines patient care, billing, and clinical support.

Training allowance: **€700–€950/month**
Post-graduation salary: **€2,200–€2,800/month**

This is an underrated option — competition from local applicants is relatively low, making it a strong opportunity for international candidates.

### 9. Automotive Mechatronics Technician (Kraftfahrzeugmechatroniker/in – KFZ)

Different from general mechatronics, this specialization focuses on cars, trucks, and electric vehicles. With Germany's EV transition, the demand for KFZ technicians who understand electric drivetrains is growing fast.

Training duration: 3.5 years
Training allowance: **€800–€1,100/month**
Post-graduation salary: **€2,800–€3,600/month**

### 10. Construction Drafter / Technical Architect (Technische/r Zeichner/in – Fachrichtung Gebäude)

As Germany faces a housing shortage, the construction sector needs more technical drawing and planning professionals. This 3-year program combines CAD software skills with structural knowledge.

Training allowance: **€850–€1,100/month**
Post-graduation salary: **€2,800–€3,500/month**

## How to Choose the Right Ausbildung Profession for You

Don't just pick the highest salary. Think about:

- **Your current German level** — Nursing and social care require B2; logistics can work with B1
- **Your existing background** — An IT background? Fachinformatiker makes sense. Worked in hospitality? Cook or hotel management Ausbildung are natural fits
- **Physical demands** — Construction and electrical trades are physically intensive
- **Long-term goals** — Want to open your own business? Electrician and KFZ Mechatroniker Meister qualifications make that possible

Use the official job portal **make-it-in-germany.com** to search open Ausbildung positions by profession, city, and language requirement.

## German Language Requirements by Profession

| Profession | Minimum German Level |
|---|---|
| Nursing / Healthcare | B2 (often B2+ for exams) |
| IT Specialist | B1–B2 |
| Electrician | B1 |
| Logistics Specialist | B1 |
| Social Care | B2 |
| Cook | B1 |
| KFZ Mechatroniker | B1 |

Many Ausbildung employers in technical fields accept B1 candidates and provide in-company German support. However, if your German is below B1, focus on language first — it is the real bottleneck, not your qualifications.

## What People Get Wrong About Ausbildung Professions

**Mistake 1: Applying for any open position without research.**
Not all Ausbildung places are equal. A position at a small family business in a rural area may offer €650/month. A position at a large company like Bosch or Deutsche Bahn may offer €1,100+. Always compare offers before accepting.

**Mistake 2: Assuming the highest-demand professions are the easiest to enter.**
Nursing is extremely in demand — but it also requires you to pass the Anerkennungsberatung process for recognition of any prior healthcare experience, and your German must be solid by the start date.

**Mistake 3: Ignoring state-specific differences.**
Germany's 16 states (Bundesländer) have different allowances, different training structures, and different labor markets. Bavaria (München) and North Rhine-Westphalia (NRW) tend to have the most Ausbildung positions overall. Brandenburg and Saxony have lower costs of living but also fewer positions.

**Mistake 4: Not customizing the application.**
A generic Bewerbung (application) with a copied cover letter will not work. German employers — especially small and medium ones — expect a tailored Anschreiben that shows you know their company specifically. This is the most common reason international applicants get rejected at the first step.

**Mistake 5: Waiting until you arrive in Germany to start applying.**
The best Ausbildung positions are filled 6–12 months in advance. You should be sending applications while still in Morocco.

## Conclusion

Germany's Ausbildung system is one of the most accessible and well-paying vocational pathways in Europe — and for Moroccans with the right preparation, it is a realistic, structured route to a stable life in Germany. The 10 professions listed here all have genuine, sustained demand, fair training wages, and clear career paths after graduation.

Your next step is to match your German level and background to the right profession, then build an application that actually gets read. Book a free consultation to learn German and move to Germany successfully — and use our [CV builder](/cv-builder) and [Anschreiben generator](/anschreiben-generator) to create documents that German employers take seriously.

faqs.question: What is the highest-paying Ausbildung profession in Germany for 2025?
faqs.answer: IT Specialist (Fachinformatiker) and Mechatronics Technician typically offer the highest post-graduation salaries, ranging from €3,200 to €4,500/month gross. Nursing also pays well (€2,800–€3,400/month) and often includes additional shift allowances.

faqs.question: How much German do I need to start an Ausbildung in Germany?
faqs.answer: Most technical Ausbildung programs (electrician, logistics, KFZ) require B1 German. Nursing, social care, and dental assistant positions typically require B2 because patient and client communication is central to the role. You should reach your target level before applying, not after.

faqs.question: Can I apply for an Ausbildung in Germany while still living in Morocco?
faqs.answer: Yes, and you should. Most companies accept applications from abroad, and the Ausbildungsvisum allows you to enter Germany specifically to complete your training. Apply 6–12 months before your intended start date. Use platforms like make-it-in-germany.com and Ausbildung.de to find open positions.

faqs.question: Do Ausbildung companies in Germany pay you during training?
faqs.answer: Yes. Every recognized Ausbildung in Germany comes with a monthly training allowance (Ausbildungsvergütung). Depending on the sector and company, this ranges from €650 to €1,400/month. Nursing and IT tend to be at the higher end; hospitality and retail at the lower end.

faqs.question: Which Ausbildung profession is easiest for Moroccans to enter with a B1 German level?
faqs.answer: Logistics specialist (Fachkraft für Lagerlogistik), cook, and electrician are the most accessible at B1 level. They have high vacancy rates, relatively straightforward entry requirements, and many employers are experienced with recruiting international candidates.

rw-75.title: Ausbildung in Cooking and Hospitality: Your Opportunity in the Heart of Europe
rw-75.summary: Discover how Moroccan applicants can land an Ausbildung in cooking and hospitality in Germany — with real salaries, top cities, and step-by-step guidance.
rw-75.content:
Germany's hospitality and culinary industry is hungry for skilled workers — and it is actively recruiting from Morocco. If you have ever dreamed of building a professional cooking or hotel career in the heart of Europe, an Ausbildung in cooking and hospitality could be your most practical, well-funded path to getting there. This guide walks you through everything: what the training looks like, what you earn, and exactly how to apply from Morocco.

## What Is an Ausbildung in Cooking and Hospitality?

An Ausbildung (vocational training) in Germany combines hands-on work at a real employer with classes at a vocational school (Berufsschule). You are not a student paying tuition — you are a paid trainee with a contract, a salary, and full social insurance from day one.

In the cooking and hospitality sector, the most common Ausbildung programmes include:

- **Koch/Köchin** (Professional Cook) — 3 years
- **Restaurantfachmann/-frau** (Restaurant Specialist) — 3 years
- **Hotelfachmann/-frau** (Hotel Specialist) — 3 years
- **Fachkraft im Gastgewerbe** (Hospitality Worker) — 2 years, a shorter entry-level option
- **Systemgastronomiefachmann/-frau** (System Gastronomy Specialist) — 3 years

Each programme is nationally standardised, meaning your qualification is recognised across all 16 German states.

### What You Actually Do Each Week

Roughly three to four days per week, you work in your training company — a restaurant, hotel, catering firm, or large canteen. The remaining one to two days, you attend Berufsschule, where you study theory: food hygiene (HACCP), cost calculation, nutrition science, and guest communication. By the end of year three, you can run a professional kitchen or manage hotel operations independently.

## Salaries During and After Training

One of the biggest surprises for Moroccan applicants is that you get paid from the very first month. Since August 2020, Germany introduced a **minimum Ausbildung salary** (Mindestausbildungsvergütung). As of 2024, the federal minimums are:

| Training Year | Minimum Monthly Gross |
|---|---|
| Year 1 | €649 |
| Year 2 | €766 |
| Year 3 | €876 |

Many employers — especially large hotel chains like Marriott, Hilton, or Mövenpick — pay significantly above these minimums, often €900–€1,100 in year one. Tarifverträge (collective wage agreements) in the hotel and restaurant sector (DEHOGA) set higher rates in states like Bavaria, Baden-Württemberg, and Hamburg.

After completing your Ausbildung, a qualified cook (Geselle/Gesellin) earns between **€2,000 and €2,800 gross per month** to start. Hotel specialists and restaurant managers often reach €2,500–€3,200 within two to three years of qualified experience.

## Why Germany's Hospitality Sector Needs You

Germany has roughly **228,000 unfilled positions** in the gastronomy and hotel sector (DEHOGA statistics, 2023). The country's domestic workforce is ageing and shrinking, and the industry cannot fill training spots fast enough. This is a structural gap — not a temporary trend.

Key cities with the highest demand include:

- **Munich (München)** — luxury hotels, Oktoberfest infrastructure, Michelin-starred restaurants
- **Berlin** — Europe's largest hotel market by room count, vibrant restaurant scene
- **Hamburg** — major port city with premium hospitality demand
- **Frankfurt** — international business travel drives year-round hotel occupancy
- **Cologne (Köln)** — trade fairs (Messe Köln) create spikes in catering demand

For Moroccan applicants, this demand translates into a realistic chance of finding a training contract even with intermediate German skills — provided your application is well-prepared.

## German Language Requirements and Preparation

You need at least **B1 German** to be accepted into most Ausbildung programmes in hospitality. Many employers prefer B2 because you will be in daily contact with German-speaking guests, colleagues, and suppliers. The Goethe-Institut has centres in Casablanca and Rabat where you can sit for official exams.

### Language Tips That Actually Work

- Start with a structured A1–B1 course (roughly 6–9 months of consistent study)
- Supplement with German cooking videos on YouTube — you pick up vocabulary in context
- Practise guest dialogues: "Wie kann ich Ihnen helfen?" (How can I help you?) is something you will say dozens of times a day
- Use the Deutsche Welle free online German courses (dw.com/en/learn-german)
- Once you reach B1, begin applying — many employers will hire you and support further language development on the job

## How to Apply for an Ausbildung in Cooking and Hospitality from Morocco

The application process has several stages. Do not skip any of them.

### Step 1 — Find Open Training Positions

Search on:
- **Bundesagentur für Arbeit** (arbeitsagentur.de) — Germany's official job agency, filter by Ausbildung and sector
- **Ausbildung.de** — dedicated Ausbildung portal
- **Make it in Germany** (make-it-in-germany.com) — federal government's immigration portal
- Hotel chains' own career pages: Marriott Careers, Hilton Careers, NH Hotels

### Step 2 — Prepare Your Application Documents

A German Ausbildung application typically requires:

- A **Lebenslauf** (CV) in German, formatted to DIN 5008 standard
- An **Anschreiben** (cover letter) tailored to the specific employer
- Certified copies of your school certificates (Baccalauréat or equivalent) — these must often be translated into German by a sworn translator
- Language certificate (Goethe-Institut B1 or B2)
- Any relevant work experience documents (even part-time kitchen or service jobs count)

### Step 3 — Apply for the Right Visa

As a Moroccan national, you need a **Ausbildungsvisum** (training visa). You apply at the German Consulate in Casablanca or Rabat. Required documents for the visa include:

- Signed Ausbildungsvertrag (training contract) from your employer
- Proof of accommodation in Germany
- Language proof (B1 minimum)
- Proof your qualifications are recognised (or an equivalency letter from the employer)
- Consulate fees: approximately **€75**

Processing time is typically 6–12 weeks. Book your appointment early — slots fill up fast.

### Step 4 — Prepare for Life in Germany

Before you travel:
- Open a **blocked account (Sperrkonto)** — not required for Ausbildung visa (unlike student visa), but having €2,000–€3,000 saved is strongly recommended for the first month
- Arrange health insurance — your employer will register you for statutory insurance (gesetzliche Krankenversicherung) from day one
- Find a room in a Wohnheim (shared student/trainee housing) or a WG (Wohngemeinschaft/shared flat). Budget €400–€700 per month for rent in most cities

## What People Get Wrong About This Path

**Mistake 1: Applying without a German CV.**
Many Moroccan applicants send a French or English CV. German employers expect a Lebenslauf in German, with a photo, formatted correctly. This alone can disqualify an otherwise strong application.

**Mistake 2: Underestimating the language requirement.**
Arriving with A2 German hoping to "learn on the job" creates real problems at the Berufsschule. Classes are taught entirely in German. Reach B1 before you apply.

**Mistake 3: Targeting only big cities.**
Munich and Berlin are competitive. Cities like Nuremberg (Nürnberg), Freiburg, Augsburg, or Mainz have strong hospitality sectors and noticeably less competition for training spots.

**Mistake 4: Forgetting to get documents officially translated.**
Your Baccalauréat needs a certified German translation. The German Consulate will not accept Arabic or French originals alone. Budget €80–€150 for translation services.

**Mistake 5: Not following up on applications.**
German employers respect initiative. If you sent your application and heard nothing after two weeks, a polite follow-up email is not just acceptable — it is expected.

## What Comes After Your Ausbildung

Finishing your Ausbildung opens multiple doors:

- Work directly in Germany with a **skilled worker residence permit (Fachkräftevisum)** — your Ausbildung certificate qualifies you automatically
- Sit the **Meisterprüfung** (master craftsman exam) to open your own restaurant or hotel in Germany
- Pursue a **Weiterbildung** (advanced training) in hotel management or culinary arts
- Apply to a Hochschule für Angewandte Wissenschaften (university of applied sciences) — several accept Ausbildung graduates with practical experience into hospitality management bachelor programmes

Germany's Chancenkarte (Opportunity Card), introduced in 2024, also makes it easier to come to Germany first and search for an Ausbildung spot in person.

## Conclusion

An Ausbildung in cooking and hospitality is one of the most accessible, well-structured routes for Moroccans to build a real career in Germany. You earn from day one, gain a recognised qualification, and step into a sector that genuinely needs you. The key is preparation: reach B1 German, build a strong German-format application, and start searching early.

Ready to put together a compelling Ausbildung application? [Build your German CV and cover letter now](/cv-builder) or [book a free consultation](/anschreiben-generator) to learn German and move to Germany successfully.

faqs.question: Do I need German language skills to apply for an Ausbildung in cooking and hospitality?
faqs.answer: Yes. Most employers require at least B1 German, and B2 is preferred since you will work with German-speaking guests daily. You can prepare through the Goethe-Institut in Casablanca or Rabat, or use free resources like Deutsche Welle's online courses at dw.com.

faqs.question: How much will I earn during an Ausbildung in the hospitality sector in Germany?
faqs.answer: Germany's legal minimum for Ausbildung trainees starts at €649 per month in year one (2024 rates), rising to €876 in year three. Many hotel chains and restaurants pay €900–€1,100 or more in year one, especially in Bavaria and Hamburg under DEHOGA collective agreements.

faqs.question: Which cities in Germany have the most Ausbildung positions in cooking and hotels?
faqs.answer: Munich, Berlin, Hamburg, Frankfurt, and Cologne have the highest overall demand. However, cities like Nuremberg, Freiburg, and Mainz offer strong hospitality markets with less competition for training spots — a smart choice for first-time applicants.

faqs.question: What visa do I need as a Moroccan to do an Ausbildung in Germany?
faqs.answer: You need an Ausbildungsvisum (training visa), applied for at the German Consulate in Casablanca or Rabat. You must present a signed training contract, proof of German language skills (B1 minimum), accommodation details, and pay a consulate fee of approximately €75. Processing typically takes 6–12 weeks.

faqs.question: What can I do in Germany after finishing my Ausbildung in hospitality?
faqs.answer: Your completed Ausbildung certificate qualifies you automatically for a skilled worker residence permit (Fachkräftevisum), allowing you to work anywhere in Germany. You can also pursue the Meisterprüfung to open your own business, advance into hotel management through a Weiterbildung, or even apply to a university of applied sciences.

rw-19.title: How to Write a German-Style CV (Lebenslauf) That Gets You Hired in Germany
rw-19.summary: Learn exactly how to write a German-style CV (Lebenslauf) that impresses employers — format, sections, photos, and common mistakes to avoid.
rw-19.content:
Landing a job or Ausbildung in Germany starts with one document that can make or break your application: the Lebenslauf. If you've been sending the same CV you use in Morocco, you're almost certainly missing the mark — German employers have very specific expectations that differ sharply from what's standard in Arab countries or even the rest of Europe. This guide walks you through exactly how to write a German-style CV, step by step, with real examples and numbers, so you can apply with confidence.

## What Is a German Lebenslauf and Why Is It Different?

The word *Lebenslauf* literally means "course of life" in German. It's the equivalent of a CV or résumé, but the German format follows strict conventions that employers and HR departments treat as a signal of professionalism and cultural fit.

Here's what makes it different from a Moroccan or international CV:

- **It must include a professional photo** — unlike in the US or UK, this is expected and omitting it can hurt your chances.
- **Reverse chronological order** — your most recent job or education comes first.
- **Personal details section** is standard — including your date of birth, nationality, and marital status (optional but common).
