new-public-health-insurance-ausbildung-g.title: Public Health Insurance Germany Ausbildung: Your Complete GKV Guide for Trainees
new-public-health-insurance-ausbildung-g.summary: Learn how public health insurance (GKV) works during your Ausbildung in Germany — who pays, what it costs, what's covered, and how to enroll from day one.
new-public-health-insurance-ausbildung-g.content:
Starting your Ausbildung in Germany is exciting, but the paperwork that comes with it — especially around health insurance — can feel overwhelming if you've never dealt with the German system before. Public health insurance in Germany (called Gesetzliche Krankenversicherung, or GKV) is not optional: every Ausbildung trainee must be covered from the very first day of training. The good news is that the system is straightforward once you understand who pays what, how much comes out of your pocket, and exactly how to sign up before your start date.

## What Is GKV and Why Does It Apply to Your Ausbildung?

GKV stands for **Gesetzliche Krankenversicherung**, which translates directly as "statutory health insurance." It is the public, legally mandated health insurance system that covers roughly 90% of people living in Germany. The alternative — private health insurance (PKV) — is generally not available to Ausbildung trainees, because your training salary is below the income threshold (€69,300 per year in 2024) that would allow you to opt out of GKV.

As an Ausbildung trainee, you are classified as an employee under German law. That means you are automatically subject to the same social security contributions as any other worker, including health insurance contributions. There is no grey area here: if you show up on day one without proof of GKV membership, your company's HR department will ask for it immediately.

### The Five Main Social Security Contributions

GKV is one of five contributions deducted from your gross training salary every month:

- **Krankenversicherung** (health insurance) — GKV
- **Pflegeversicherung** (long-term care insurance)
- **Rentenversicherung** (pension insurance)
- **Arbeitslosenversicherung** (unemployment insurance)
- **Unfallversicherung** (accident insurance — paid entirely by the employer)

This article focuses on health insurance, but it helps to know these others exist so you aren't surprised when you see your first payslip.

## How Much Does GKV Cost for Ausbildung Trainees?

Here is the part that surprises many trainees from Morocco: you don't pay the full contribution yourself. The cost is **split between you and your employer**.

### The Standard Contribution Rate

The total GKV contribution rate in 2024 is **14.6%** of your gross salary, plus a fund-specific additional contribution (Zusatzbeitrag) that averages around **1.6%** — making the effective total roughly **16.2%**.

This is split almost equally:
- **You pay:** approximately 8.1% of your gross salary
- **Your employer pays:** approximately 8.1% of your gross salary

### Real Numbers: What You Actually Pay

Let's use concrete figures. Ausbildung salaries vary by sector and year of training, but here are some typical examples:

| Sector | Year 1 Gross Salary | Your Monthly GKV Contribution |
|---|---|---|
| IT (Fachinformatiker) | ~€800/month | ~€65/month |
| Retail (Kaufmann/frau) | ~€620/month | ~€50/month |
| Healthcare (Pflegefachmann) | ~€1,190/month | ~€96/month |
| Construction (Maurer) | ~€700/month | ~€57/month |

These are approximate figures — the exact amount depends on which GKV fund you choose and that fund's current Zusatzbeitrag. The employer automatically deducts your share and transfers the combined contribution directly to your health insurance fund. You never have to send a payment yourself.

### Long-Term Care Insurance (Pflegeversicherung) — An Add-On to GKV

Pflegeversicherung is always tied to your GKV and adds another **3.4%** (2024 rate for people without children). Half is paid by your employer. This is worth knowing because it appears as a separate line on your payslip alongside GKV.

## What Does GKV Actually Cover?

GKV coverage is comprehensive by international standards. As an Ausbildung trainee enrolled in any statutory health insurance fund, you are entitled to:

- **Doctor visits:** General practitioners (Hausarzt) and specialists — no per-visit fee beyond the first visit to a new specialist chain in a quarter
- **Hospital treatment:** Inpatient stays covered; you pay a co-pay of €10 per day, capped at 28 days per year (max €280/year)
- **Prescription medications:** You pay a co-pay of €5–€10 per prescription, never more than the medication's actual price
- **Dental care:** Basic dental treatment (fillings, extractions) is fully covered; higher-quality fillings or implants require a partial top-up from you
- **Mental health care:** Psychotherapy sessions are covered — waiting times can be long, but the coverage exists
- **Preventive care:** Vaccinations, cancer screenings, and regular check-ups (Vorsorgeuntersuchungen) are fully covered
- **Sick leave (Krankengeld):** If you are ill for more than 6 weeks, GKV pays you Krankengeld — approximately 70% of your gross salary — starting from week 7

### What GKV Does NOT Cover

- Private hospital rooms or personal attending physicians (Chefarztbehandlung)
- Most vision correction (glasses, contact lenses) — there are exceptions for severe prescriptions
- Many alternative medicine treatments
- Dental implants beyond the statutory fixed-cost subsidy

## Which GKV Fund Should You Choose?

Germany has over 90 statutory health insurance funds (Krankenkassen). The most well-known and widely available ones include:

- **TK (Techniker Krankenkasse)** — popular with young people, strong app and digital services, Zusatzbeitrag ~1.2% in 2024
- **AOK** — regional funds with strong local networks; good if you live outside major cities
- **Barmer** — nationwide, solid digital tools, Zusatzbeitrag ~1.7%
- **DAK-Gesundheit** — another nationwide option, known for good customer service
- **BKK (Betriebskrankenkassen)** — employer-linked funds; sometimes available to you through your training company

### How to Compare Funds

The main things to compare are:
- **Zusatzbeitrag** (additional contribution) — lower means cheaper for you
- **Additional benefits** — some funds offer extras like professional teeth cleaning reimbursement (up to €100/year), hearing aids, or fitness studio subsidies
- **App quality and English-language support** — TK and Barmer both offer partial English-language service, which matters when your German is still developing

You can compare current Zusatzbeiträge at **krankenkasseninfo.de** or directly on each fund's website. All funds cover the same legally required services — you are only choosing the price and extras.

## How to Enroll in GKV Before Day One of Your Ausbildung

This is the step that trips up many trainees. You must choose your GKV fund and receive a **membership confirmation document** (Mitgliedsbescheinigung) before your Ausbildung starts. Your employer needs this document to register you in the social security system.

### Step-by-Step Enrollment Process

1. **Choose your fund** — compare Zusatzbeitrag and benefits online at krankenkasseninfo.de
2. **Apply online** — go directly to the fund's website (e.g., tk.de, barmer.de) and fill in the online Beitrittserklärung (membership application). Most take 5–10 minutes
3. **Submit your documents** — you'll typically need your passport/ID and your training contract (Ausbildungsvertrag)
4. **Receive your Mitgliedsbescheinigung** — this confirmation usually arrives within 2–5 business days by email or post
5. **Give the document to your employer's HR department** — they handle everything else from here
6. **Receive your GKV card (Gesundheitskarte)** — a physical card arrives by post within a few weeks; use it at every doctor visit

**Important:** If you do not actively choose a fund, your employer will assign you to one automatically. You keep the right to switch funds — but only after being a member for at least 12 months.

### What If You Arrive in Germany Just Before Starting?

Many trainees from Morocco arrive only days before their Ausbildung begins. Apply to your chosen fund online as soon as you have your training contract — even if you are still in Morocco. Funds like TK accept applications from abroad and can email you the Mitgliedsbescheinigung.

## Common Pitfalls — What People Get Wrong

**1. Waiting until after day one to apply.**
Your coverage must start on your first day of training. Apply at least two weeks before your start date to have the Mitgliedsbescheinigung in hand on time.

**2. Confusing GKV with private insurance.**
If someone offers you "private health insurance" as an Ausbildung trainee in Germany, be cautious. You are almost certainly legally required to be in GKV. Private insurance as a supplement is fine, but it cannot replace GKV at your income level.

**3. Not understanding the Zusatzbeitrag difference.**
A 0.5% difference in Zusatzbeitrag on a €800/month salary is only €4/month — not life-changing. Don't agonize over this decision for weeks; the core coverage is identical across all GKV funds.

**4. Assuming your home country insurance covers you.**
Your Moroccan health insurance does not work in Germany once you become a resident and start Ausbildung. You need German GKV.

**5. Missing the free family coverage window.**
If your spouse or children join you in Germany and they are not working, they can be covered under your GKV at no extra cost (Familienversicherung). Many trainees don't claim this and pay unnecessarily.

**6. Not registering an address (Anmeldung) first.**
Some GKV funds require a German address to complete registration. Get your Anmeldung done at your local Einwohnermeldeamt as soon as you have a place to live — this document is useful for almost every bureaucratic step in Germany.

## Conclusion

Public health insurance in Germany during your Ausbildung is mandatory, affordable, and genuinely comprehensive. You pay roughly 8% of your training salary, your employer matches it, and in return you get access to doctors, hospitals, medications, mental health care, and preventive screenings — all from day one. The key action is simple: pick a GKV fund before your training starts, apply online, and hand the Mitgliedsbescheinigung to your HR team.

If you're still navigating the paperwork side of moving to Germany for Ausbildung — from your application documents to your CV and cover letter — [book a free consultation to learn German and move to Germany successfully](/cv-builder). Getting the administrative details right from the start means you can focus on what actually matters: building your career.

faqs.question: Can I choose any GKV fund as an Ausbildung trainee, or is it assigned by my employer?
faqs.answer: You have the right to choose any GKV fund yourself. Your employer cannot force you into a specific fund. If you don't choose one before your start date, your employer will assign you to a fund automatically — but you can switch after 12 months of membership.

faqs.question: How much will I pay per month for GKV during my Ausbildung?
faqs.answer: It depends on your salary. At a typical first-year salary of €800/month, you pay roughly €65/month for GKV. Your employer pays an equal share on top of that. The exact amount is around 8.1% of your gross training salary, including the fund's Zusatzbeitrag.

faqs.question: Can my family members be covered under my GKV for free?
faqs.answer: Yes. If your spouse or children move to Germany with you and they are not working (or earning under €505/month), they can be added to your GKV as family members (Familienversicherung) at no extra cost. Contact your GKV fund to register them.

faqs.question: What happens if I get sick during my Ausbildung — do I still get paid?
faqs.answer: Yes. Your employer must continue paying your full training salary for up to 6 weeks of illness per year (Entgeltfortzahlung). If you are still sick after 6 weeks, your GKV fund pays Krankengeld — approximately 70% of your gross salary — until you recover or for a maximum of 78 weeks for the same illness.

faqs.question: Is TK (Techniker Krankenkasse) really the best GKV fund for Ausbildung trainees from abroad?
faqs.answer: TK is often recommended because it has a strong English-language support option, a well-rated app, and a relatively low Zusatzbeitrag. However, "best" depends on your situation. If you live in a smaller city, AOK may have better local doctor networks. Compare current Zusatzbeiträge at krankenkasseninfo.de before deciding.

new-public-vs-private-health-insurance-g.title: Public vs Private Health Insurance Germany: What Ausbildung Trainees from Morocco Need to Know
new-public-vs-private-health-insurance-g.summary: GKV or PKV? Learn the real cost differences, who can actually choose, and whether private health insurance in Germany is worth it for Ausbildung trainees.
new-public-vs-private-health-insurance-g.content:
Choosing between public and private health insurance in Germany feels like picking a phone plan in a language you barely speak — the options look similar on the surface, but the details can cost you thousands of euros. For Moroccans moving to Germany for an Ausbildung or skilled work, this decision matters more than most people realise. Get it wrong and you could spend years paying far too much, or worse, find yourself locked out of the cheaper option when you need it most.

## Public vs Private Health Insurance Germany: The Basic Difference

Germany has two parallel health insurance systems running side by side, and they work completely differently.

**GKV (Gesetzliche Krankenversicherung)** is the statutory, public health insurance system. About 90% of people in Germany use it. Your monthly contribution is calculated as a percentage of your gross income — currently around 14.6% of your salary, split roughly 50/50 between you and your employer, plus a supplemental contribution (Zusatzbeitrag) that averages around 1.7% in 2024. Major public funds include **AOK**, **TK (Techniker Krankenkasse)**, **Barmer**, and **DAK**.

**PKV (Private Krankenversicherung)** is private health insurance. Premiums are not based on your income — they're calculated based on your age, health status, and the specific benefits package you choose. A young, healthy 22-year-old might pay as little as €150–€200/month for a basic private plan, which can look very attractive compared to public contributions. Companies like **Allianz**, **DKV**, **AXA**, and **Debeka** offer PKV policies.

### How GKV Contributions Work in Practice

If you're doing an Ausbildung and earning €800/month gross (a common starting salary in year one), your total health insurance contribution would be roughly:

- 14.6% + ~1.7% = ~16.3% of €800 = ~€130/month total
- Your employer pays approximately half: ~€65/month
- You pay: ~€65/month

That's genuinely affordable. And your family members (spouse, children) can be added for free under **Familienversicherung** — one of the biggest advantages of GKV.

## Who Can Actually Choose Between GKV and PKV?

This is where most people get surprised. In Germany, **not everyone gets to choose freely**.

If you're an Ausbildung trainee, you are compulsorily insured in GKV. There is no opt-out. Your employer automatically registers you with a public fund, and that's it. You can choose *which* GKV fund, but you cannot switch to PKV during your Ausbildung.

The right to choose PKV is reserved for:

- **Self-employed people** (Selbstständige) — they can choose from day one
- **Civil servants** (Beamte) — they often choose PKV because the government (Beihilfe) covers 50–80% of their costs
- **Employees earning above the income threshold** (Jahresarbeitsentgeltgrenze / JAEG) — in 2024, this is **€69,300/year gross** (about €5,775/month). Only if you earn above this for at least one year can you opt out of GKV

As an Ausbildung trainee earning €800–€1,100/month, you will not come close to this threshold. PKV is simply not on the table during your training years.

## When Private Health Insurance Might Be Worth Considering

Once you finish your Ausbildung and move into a full-time position, the calculation changes — but only under specific circumstances.

### You Earn Above the Income Threshold

If your post-Ausbildung job offers a salary above €69,300/year from the start (this happens in IT, engineering, or if you move into a management role quickly), you become eligible to switch to PKV. At that point, it's worth comparing seriously.

### You're Young, Single, and Healthy

PKV premiums are age-locked at entry. A 26-year-old signing up pays a lower base rate than a 35-year-old for the same plan — forever. If you're young, have no pre-existing conditions, and plan to stay in Germany long-term, locking in a low PKV premium early *can* make financial sense.

### Better Benefits for Specific Needs

Private insurance typically offers:
- Single or double rooms in hospitals (Chefarztbehandlung)
- Shorter waiting times for specialist appointments
- Broader dental and optical coverage
- Access to senior consultants rather than junior staff

For most basic healthcare needs, however, GKV in Germany is genuinely good. The difference in day-to-day care is smaller than private insurers advertise.

## The Real Costs: GKV vs PKV Side by Side

Let's put real numbers to this.

**Scenario A: Ausbildung trainee, year two, €900/month gross**
- GKV contribution: ~€73/month (your share)
- PKV: Not available (compulsory GKV)

**Scenario B: IT specialist, 27 years old, €6,000/month gross, no pre-existing conditions**
- GKV contribution: contribution is capped at the Beitragsbemessungsgrenze (€5,175/month in 2024), so you pay roughly €422/month (your share)
- PKV (e.g., DKV basic plan): approximately €200–€280/month with a good benefits package

In Scenario B, PKV saves you €140–€220/month. That sounds compelling. But factor in:

- **No free family coverage** — a spouse and two children on PKV could add €400–€600/month
- **Premiums rise with age** — at 50, that €250/month plan could be €500–€700/month
- **Pre-existing conditions are excluded or cost extra**
- **Switching back to GKV later is very difficult** (see below)

## The Trap of Switching Back from PKV to GKV

This is the most common and painful mistake people make. Many Moroccans who switch to PKV in their late 20s or early 30s discover at 45 or 50 that they want to go back to GKV — because they've started a family, their income dropped, or premiums became unmanageable.

**Getting back into GKV is extremely hard once you leave.**

Your main options are:
- Become an employee earning *below* the JAEG threshold — but your employer would need to report this, and PKV companies fight hard to keep you
- Become unemployed and receive ALG I/ALG II (Jobcenter pays GKV contributions automatically)
- Retire (at which point you may enter KVdR — but only if you were in GKV for most of your working life)

For Moroccan immigrants who may have variable income over a career, or who plan to bring family members to Germany, staying in GKV is almost always the safer, more flexible choice.

## What People Get Wrong About Health Insurance in Germany

**"PKV is always cheaper."** Only when you're young, childless, and high-earning. The math flips fast when family or age enters the picture.

**"I can switch to PKV during my Ausbildung."** No. This is legally not allowed. Any broker telling you otherwise is misleading you.

**"All GKV funds are the same."** Not quite. While the main benefit catalogue is standardised, supplemental benefits (Zusatzleistungen), customer service quality, and digital tools vary significantly. TK and Barmer are known for excellent English-language support — important for newcomers. AOK offers strong regional networks in cities like **Munich**, **Hamburg**, and **Cologne**.

**"I don't need insurance for the first few weeks."** Wrong and dangerous. Germany requires health insurance from day one of employment. If you arrive before your Ausbildung starts, arrange a short-term policy (Reisekrankenversicherung or a pre-enrollment GKV) to cover the gap.

**"PKV premiums stay affordable forever."** Premiums increase as you age and as healthcare costs rise. The German Association of Private Health Insurers (PKV-Verband) data shows average premiums for 60-year-old PKV members can be 2–3× what they paid at 30.

## Practical Steps for Moroccans Starting Their Ausbildung

1. **Before arriving:** Check that your visa application mentions the correct insurance type. For Ausbildung, you'll be covered by GKV — confirm this with your employer before departure.
2. **On arrival:** Ask your employer which GKV fund they use by default, then compare with TK, Barmer, or AOK in your city. You have a right to choose your own GKV fund.
3. **Registration:** Your employer handles the bulk of registration, but you must fill out a Mitgliedschaftsantrag (membership application) with your chosen fund.
4. **Family planning:** If your spouse or children will join you later, notify your GKV fund — Familienversicherung is free and starts immediately.
5. **After Ausbildung:** Reassess only if your new salary exceeds €69,300/year AND you are single or your spouse also earns well.

## Conclusion

For almost every Moroccan starting an Ausbildung in Germany, public health insurance (GKV) is not just the default — it's the right choice. It's affordable on a training salary, protects your family for free, and keeps your options open. Private health insurance becomes worth a serious look only if you're earning well above average, young, and genuinely committed to staying in Germany without starting a family. The trap of switching back from PKV is real, and many people wish they had never left GKV in the first place.

If you're still figuring out the paperwork, documents, and steps needed to land your Ausbildung place in Germany, [book a free consultation and use our CV builder](/cv-builder) to put your best application forward — and get started on the right financial foot from day one.

faqs.question: Can I choose private health insurance (PKV) during my Ausbildung in Germany?
faqs.answer: No. Ausbildung trainees are compulsorily enrolled in GKV (public health insurance) by law. You can choose which GKV fund to join, but switching to PKV is not legally possible during your training.

faqs.question: How much will I pay for GKV as an Ausbildung trainee earning €900/month?
faqs.answer: Your personal share is roughly €65–€75/month. Your employer pays approximately the same amount. The combined rate is around 14.6% plus a supplemental contribution of ~1.7%, split 50/50 between you and your employer.

faqs.question: Which public health insurance fund is best for Moroccan newcomers to Germany?
faqs.answer: TK (Techniker Krankenkasse) and Barmer are widely recommended for non-German speakers because both offer strong English-language support, good digital apps, and nationwide coverage. AOK is another strong option with deep regional networks in cities like Munich, Hamburg, and Cologne.

faqs.question: Can I add my spouse and children to my GKV for free?
faqs.answer: Yes. GKV offers free family coverage (Familienversicherung) for non-working spouses and children, as long as their own income is below a small threshold (€505/month in 2024). This is one of the biggest financial advantages of public insurance over PKV.

faqs.question: Is it hard to switch back from private to public health insurance in Germany?
faqs.answer: Very hard. Once you leave GKV for PKV, returning is only possible in limited situations — such as your income dropping below the threshold through a new job, becoming unemployed, or retirement. Many people in their 40s and 50s regret switching and find themselves stuck with rising PKV premiums they can no longer afford.

new-find-hausarzt-foreigner-germany.title: How to Find a Hausarzt in Germany as a Foreigner (Step-by-Step Guide)
new-find-hausarzt-foreigner-germany.summary: Learn how to find a Hausarzt in Germany as a foreigner — from using Doctolib and Jameda to your first appointment and routine check-ups.
new-find-hausarzt-foreigner-germany.content:
Moving to Germany is exciting, but the moment you catch a cold or need a prescription refilled, you realize you need a Hausarzt — a family doctor — and fast. Finding one as a foreigner can feel overwhelming when you don't know the system, speak limited German, or aren't sure whether your insurance even covers you yet. The good news: with the right tools and a little preparation, you can find a Hausarzt in Germany as a foreigner within a week, even in a big city.

## What Is a Hausarzt and Why Do You Need One?

A Hausarzt (literally "house doctor") is your primary care physician in Germany. Think of them as your first stop for almost everything medical — a cough that won't go away, a referral to a specialist, a sick note for your employer (Krankmeldung), or managing a chronic condition like diabetes or high blood pressure.

In Germany, the healthcare system is built around the Hausarzt model. You are not required by law to register with one, but in practice you need one because:

- Specialists (Fachärzte) almost always require a referral letter (Überweisung) from a Hausarzt
- Your Hausarzt keeps your complete medical history in one place
- Statutory health insurance (gesetzliche Krankenversicherung, or GKV) covers nearly all Hausarzt visits at no additional cost
- You get a Krankmeldung — the sick certificate your employer legally requires — only from a licensed doctor

If you have private health insurance (PKV), the process is slightly different but you still benefit from having a regular Hausarzt.

## The Fastest Ways to Find a Hausarzt in Germany

### Use Doctolib

[Doctolib](https://www.doctolib.de) is the most popular online booking platform in Germany. You can filter by:

- City (try Berlin-Mitte, München-Schwabing, or your specific district)
- "Neue Patienten" (new patients accepted — **this filter is crucial**)
- Language (English, French, Arabic, and others are listed in many profiles)
- Insurance type (GKV or PKV)

Create a free account, search "Allgemeinmedizin" (general medicine), and book an appointment directly. Many practices confirm within 24 hours.

### Use Jameda

[Jameda](https://www.jameda.de) works similarly but also shows patient ratings and doctor bios. It's particularly useful for finding English-speaking or multilingual doctors. Search for "Hausarzt" in your city and check the "Sprachkenntnisse" (language skills) section on each profile. Doctors who speak Arabic, French, or English often list it here.

### Call the Kassenärztliche Vereinigung (KV)

Every German state has a Kassenärztliche Vereinigung — the association that manages licensed GKV doctors. They run a national hotline: **116 117**. Call this number and explain you are a new resident looking for a Hausarzt in your area. They can give you a list of practices currently accepting new patients.

### Ask Your Health Insurance Provider

Your GKV provider — AOK, TK (Techniker Krankenkasse), Barmer, DAK — often has a doctor-finder tool on their own website or app. TK's app, for example, lets you filter by language and shows real-time availability. This is worth using because results are pre-filtered to doctors in your specific insurance network.

### Walk In and Ask

This is old-fashioned but still works, especially in smaller cities like Freiburg, Erfurt, or Augsburg. Walk into a practice, introduce yourself at reception, and ask if they are accepting new patients ("Nehmen Sie neue Patienten an?"). Bring your insurance card. Some practices will register you on the spot.

## Finding an English-Speaking or Arabic-Speaking Doctor

Language is a real barrier, and you have options beyond just hoping the doctor speaks English.

- **Doctolib language filter**: Type your language in the search and many profiles will surface immediately
- **Expat Facebook groups**: In cities like Berlin, Hamburg, and Munich, expat groups on Facebook have pinned posts with community-recommended English-speaking Hausärzte. Search "[your city] expats" and browse recommendations
- **International practices**: Major cities have practices specifically designed for international patients. Examples include the International Health Centre Berlin (Ku'damm area) and Medicover in Munich and Hamburg — both with multilingual staff
- **University towns**: Heidelberg, Göttingen, and Münster have practices near university campuses that are accustomed to international students and often have English-speaking staff
- **Translation apps as backup**: If your German is limited and you can't find an English speaker nearby, bring Google Translate or a trusted friend to your first appointment

## What to Bring to Your First Hausarzt Appointment

German doctors are thorough record-keepers. Show up prepared and your first visit will go much more smoothly.

**Required documents:**
- Krankenversicherungskarte (your health insurance card) — you receive this from your GKV provider after registration
- Your passport or residence permit (Aufenthaltstitel)
- Anmeldebescheinigung (proof of address registration in Germany)

**Helpful to bring:**
- A written summary of your medical history in German or English — chronic conditions, surgeries, allergies
- Any current medications you take, with dosage (a photo of the packaging works)
- Previous lab results or vaccination records if you have them
- Name and contact details of any specialist you already see

If you're on regular medication from Morocco, bring the Arabic/French prescription and the medication itself. The Hausarzt can issue a German prescription for the equivalent drug, though this may take a follow-up visit.

## What Happens at Your First Appointment

Your first visit (Erstgespräch) typically lasts 20–30 minutes. Here's what to expect:

1. **Registration at reception**: You hand over your insurance card and it's scanned electronically. No paper forms usually.
2. **Medical history intake**: The doctor asks about existing conditions, current medications, family history, and lifestyle (smoking, alcohol, exercise).
3. **Basic measurements**: Blood pressure, weight, and sometimes an ECG (electrocardiogram) if you're over 35.
4. **Routine blood tests**: Your Hausarzt may order a Blutbild (blood panel) — this includes cholesterol, blood sugar (HbA1c), liver and kidney values, and a complete blood count. This is standard and costs you nothing with GKV.
5. **Vaccinations check**: Germany follows a vaccination schedule from the Robert Koch Institut (RKI). Your doctor will check if you're up to date and may recommend boosters.

Follow-up appointments are usually shorter — 10 to 15 minutes — and focused on a specific issue.

## Routine Tests Your Hausarzt Will Likely Recommend

German preventive care (Vorsorge) is comprehensive and largely free with GKV. Once registered, you're entitled to regular screenings:

- **Check-up 35** (Gesundheits-Check-up): A full health screening offered to all GKV members from age 35, then every three years. Covers blood sugar, cholesterol, kidney function, and a urine test.
- **Cancer screenings**: Bowel cancer screening from age 50, skin cancer screening every two years from age 35, cervical smear for women, prostate check for men from age 45.
- **Dental check-up**: Twice a year, covered by GKV — handled by a Zahnarzt (dentist), not your Hausarzt, but your Hausarzt can refer you.
- **Eye pressure test**: Relevant if you have a family history of glaucoma.

## What People Get Wrong When Looking for a Hausarzt in Germany

**Waiting until you're sick**: Many foreigners only look for a Hausarzt when they're already ill. Then they discover the nearest practice isn't accepting new patients. Register within your first month in Germany, before you need it urgently.

**Ignoring the "neue Patienten" filter**: Booking platforms show all doctors, including those with full patient lists. Always filter for "neue Patienten" or call ahead. Showing up without confirmation wastes everyone's time.

**Assuming the emergency room is the answer**: In Germany, the Notaufnahme (emergency room) is for genuine emergencies only. For a fever, ear infection, or back pain, you go to your Hausarzt or call 116 117 for an after-hours appointment. Using the ER for non-emergencies is expensive and frowned upon.

**Not bringing your insurance card on day one**: Without your Krankenversicherungskarte, many practices will ask you to pay out of pocket (around €50–€100 for a standard visit) and claim it back later. Avoid the hassle — carry the card.

**Expecting a walk-in system**: Germany is appointment-based. Only true medical emergencies allow walk-ins. Book ahead, always.

## Conclusion

Finding a Hausarzt in Germany as a foreigner is one of the most practical things you can do in your first weeks here. It protects your health, gives you access to the full German healthcare system, and saves you from expensive ER visits for routine problems. Use Doctolib or Jameda, filter by language and "neue Patienten," bring your insurance card and a short medical history summary, and you'll have a doctor registered within days.

Getting your health sorted is just one piece of settling into Germany. If you're still working on your application documents, [use our free CV builder](/cv-builder) to create a professional German-style Lebenslauf, or [generate a cover letter](/anschreiben-generator) tailored to German employers. Book a free consultation to learn German and move to Germany successfully — so you can focus on building your new life, not navigating paperwork alone.

faqs.question: Do I need a Hausarzt if I have private health insurance (PKV) in Germany?
faqs.answer: You're not required to register with one, but it's still strongly recommended. With PKV you can often book specialist appointments directly, but having a Hausarzt ensures continuity of care, keeps your full medical history in one place, and issues sick certificates (Krankmeldung) your employer requires. Private patients are generally easier to accept since practices earn higher fees from PKV.

faqs.question: What do I do if no Hausarzt in my area is accepting new patients?
faqs.answer: Call 116 117 (the Kassenärztliche Vereinigung hotline) — they are legally required to find you a doctor. Also try expanding your search radius slightly on Doctolib or Jameda, contact your health insurance provider's hotline, or ask at local expat Facebook groups. In urgent cases, walk-in Bereitschaftspraxen (on-call practices) run by the KV can treat you without registration.

faqs.question: How much does a Hausarzt visit cost in Germany?
faqs.answer: With statutory health insurance (GKV), standard Hausarzt visits are free — your insurance card covers the cost completely. You only pay out of pocket for services explicitly excluded from your plan, such as certain travel vaccinations or cosmetic treatments. If you don't yet have your insurance card, a standard visit typically costs €50–€80 privately, which you can usually claim back from your insurer later.

faqs.question: Can I see a Hausarzt if I only just arrived and haven't registered for health insurance yet?
faqs.answer: You must have valid health insurance to access standard GKV services. If you're starting an Ausbildung or job, your employer registers you with a GKV provider and your coverage begins on day one of work — your card arrives within 2–3 weeks. In the meantime, your insurer can issue a temporary confirmation letter (Versicherungsnachweis) that most practices will accept. For genuine emergencies before coverage starts, hospitals must treat you regardless.

faqs.question: Do German Hausärzte speak English?
faqs.answer: Many do, especially in larger cities like Berlin, Hamburg, Munich, Frankfurt, and university towns. The Doctolib and Jameda platforms both let you filter by language, so you can search specifically for English-speaking, Arabic-speaking, or French-speaking doctors. International health centres in major cities are also specifically set up for non-German-speaking patients. In smaller towns, language access is more limited, so prepare a written summary of your medical history in German as a backup.

new-dental-care-germany-ausbildung.title: Dental Care in Germany as an Ausbildung Trainee: Costs, Coverage, and What to Expect
new-dental-care-germany-ausbildung.summary: Discover what public health insurance covers for dental care in Germany as an Ausbildung trainee, what you pay out of pocket, and when extra dental insurance is worth it.
new-dental-care-germany-ausbildung.content:
Moving to Germany for your Ausbildung is exciting — but your first toothache can quickly turn into a stressful financial surprise if you haven't looked into how dental care works here. Germany's public health insurance (gesetzliche Krankenversicherung, or GKV) does cover some dental treatments, but "some" is doing a lot of heavy lifting in that sentence. Knowing exactly what you're entitled to as an Ausbildung trainee, what comes out of your own pocket, and when it makes sense to top up your coverage with supplementary dental insurance can save you hundreds of euros and a lot of headaches — both literal and financial.

## How Public Health Insurance Covers Dental Care for Ausbildung Trainees

As an Ausbildung trainee in Germany, you are automatically enrolled in the public health insurance system through your employer. Your monthly contribution — split between you and your training company — is calculated as a percentage of your gross Ausbildungsvergütung (training salary). In 2024, the total contribution rate is around 14.6% plus a fund-specific additional rate (Zusatzbeitrag) averaging about 1.7%, so your share comes to roughly 8–9% of your gross salary.

This means if you earn €800 gross per month (typical for a first-year retail or office Ausbildung), you pay around €65–72 per month for your public health coverage. That's not bad — and it includes dental care, just not all of it.

### What GKV Pays For

Your statutory health insurance covers:

- **Annual dental check-up** (Kontrolluntersuchung) — fully covered, once per year
- **Dental X-rays** when medically necessary
- **Basic fillings** using standard materials (amalgam or simple composite for back teeth)
- **Tooth extractions**
- **Root canal treatment** on certain teeth
- **Basic dentures** — GKV pays a fixed grant (Festzuschuss) toward dentures, typically covering 50–60% of the standard treatment cost

The key word throughout is *basic*. If the dentist recommends something above the standard treatment — a white composite filling on a back molar, a porcelain crown instead of a metal one, an implant — the extra cost is yours to carry.

### The Bonusheft: Why You Need to Start It Immediately

One of the most important things you can do in your first weeks in Germany is get a **Bonusheft** (bonus booklet) from your health insurer or dentist. Every time you attend your annual check-up, the dentist stamps the booklet. After 5 consecutive years of documented check-ups, GKV raises its fixed grant on dentures from 50% to 60%. After 10 years, it goes to 65%.

If you're coming from Morocco and you're 22 years old when you start your Ausbildung, starting your Bonusheft now means that by your early 30s you'll get significantly better coverage for major dental work. Do not skip this step.

## What You Pay Out of Pocket: Real Numbers

Here's where Ausbildung trainees often get caught off guard. Germany operates on a co-payment and "top-up" model for most dental work beyond check-ups.

### Fillings

A basic amalgam filling on a back tooth: **fully covered by GKV**.
A white composite filling on the same tooth: you pay the difference, which is typically **€30–€80 per tooth** depending on size and location.

### Crowns

GKV covers the cost of a standard metal crown as its Festzuschuss. A porcelain-fused-to-metal crown costs around **€400–€700 total**, and you'd pay roughly **€200–€400** on top of the GKV grant.
A full ceramic crown (the kind that looks most natural) can run **€800–€1,200**, leaving you with **€500–€800** to pay yourself.

### Implants

GKV does **not** cover dental implants. A single implant in Germany — including the post, abutment, and crown — typically costs **€2,000–€3,500**. This is entirely out of pocket unless you have supplementary insurance.

### Orthodontics (Braces)

For adults (18+), orthodontic treatment is almost never covered by GKV. Braces or aligners can cost **€3,000–€8,000** depending on the case. For children and adolescents up to 18 with medically indicated cases, GKV covers a larger share.

## Finding a Dentist in Germany as a Trainee

Germany has no shortage of dentists. You are free to choose any dentist (Zahnarzt) who accepts GKV patients — and the majority do, although some practices have shifted to private-only.

### How to Find One

- **Kassenzahnärztliche Vereinigung (KZV)**: Each German state has one. Their websites have searchable directories of GKV-accepting dentists. For example, in Bavaria it's kzvb.de; in North Rhine-Westphalia it's kzv-wl.de or kzv-nordrhein.de.
- **Jameda.de**: Germany's largest doctor-rating platform. Filter by "Kassenpatient" (GKV patient) and your city.
- **Your health insurer's website**: AOK, TK (Techniker Krankenkasse), Barmer, DAK — all have dentist-finder tools.

### Practical Tips

- Book your first check-up within the first few months of arriving. Don't wait until something hurts.
- Bring your **Krankenkassenkarte** (health insurance card) — you'll receive it by post shortly after registration.
- If you need a specialist (e.g., an oral surgeon), your general dentist will refer you.
- Language: In larger cities like Frankfurt, Berlin, Munich, or Cologne, many dental practices have English-speaking staff or at least one staff member who speaks French. In smaller towns, bring a German-speaking friend or use a translation app for your first visit.

## When Zahnzusatzversicherung (Supplementary Dental Insurance) Is Worth It

Zahnzusatzversicherung is supplementary private dental insurance that sits on top of your GKV coverage and pays for the gap. It's one of the most popular optional insurance add-ons in Germany — and for good reason.

### What It Covers

Depending on the policy, a good Zahnzusatzversicherung can reimburse **70–100% of the costs** that GKV leaves to you, including:
- High-quality composite or ceramic fillings
- Porcelain crowns and inlays
- Dental implants (some policies, after a waiting period)
- Professional teeth cleaning (Professionelle Zahnreinigung, or PZR) — which GKV does not cover and costs **€60–€120 per session**

### What It Costs

Monthly premiums vary by age, health history, and coverage level:
- A basic plan (covering 70–75% of top-up costs, no implants): **€8–€15/month**
- A mid-range plan (80–90% coverage, including PZR): **€15–€25/month**
- A comprehensive plan (90–100%, implants included): **€25–€50/month**

For a trainee earning €800–€1,000/month, a mid-range plan at €15–€20/month is usually the sweet spot.

### Is It Worth It for You?

It depends on your dental health. If your teeth are generally healthy and you just want cover for one decent cleaning per year and better fillings, a basic plan makes sense. If you need crowns, implants, or extensive work in the next few years, get a comprehensive plan — but be aware that most policies have **waiting periods of 3–8 months** before you can claim major treatments. Apply before you need the dentist urgently.

Good providers to compare: **DKV**, **Allianz**, **AXA**, **ARAG**, and **HanseMerkur**. Use comparison portals like **Check24.de** or **Verivox.de** to see real quotes based on your age and postcode.

## What People Get Wrong About Dental Care as a Trainee

**Assuming everything is free because you have insurance.** GKV is solid for check-ups and emergencies, but for anything cosmetic or above the basic standard, you'll have a co-payment. Don't be shocked at the dentist's reception desk.

**Not keeping the Bonusheft.** Many people who've lived in Germany for years discover too late that they never got the booklet stamped. You cannot retroactively fill in missed years.

**Waiting until pain forces a visit.** Preventive care is much cheaper than emergency treatment. A check-up is free; an emergency root canal at a weekend dental clinic can involve significant private fees.

**Signing treatment plans without reading them.** Before any non-emergency work, your dentist must give you a **Heil- und Kostenplan (HKP)** — a written cost and treatment plan. You can take this to your health insurer for pre-approval and to a second dentist for a second opinion. Never skip this step for expensive treatments.

**Choosing a dentist who only accepts Privatpatienten.** Some upscale practices have moved to private-only billing. Always confirm upfront that they accept GKV patients, or you'll pay full private rates for everything.

## Conclusion

Dental care in Germany as an Ausbildung trainee is manageable if you understand the system. Your GKV covers the basics — check-ups, extractions, standard fillings, and partial denture costs — but anything beyond that comes with a co-payment. Starting your Bonusheft immediately, finding a GKV-accepting dentist early, and considering a mid-range Zahnzusatzversicherung for around €15–€20/month puts you in a strong position.

Getting the most out of Germany's healthcare system starts with the right preparation before you even land. If you're still in the planning phase of your Ausbildung journey and need help with your application documents, [use our CV builder](/cv-builder) to create a German-standard Lebenslauf, or [book a free consultation](/anschreiben-generator) to get personalised guidance on moving to Germany successfully.

faqs.question: Does public health insurance in Germany cover dental implants for Ausbildung trainees?
faqs.answer: No. GKV (public health insurance) does not cover implants regardless of your employment status. A single implant costs €2,000–€3,500 out of pocket. If you want implant coverage, you need a comprehensive Zahnzusatzversicherung — ideally taken out before you need the procedure, as most policies have a 3–8 month waiting period.

faqs.question: How much does a professional teeth cleaning (PZR) cost in Germany, and is it covered?
faqs.answer: Professional teeth cleaning (Professionelle Zahnreinigung) is not covered by GKV. It costs between €60 and €120 per session depending on the practice and city. Many Zahnzusatzversicherung plans cover one or two PZR sessions per year, which is one of the main reasons trainees find supplementary dental insurance worthwhile.

faqs.question: What is a Bonusheft and how do I get one as a new arrival in Germany?
faqs.answer: A Bonusheft is a booklet where your dentist stamps proof of your annual dental check-up. After 5 consecutive years of stamps, GKV raises its denture grant from 50% to 60%; after 10 years, to 65%. Ask for one at your first dental visit or from your health insurer (AOK, TK, Barmer, etc.). You can also download a template from your insurer's website. Start it at your very first check-up.

faqs.question: How do I find a GKV-accepting dentist in Germany as a foreigner?
faqs.answer: Use the official KZV (Kassenzahnärztliche Vereinigung) directory for your federal state — for example, kzvb.de in Bavaria. You can also search on Jameda.de and filter for "Kassenpatient." Always call ahead to confirm the practice is still accepting new GKV patients, as availability varies by city and neighbourhood.

faqs.question: Can I get supplementary dental insurance (Zahnzusatzversicherung) right after arriving in Germany?
faqs.answer: Yes, you can apply as soon as you are enrolled in GKV. However, most policies impose a waiting period of 3–8 months before you can claim major treatments like crowns or implants. Routine check-ups and teeth cleaning coverage often starts sooner. Use comparison sites like Check24.de or Verivox.de to compare plans from DKV, Allianz, AXA, ARAG, and HanseMerkur based on your age and postcode.

new-mental-health-support-germany-intern.title: Mental Health Germany International Trainee: How to Find a Therapist and Get Support
new-mental-health-support-germany-intern.summary: Navigating mental health care in Germany as an international trainee can feel overwhelming. Here's exactly how to find support, fast.
new-mental-health-support-germany-intern.content:
Moving to Germany for an Ausbildung is exciting — but nobody tells you how lonely, exhausting, and disorienting the first months can really be. If you're struggling with anxiety, depression, or just the weight of being far from home, you are not alone, and you do have real options for professional support. This guide explains exactly how mental health Germany international trainee access works — from public insurance to crisis lines — in plain, honest language.

## Why Mental Health Support Matters for International Trainees

Starting an Ausbildung in a new country means managing a language you're still learning, a work culture that can feel cold, homesickness, financial stress, and often racial or social isolation — all at the same time. Research from the German Federal Chamber of Psychotherapists (BPtK) consistently shows that migrants and international students face higher rates of anxiety and depressive episodes than the general population, yet they use mental health services far less. The barriers are real: language, cost confusion, fear of stigma, and simply not knowing where to start.

The good news? Once you know the system, it is more accessible than it looks.

## How the German Public Health Insurance System Covers Therapy

As an Ausbildung trainee, you are almost certainly enrolled in statutory health insurance (gesetzliche Krankenversicherung, or GKV). This means your therapy costs are covered — in full — once you navigate the right steps. The main insurers you will deal with include **AOK**, **TK (Techniker Krankenkasse)**, **Barmer**, **DAK**, and **IKK**. All of them must legally cover psychotherapy.

### The Three Main Types of Covered Therapy

- **Verhaltenstherapie (Cognitive Behavioural Therapy / CBT):** Most widely available; focuses on changing thought and behaviour patterns.
- **Tiefenpsychologisch fundierte Psychotherapie:** Depth psychology approach, exploring emotional patterns over time.
- **Analytische Psychotherapie:** Long-term psychoanalytic therapy; less commonly offered to new patients.

CBT is usually your fastest route to an appointment, so if you have no strong preference, ask specifically for a Verhaltenstherapeut.

### The "Probatory Session" System (Probatorische Sitzungen)

Before formal therapy begins, you are entitled to up to **5 free introductory sessions** (probatorische Sitzungen) with any licensed therapist. These sessions are fully covered by your insurance and have no commitment on either side. You use them to see if you and the therapist are a good fit. After that, the therapist applies to your insurance for a full course of therapy — typically 24 to 80 sessions depending on need.

**You do not need a referral from your GP to start these sessions.** You can call a licensed therapist directly.

## Finding an Arabic, French, or English-Speaking Therapist in Germany

This is the single biggest practical challenge. Here are the resources that actually work:

### Online Therapist Directories

- **[BPtK Therapeutensuche](https://www.bptk.de):** The official search tool of the German Federal Psychotherapist Chamber. Filter by postcode, insurance type, and — crucially — by language (Sprache).
- **[Therapie.de](https://www.therapie.de):** User-friendly search. You can select "Arabisch" or "Französisch" under language filters. Real availability calendars are shown.
- **[Psych-Info](https://www.psychinfo.de):** Regional directories with language tagging.
- **[Psychology Today Germany](https://www.psychologytoday.com/de/therapeuten):** English-language interface, strong filter for English-speaking therapists.

### Practical Search Tips

- Search in large cities first. **Berlin, Hamburg, Munich, Cologne, Frankfurt, and Stuttgart** have the highest concentration of multilingual therapists.
- Even if you live in a smaller city like Kaiserslautern or Erfurt, you can combine in-person sessions in a nearby city with online sessions in between.
- When you call a practice, ask: *"Haben Sie Kapazitäten für Kassenpatienten?"* (Do you have capacity for public insurance patients?) Waitlists of 3–6 months are common, so call multiple practices simultaneously.
- Many Arabic-speaking therapists in Germany are themselves from Lebanon, Syria, Egypt, or Morocco — they understand the migration experience from the inside.

### University Psychological Counselling Services

If you are near a university town, most universities offer **free psychological counselling (Psychologische Beratung)** open to the public or specifically to trainees. These are not full therapy but are excellent for short-term support while you wait for a therapist. Examples:
- **Studierendenwerk München** – free counselling, available in English
- **Beratungsstellen of Caritas and AWO** in most German cities – often multilingual

## Online Therapy Options That Accept German Public Insurance

Waitlists for in-person therapists can stretch 3–6 months. Online therapy is a legitimate, GKV-covered option that can start within days.

- **[Selfapy](https://www.selfapy.com):** Online CBT courses covered by most GKV insurers. German-language but structured and effective. Some AOK and TK branches cover 100% of costs.
- **[HelloBetter](https://hellobetter.de):** Evidence-based digital programmes for depression, anxiety, and stress. TK covers it free for members.
- **[Instahelp](https://www.instahelp.me/de):** Pay-per-session video therapy in multiple languages including Arabic and French. Not always GKV-covered but sessions cost around **€59–€79** each — ask your insurer first.
- **BetterHelp / Talkspace:** These US-based platforms are not covered by GKV but offer English and sometimes Arabic-speaking therapists starting from around **€40–€60/week**. Use as a bridge, not a permanent solution.

## What to Do in a Crisis

If you are in emotional crisis right now — not just struggling, but in acute distress or having thoughts of self-harm — use these resources immediately. They are free, confidential, and available around the clock.

- **Telefonseelsorge:** 0800 111 0 111 or 0800 111 0 222. Free, 24/7, German-language. No call tracing.
- **TelefonSeelsorge online chat:** [online.telefonseelsorge.de](https://online.telefonseelsorge.de) — useful if speaking German on the phone feels hard.
- **112** (emergency services) or **110** (police): If you or someone else is in immediate danger.
- **Arab-speaking support — Ethno-Medizinisches Zentrum (EMZ) Hannover:** Specialises in counselling for migrants including Arabic speakers: [www.emz-hannover.de](https://www.emz-hannover.de)
- **International Helpline Berlin:** +49 30 4401 0607 — English, some multilingual capacity.

If you go to a German hospital emergency room (Notaufnahme) in a mental health crisis, they are legally required to see you and cannot turn you away due to insurance issues.

## Common Pitfalls: What People Get Wrong

**"I need a referral from my doctor first."**
You do not. You can contact a licensed psychotherapist (Psychologischer Psychotherapeut or Kinder- und Jugendlichenpsychotherapeut) directly. A GP referral is optional and may actually slow things down.

**"My insurance won't cover it if I'm still in probation."**
GKV mental health coverage begins on day one of your insurance enrollment. Your Ausbildung probation period has no impact on mental health entitlements.

**"I'll wait until I feel worse."**
Therapy waitlists in Germany are long. Starting your search now — even if you are managing — means you get access sooner. You can always cancel if things improve.

**"Online therapy isn't real therapy."**
Clinical evidence published in journals like *JAMA Psychiatry* shows online CBT produces outcomes comparable to in-person therapy for anxiety and depression. German insurers accept this — which is why they fund it.

**"I can't afford private therapy while I wait."**
Before paying out of pocket, check whether your employer's Betriebskrankenkasse (company health fund) offers mental health programmes. Many do, especially at larger companies. Also ask your insurer directly about their "Präventionskurse" — stress-reduction courses they will fund for €0.

## Conclusion

Your mental health is not a luxury. It is the foundation on which your Ausbildung, your German language progress, and your new life are built. The German system does cover therapy as an international trainee — you just need to know where to look and what to ask for. Start with the BPtK therapist search today, call three practices this week, and use HelloBetter or Selfapy while you wait.

You took a huge step moving to Germany. Getting support when you need it is not weakness — it is exactly the kind of smart planning that makes everything else possible.

faqs.question: Does German public health insurance (GKV) cover therapy for Ausbildung trainees?
faqs.answer: Yes, fully. As soon as you are enrolled in GKV — which happens automatically when your Ausbildung starts — you are entitled to covered psychotherapy sessions. You can have up to 5 free introductory sessions with any licensed therapist before formal therapy is approved.

faqs.question: How do I find an Arabic or French-speaking therapist in Germany?
faqs.answer: Use the BPtK Therapeutensuche at bptk.de or Therapie.de and filter by language (Arabisch or Französisch). Large cities like Berlin, Hamburg, and Frankfurt have the highest number of multilingual therapists. The Ethno-Medizinisches Zentrum in Hannover also specialises in Arabic-speaking migrants.

faqs.question: How long is the waiting list for a therapist in Germany?
faqs.answer: Typically 3 to 6 months for an in-person therapist. To reduce your wait, call multiple practices at once, and use GKV-covered online programmes like HelloBetter (free for TK members) or Selfapy while you wait.

faqs.question: What should I do if I am in a mental health crisis right now?
faqs.answer: Call Telefonseelsorge for free on 0800 111 0 111 (24/7, German-language) or use their online chat at online.telefonseelsorge.de. For English support, try the International Helpline Berlin at +49 30 4401 0607. In a life-threatening emergency, go directly to any hospital Notaufnahme or call 112.

faqs.question: Can I do therapy online and have it covered by my German insurance?
faqs.answer: Yes. Several platforms are GKV-approved. HelloBetter is free for TK members; Selfapy is covered by AOK and other insurers. Ask your specific insurer which digital programmes they fund — many cover them at 100% as part of their prevention budget.

new-krankschreibung-sick-leave-ausbildun.title: Krankschreibung Ausbildung: How to Handle Sick Leave in Germany as a Trainee
new-krankschreibung-sick-leave-ausbildun.summary: Learn how to call in sick during your Ausbildung in Germany, when you need a doctor's note, and what happens to your pay and vacation days.
new-krankschreibung-sick-leave-ausbildun.content:
Getting sick is stressful enough on its own — but when you're in the middle of your Ausbildung in Germany and you don't know the rules, it can feel like a crisis. Understanding how Krankschreibung (sick leave certification) works during your Ausbildung is not just useful, it's essential for protecting your rights as a trainee. This guide walks you through exactly what to do on day one of illness, when you need a doctor's note, and what happens to your money and vacation days while you're off.

## What "Krankschreibung" Actually Means in the Context of Ausbildung

The word **Krankschreibung** literally means "sick-writing" — it refers to the official process of a doctor certifying that you are unable to work due to illness. In German law, this document is called an **Arbeitsunfähigkeitsbescheinigung (AU)**, sometimes just called a "gelbe Schein" (yellow slip), though in 2023 Germany transitioned to a fully digital system for most employees and trainees.

As an Auszubildender (trainee), you are covered under the **Berufsbildungsgesetz (BBiG)** — Germany's Vocational Training Act — which gives you the same sick leave protections as regular employees. That's a big deal. You cannot be fired simply because you got sick, and you are entitled to continued pay during your illness under specific conditions.

### Ausbildung vs. Regular Employment: Any Difference?

The rules are nearly identical. The main thing to remember is that your **training company is your employer**, so all notification and documentation requirements go to them (and your Berufsschule if you're also missing school days). Berufsschule attendance is a separate obligation — even if your company excuses you, your school absence is tracked independently.

## What to Do on the First Day You're Sick

This is where many trainees make mistakes because they panic or don't know the procedure. Here's what you need to do, step by step:

- **Notify your training company as early as possible** on the first day — ideally before your shift starts, or at the latest by the time you would normally arrive. Call your Ausbilder (trainer) or supervisor directly. A WhatsApp message is usually not sufficient unless your company has explicitly said it's acceptable.
- **Notify your Berufsschule** if you would have had school that day. Schools typically require a separate phone call or online notification through their portal.
- **State that you are sick**, not why. You are not legally required to tell your employer your diagnosis.
- **Get a doctor's appointment** if your illness extends (more on the exact timeline below).

A simple phone call script: *"Guten Morgen, ich bin [your name], ich bin heute krank und kann nicht zur Arbeit kommen."* That's all you need to say.

## When Do You Actually Need a Doctor's Note?

This is one of the most confusing points for international trainees coming from Morocco, where workplace sick leave rules work differently.

### The Standard Rule: From Day 4

Under the default rule in German law (§ 5 EFZG — Entgeltfortzahlungsgesetz), you must submit a medical certificate if your illness lasts **more than three calendar days**. So if you're sick on Monday, Tuesday, and Wednesday, you can stay home without a note. But if you're also sick on Thursday, you must see a doctor and present the AU by that Thursday (the fourth day).

### When Your Employer Can Demand It Earlier

Your training contract or company policy may require a doctor's note **from day one**. This is completely legal. Check your **Ausbildungsvertrag** — it's usually stated explicitly. Many larger companies like Deutsche Bahn, Siemens, or big retail chains require immediate documentation. If your contract says "ab dem ersten Krankheitstag," you need to visit a doctor on day one.

### School Rules Add Another Layer

Your Berufsschule may require a note from day one regardless of what your company says. Ask your class teacher (Klassenlehrer) at the start of your Ausbildung so you're not caught off guard.

## The Electronic AU (eAU): Germany's Digital Sick Note System

Since January 2023, Germany has officially switched to the **elektronische Arbeitsunfähigkeitsbescheinigung (eAU)** for all statutory health insurance members (gesetzliche Krankenversicherung, or GKV). This affects most trainees.

Here's how it works now:

- You go to the doctor and they certify your illness digitally in their system.
- The doctor's practice transmits the certificate **directly to your employer's health insurance interface** — you no longer have to physically deliver the yellow paper slip to your employer.
- You still receive a **paper printout for yourself** (the "Ausdruck für den Versicherten"), which you should keep.
- You still need to **inform your employer by phone/email** that you are sick — the eAU does not replace that notification.

**Important caveat:** If you have **private health insurance (PKV)** — which is less common for trainees but possible — the old paper system still applies. You must deliver the AU yourself.

If you're registered with a GKV like **AOK, TK (Techniker Krankenkasse), BARMER, or DAK**, you are part of the eAU system. You can check your AU status online through your insurer's app (e.g., the TK-App or My AOK).

## Your Pay During Sick Leave: What You're Entitled To

Here's the good news: as an Auszubildender in Germany, you are entitled to **continued pay (Entgeltfortzahlung)** during illness, up to **six weeks** per illness episode, from your very first day of training — provided you've been in your Ausbildung for at least **four weeks**.

- Your training allowance (**Ausbildungsvergütung**) continues 100% for up to six weeks.
- Example: If you earn €900/month gross in your first year, you receive the same €900 while sick for up to six weeks.
- After six weeks of continuous illness, your health insurance steps in with **Krankengeld** — sickness benefit, which is approximately **70% of your gross income**, paid directly by your Krankenkasse.
- Krankengeld is only available if you've paid into GKV for at least 12 months and are over 18, so check with your insurer early.

**Your vacation days are NOT deducted** during a certified sick leave period. If you fall ill during your annual leave and have a valid AU, those days are converted back to vacation days — you don't lose them. This is guaranteed under § 9 BUrlG (Bundesurlaubsgesetz).

## What Happens If You Don't Follow the Rules?

Failing to notify your employer correctly or missing the AU deadline can have real consequences:

- **No notification = no pay**: Your employer is not obligated to pay you for days where you didn't properly call in sick.
- **Repeated unexcused absences** can be grounds for a warning (**Abmahnung**) and ultimately termination of your Ausbildung contract.
- **Berufsschule absences without excuse** can be reported to the company and the Berufsschule authorities, creating official problems for your training record.
- If you're caught lying about being sick — for example, posting party photos on social media while claiming to be ill — your employer has grounds for **fristlose Kündigung** (immediate termination without notice).

## Common Pitfalls: What Trainees from Morocco Often Get Wrong

Moving from Morocco to Germany means adapting to a much more formal, documentation-heavy culture around workplace absence. Here are the mistakes we see most often:

- **Sending a text message instead of calling**: In Germany, a phone call is the expected method for notifying sick leave. Text-only communication is often not accepted.
- **Assuming the doctor automatically handles everything**: With the eAU system, your doctor does transmit the note digitally, but you still have to notify your employer personally.
- **Not notifying the Berufsschule separately**: Many trainees assume their company handles this — they don't. You are responsible for contacting both institutions.
- **Missing the four-day deadline**: Thinking you have four *working* days instead of four *calendar* days. Weekends count. If you got sick on a Friday and are still ill on Monday, you need a note by Monday.
- **Not knowing your Ausbildungsvertrag rules**: Some companies require notes from day one. Not reading your contract is the most avoidable mistake.
- **Forgetting about Berufsschule makeup work**: Being sick doesn't exempt you from Berufsschule exams or submitted coursework in most cases. Contact your teacher early.

## Conclusion

Navigating Krankschreibung during your Ausbildung in Germany doesn't have to be overwhelming once you know the steps. Call in on day one, check your contract for doctor's note requirements, understand how the eAU system works with your Krankenkasse, and know that your pay is protected for up to six weeks. These aren't just bureaucratic hurdles — they're protections that work in your favor.

If you're still in the process of preparing your Ausbildung application or want guidance on understanding German workplace documents, [book a free consultation to learn German and move to Germany successfully](/anschreiben-generator). The earlier you understand your rights, the more confidently you can focus on your training.

faqs.question: Do I need a doctor's note from the first day of illness during my Ausbildung?
faqs.answer: It depends on your training contract. German law requires a note only from the 4th calendar day of illness. However, your employer can legally require a note from day one if it's stated in your Ausbildungsvertrag. Always check your contract and ask your Ausbilder at the start of your training.

faqs.question: Does being sick during Ausbildung affect my vacation days?
faqs.answer: No. If you fall ill during your annual vacation and have a valid Krankschreibung (AU), those sick days are not counted as vacation days. They are returned to your vacation balance under § 9 of the Bundesurlaubsgesetz. You must submit the AU to your employer promptly for this to apply.

faqs.question: How does the new electronic AU (eAU) work for Ausbildung trainees in Germany?
faqs.answer: Since January 2023, doctors transmit your sick certificate digitally to your employer's system if you have statutory health insurance (GKV) like TK, AOK, or BARMER. You receive a paper printout for yourself, but you no longer need to physically deliver a yellow slip to your company. You still must notify your employer by phone that you're sick — the eAU does not replace that call.

faqs.question: How much money do I receive when I'm sick during my Ausbildung?
faqs.answer: For the first six weeks of a single illness episode, you receive your full Ausbildungsvergütung (training allowance) — for example, if you earn €850/month, you continue to receive €850. After six weeks, your statutory health insurance (Krankenkasse) pays Krankengeld, which is roughly 70% of your gross income, directly to you.

faqs.question: Can my Ausbildung be terminated because I was sick too often?
faqs.answer: Being sick is not itself a legal reason for termination. German law protects trainees from dismissal due to illness. However, if you repeatedly fail to notify your employer properly, miss the AU deadline, or are absent without valid excuse, you can receive an Abmahnung (formal warning) and eventually face contract termination. Always follow the notification procedure correctly.

new-pregnancy-mutterschutz-ausbildung-ge.title: Pregnancy & Mutterschutz During Ausbildung in Germany: Your Complete Guide
new-pregnancy-mutterschutz-ausbildung-ge.summary: Pregnant during your Ausbildung in Germany? Learn your Mutterschutz rights, financial support options, and how to protect your training contract.
new-pregnancy-mutterschutz-ausbildung-ge.content:
Finding out you're pregnant while doing your Ausbildung in Germany can feel overwhelming — especially when you're still navigating a new country, a new language, and a demanding training program. The good news is that Germany has some of the strongest maternity protection laws in Europe, and they apply to you as an Azubi (trainee) just as much as to any regular employee. Understanding your rights under the Mutterschutzgesetz (Maternity Protection Act) can make the difference between a smooth experience and unnecessary stress.

## What Is Mutterschutz and How Does It Apply to Your Ausbildung?

Mutterschutz literally means "mother protection," and it's the legal framework that protects pregnant women and new mothers in the workplace — including during vocational training. The governing law is the **Mutterschutzgesetz (MuSchG)**, which was significantly updated in 2018 to cover more groups, including Azubis.

As a trainee, you have the same Mutterschutz rights as a regular employee. That means:

- Your training contract **cannot be terminated** because of your pregnancy.
- Your employer must be informed of your pregnancy as soon as you know — this triggers the legal protections.
- You are protected from dismissal from the moment you tell your employer until **four months after giving birth**.

### When Should You Tell Your Employer?

You are legally required to inform your employer of your pregnancy "as soon as you know." In practice, this means telling your Ausbildungsbetrieb (training company) and your Berufsschule (vocational school) as early as possible. Your employer is then required to notify the relevant authority (the Gewerbeaufsichtsamt or Aufsichtsbehörde) within three working days.

You do not need to tell your employer immediately if you are not ready — but the legal protections only kick in once your employer has been informed. If you are dismissed before telling them and they later claim they didn't know, you typically have **two weeks** after dismissal to inform them retrospectively and have the dismissal reversed.

## Your Rights at the Workplace During Pregnancy

Once your employer knows you are pregnant, a wide range of protections come into force automatically.

### Working Hour Restrictions

- You may **not work more than 8.5 hours per day** (and no more than 90 hours in any two-week period).
- Night work (between 8 PM and 6 AM) is generally prohibited.
- Weekend and public holiday work is banned unless you explicitly agree and your doctor confirms it is safe.

### Hazardous Work Restrictions

Your employer must carry out a **risk assessment (Gefährdungsbeurteilung)** specific to your role. If your regular tasks involve:

- Heavy lifting (generally over 5 kg regularly, or over 10 kg occasionally)
- Exposure to chemicals, radiation, or infectious materials
- Prolonged standing or sitting without breaks
- High levels of stress or noise

...then your employer must reassign you to safer tasks or, if that's not possible, excuse you from work entirely — **with full pay**.

### Prenatal Appointments (Vorsorgeuntersuchungen)

You have the right to attend all prenatal care appointments during working hours **without losing pay**. These check-ups happen roughly every four weeks in early pregnancy and more frequently later. Your employer cannot count these absences against your training time or training record.

## The Mutterschutzfrist: Mandatory Leave Before and After Birth

The Mutterschutzfrist is the core period of mandatory maternity leave:

- **6 weeks before your due date**: You cannot be required to work during this period, though you can choose to work if you want.
- **8 weeks after birth**: Strictly mandatory — you absolutely cannot work during this time.
- **12 weeks after birth**: If you give birth to twins or a premature baby, the post-birth period extends to 12 weeks.

During the Mutterschutzfrist, your Ausbildung contract is effectively paused. This is important: **the time you are on Mutterschutz does not count toward your total training period**, which means your Ausbildung end date may shift. Talk to your Ausbildungsbetrieb early to plan how this will be handled.

## Financial Support: Mutterschaftsgeld and Elterngeld

Germany's financial support system during and after pregnancy is generous — here's what you can actually expect to receive.

### Mutterschaftsgeld (Maternity Allowance)

If you are covered by German public health insurance (gesetzliche Krankenversicherung, or GKV), you are entitled to Mutterschaftsgeld during the Mutterschutzfrist. This is paid by your health insurance fund (Krankenkasse) — typically **up to €13 per calendar day**.

Your employer must top this up to 100% of your average net pay. So if you earn €800/month net as an Azubi, your Krankenkasse pays roughly €390 and your employer tops up the remaining ~€410.

To apply, contact your Krankenkasse directly (e.g., TK, AOK, Barmer) about 7 weeks before your due date and request the Mutterschaftsgeld application form. You will need a certificate from your midwife or doctor confirming your expected due date.

**If you are not covered by GKV** (e.g., you are family-insured or uninsured), you can apply to the **Bundesamt für Soziale Sicherung** and receive a one-time payment capped at €210 total. This is significantly less, so it's worth checking your insurance status early.

### Elterngeld (Parental Allowance)

After the Mutterschutzfrist ends, you can apply for **Elterngeld**, which is Germany's parental allowance designed to replace lost income while you care for your newborn.

- **Basiselterngeld**: 65–67% of your average net income before birth, for up to 14 months (if both parents participate; 12 months for one parent alone).
- Minimum payment: **€300/month**
- Maximum payment: **€1,800/month**

As an Azubi earning around €700–900/month, you can expect roughly **€455–600/month** in Elterngeld. You apply through your local **Elterngeldstelle** (part of the Jugendamt or Familienkasse). The application should be submitted within the first three months after birth.

You can also choose **ElterngeldPlus**, which gives you half the monthly amount but for twice as long — useful if you return to your Ausbildung part-time.

### Kindergeld (Child Benefit)

Don't forget **Kindergeld** — a monthly child benefit of **€250 per child** (as of 2024), paid regardless of your employment status. Apply through the Familienkasse at your local Agentur für Arbeit.

## Impact on Your Ausbildung: What Happens to Your Training?

This is the practical question most Azubis worry about. Here's what typically happens:

- **Your contract is suspended**, not terminated. You pick up where you left off.
- The missing training time must be made up, which means your Ausbildung end date is pushed back by the duration of your leave.
- In some cases, you and your employer can agree that the missed time is short enough that the final exam can still take place on the original date — this requires an agreement with the chamber (IHK or HWK).
- Your Berufsschule may require you to repeat a school year or semester depending on how much time you missed.

**Example**: If your Ausbildung in Cologne was due to end in July 2025 and you took 6 months of Mutterschutz + Elternzeit, your new end date would likely be January 2026.

## Common Pitfalls: What People Get Wrong

- **Waiting too long to notify your employer**: The protections only apply once your employer knows. Delaying costs you coverage.
- **Not applying for Mutterschaftsgeld early enough**: Applications should go in roughly 7 weeks before your due date. Late applications can delay payment.
- **Assuming the Ausbildung contract will be terminated**: Dismissal due to pregnancy is illegal. If your employer suggests otherwise, contact your **Gewerkschaft** (union), the **IHK/HWK**, or a legal aid service immediately.
- **Confusing Elternzeit with Elterngeld**: Elternzeit is the legal leave period (up to 3 years); Elterngeld is the financial support (up to 14 months). You can take Elternzeit without Elterngeld after the paid months run out — but you won't receive income during that extra unpaid period.
- **Forgetting to inform the Berufsschule**: Your vocational school must also know so they can manage attendance records and exams accordingly.
- **Not checking your health insurance status**: If you're on a family insurance plan (Familienversicherung) through a parent, your Mutterschaftsgeld situation is very different from someone with their own GKV membership.

## Practical Resources and Where to Get Help

- **Your Krankenkasse** (TK, AOK, Barmer, DAK, etc.) — for Mutterschaftsgeld applications
