- A public authority has explicitly told you to apply for the "behördliches Führungszeugnis"
- You are applying for a firearms licence or similar regulated activity

**Important:** When applying for Belegart N, you must provide the exact name and address of the receiving authority. Without it, the application will be rejected.

## How to Request a Polizeiliches Führungszeugnis: Step by Step

You have two main options: online or in person at a Bürgeramt. The online route is faster and easier — but only available to people already registered in Germany (with a registered address, or Meldeadresse).

### Option 1 — Online via the Bundesamt für Justiz Portal

1. Go to **www.fuehrungszeugnis.bund.de**
2. Click "Beantragen" (Apply)
3. Log in using your **BundID** account (Germany's digital identity portal) or your **Online-Ausweis** (electronic ID — requires a German residence permit with eID chip or German ID card)
4. Select the type: Belegart O or Belegart N
5. Enter your personal details and, for Belegart N, the authority's address
6. Pay the fee of **€13** by direct debit (SEPA Lastschrift) or credit card
7. Receive the certificate by post within **3–5 business days**

**Practical note:** If you're still in Morocco and haven't registered in Germany yet, the online portal won't work for you. You'll need to apply in person once you arrive and complete your Anmeldung (registration).

### Option 2 — In Person at the Bürgeramt

If you can't use the online option, visit your local Bürgeramt (citizens' service centre). In large cities like Berlin, Munich, Frankfurt, or Cologne, you'll need to book an appointment in advance — sometimes weeks ahead.

**What to bring:**
- Your valid passport or Reiseausweis
- Your German residence permit (Aufenthaltstitel), if you have one
- Your Meldebestätigung (registration confirmation) if you registered recently
- €13 in cash (some Bürgerämter now accept card — check before you go)
- If applying for Belegart N: the name and full postal address of the receiving authority

The clerk will process your application on the spot. The certificate is then mailed to your registered address — not handed to you at the counter.

**Processing time:** Typically 3–7 business days, occasionally longer during busy periods.

## Fees and Validity

- **Standard fee:** €13 for both Belegart O and Belegart N
- **Exemptions:** If you can prove you need the certificate for social welfare applications or voluntary work (Ehrenamt), you may apply for a fee waiver. Bring documentation showing your eligibility.
- **Validity:** There is no official legal expiry date, but most employers and authorities expect a certificate dated within the last **3 months**. Some ask for no older than 6 weeks. Always check what your specific requester accepts.

## How Moroccans Can Obtain the Moroccan Equivalent for Visa Purposes

If you're applying for a German visa from Morocco — for an Ausbildung (vocational training), a work visa, or a Blue Card — the German embassy in Rabat or Casablanca will typically require proof that you have no criminal record in Morocco. The German Führungszeugnis only covers your record in Germany, so you'll need the Moroccan equivalent separately.

### The Casier Judiciaire (Bulletin N°3)

In Morocco, the document equivalent to the Führungszeugnis is the **Casier Judiciaire**, specifically **Bulletin N°3** (the third extract, which is the version issued to private individuals and employers).

**How to obtain it:**
- Visit the **tribunal de première instance** (court of first instance) in your city — Casablanca, Rabat, Marrakech, Fès, etc.
- Or request it online via **www.portail.justice.gov.ma** (available for Moroccan nationals with a CIN)
- Bring your **Carte Nationale d'Identité (CIN)** or passport
- The fee is minimal (usually around **20–30 MAD**)
- Processing time: same day in person, 2–3 days online

**For the German visa application:** The embassy usually requires the Casier Judiciaire to be issued within 3–6 months of your visa appointment and, in many cases, accompanied by a certified translation into German. Confirm the exact requirements with the **Deutsche Botschaft Rabat** (www.rabat.diplo.de) or the relevant consulate in your city.

### Apostille — Do You Need One?

For most standard Ausbildung and employment visa applications, the Casier Judiciaire does not need an apostille. However, if you are applying for a position that requires enhanced background checks (e.g., childcare, healthcare, or teaching), an apostille may be required. You can obtain an apostille from the **Ministère de la Justice** in Morocco.

## Common Pitfalls: What People Get Wrong

- **Requesting the wrong Belegart:** Many people apply for Belegart O when their employer or authority specifically needs Belegart N, or vice versa. Always ask the requester in writing which type they need before you apply.
- **Using an outdated certificate:** A Führungszeugnis issued 5 months ago might be rejected. Check the recency requirement before submitting.
- **Forgetting to register first:** The online portal requires a German Meldeadresse. If you haven't done your Anmeldung yet, you cannot apply online.
- **Not getting the Moroccan record translated:** The German embassy expects documents in German or French. A Casier Judiciaire in Arabic only will often be returned or cause delays.
- **Mixing up Führungszeugnis with Führerschein:** They sound similar. One is your criminal record certificate. The other is your driving licence. Yes, this mix-up really does happen.
- **Paying the wrong fee:** Some third-party websites charge €25–€50 to "help" you apply. The official fee is €13. Always use www.fuehrungszeugnis.bund.de or your local Bürgeramt.

## Conclusion

The Polizeiliches Führungszeugnis is a straightforward document once you understand the system — and knowing how to request it correctly, whether online or in person, and whether you need Belegart O or N, makes the whole process quick and painless. For Moroccans preparing their German visa application, pairing your German criminal record certificate with a fresh Casier Judiciaire from Morocco covers all bases.

If you're still building your application documents — from your CV to your cover letter for an Ausbildung or job — [Book a free consultation to learn German and move to Germany successfully](/cv-builder) and let us guide you through every step of the process.

faqs.question: How much does a Polizeiliches Führungszeugnis cost in Germany?
faqs.answer: The standard fee is €13, whether you apply online at www.fuehrungszeugnis.bund.de or in person at a Bürgeramt. Beware of third-party services charging much more — the official fee is always €13.

faqs.question: What is the difference between Belegart O and Belegart N?
faqs.answer: Belegart O is sent to your home address and you hand it over yourself — used for most private employer and visa requests. Belegart N is sent directly from the Bundesamt für Justiz to a specific German public authority, and you never receive a personal copy. Always confirm which type your requester needs before applying.

faqs.question: Can I apply for a Führungszeugnis online from Morocco before moving to Germany?
faqs.answer: No. The online application portal requires a registered German address (Meldeadresse) and a German digital identity (BundID or eID). If you're still in Morocco, you must apply in person at a Bürgeramt after completing your Anmeldung once you arrive in Germany.

faqs.question: What Moroccan document is equivalent to the German Führungszeugnis for visa purposes?
faqs.answer: The Moroccan equivalent is the Casier Judiciaire, specifically Bulletin N°3. You can obtain it at your local tribunal de première instance or online via portail.justice.gov.ma. The German embassy in Rabat may require a certified German translation, so plan ahead.

faqs.question: How long is a Polizeiliches Führungszeugnis valid?
faqs.answer: There is no fixed legal expiry, but most employers and authorities expect the certificate to be no older than 3 months. Some require it within 6 weeks. Always check the specific requirement of whoever is asking for it before you apply to avoid having to request a new one.

new-steuer-id-germany-explained.title: Steuer-ID Germany How to Get: Your Complete Guide as a Moroccan in Germany
new-steuer-id-germany-explained.summary: Learn what the German Steuer-ID is, how to get your 11-digit tax number, and what to do if it's lost — practical guide for Moroccans in Germany.
new-steuer-id-germany-explained.content:
Moving to Germany and starting a new job is exciting — until your employer asks for your Steuer-ID on day one and you have no idea what they're talking about. The Steueridentifikationsnummer (tax identification number) is an 11-digit code that follows you for your entire life in Germany, and without it, your employer can't pay you correctly. The good news is that getting it is mostly automatic — but only if you know what to do and when.

## What Is the Steuer-ID in Germany?

The **Steueridentifikationsnummer**, often shortened to **Steuer-ID** or **IdNr**, is a permanent, unique 11-digit number assigned to every person who registers their residence (Anmeldung) in Germany. It is issued by the **Bundeszentralamt für Steuern (BZSt)** — the Federal Central Tax Office — and it never changes, even if you move cities, change jobs, or become a German citizen.

Think of it as Germany's equivalent of Morocco's CIN number, but for the tax system. Your employer uses it to report your income to the tax authorities. The health insurance, pension fund, and even your bank may ask for it too.

### Steuer-ID vs. Steuernummer — What's the Difference?

This is one of the most common points of confusion:

- **Steuer-ID (IdNr):** 11 digits. Permanent. Issued to individuals. Stays with you for life.
- **Steuernummer:** 10–13 digits depending on the German state. Assigned by your local *Finanzamt* (tax office). Changes when you move to a different state. Used for filing tax returns.

When your employer asks for your "Steuer-ID," they want the 11-digit IdNr. When you file a tax return online via **ELSTER** (elster.de), you may also need your Steuernummer. Both matter — but they are different documents.

## How the Steuer-ID Arrives Automatically

Here's the part most people don't know: **you don't apply for a Steuer-ID.** It is automatically sent to you by post after you complete your **Anmeldung** (residence registration) at the local Bürgeramt or Einwohnermeldeamt.

The process looks like this:

1. You arrive in Germany and find accommodation (even temporary housing works).
2. You register your address at the **Bürgeramt** — this is the Anmeldung appointment.
3. The BZSt receives your registration data automatically.
4. Within **2–4 weeks**, a letter arrives at your registered address with your 11-digit Steuer-ID printed on it.

That's it. No online form, no trip to the tax office, no fee. The letter comes from *Bundeszentralamt für Steuern* and looks plain — don't throw it away thinking it's junk mail. Many newcomers make exactly this mistake.

### What If You Haven't Registered Yet?

You cannot get a Steuer-ID without an Anmeldung. If you are staying in temporary housing like an Airbnb or hotel, ask the host for a **Wohnungsgeberbestätigung** (landlord confirmation form) — most Bürgerämter accept this for registration. Cities like Berlin, Munich, and Frankfurt all process this the same way.

## When Employers Need It and What Happens Without It

German law requires employers to report salary payments to the tax authority using your Steuer-ID. If you start a job and don't yet have your number, your employer is legally required to withhold income tax at the **highest possible rate (tax class VI — Steuerklasse VI)**, which can mean losing 40–45% of your gross salary until you provide the number.

For example: if your monthly gross salary is **€2,500**, without a Steuer-ID your net pay could drop to around **€1,400** instead of the normal **€1,900–€2,100** for someone in tax class I. That's a significant difference you will eventually get back as a refund, but cash flow matters when you're just getting started.

**Tell your employer immediately** that you've completed your Anmeldung and the letter is on its way. Most HR departments will wait 4–6 weeks before escalating. Once you receive the letter, hand over the number and your correct tax class will be applied from that point forward.

## How to Get Your Steuer-ID If It's Lost or Never Arrived

If your letter never arrived — or you threw it away — don't panic. You have several options:

### Option 1: Request It Online via BZSt

Visit **www.bzst.de** and use the official online form to request your Steuer-ID to be resent. You'll need:
- Your full name (exactly as on your passport)
- Your date of birth
- Your registered German address

The BZSt will mail the number again to your registered address. Allow another **2–4 weeks**.

### Option 2: Check Old Documents

Your Steuer-ID might already appear on:
- Your last German **income tax assessment letter** (Einkommensteuerbescheid)
- Your **payslip** (Lohnabrechnung) — many German payslips print it in the top section
- A letter from your **health insurance** (Krankenkasse)
- Your **pension insurance certificate** from Deutsche Rentenversicherung

### Option 3: Visit the Finanzamt

If you're in a hurry, go to your local **Finanzamt** (tax office) in person with your passport and Anmeldebescheinigung (registration confirmation). They can look up your number directly in the system and tell it to you on the spot, though they still won't print a new letter for you immediately.

### Can You Call the BZSt?

Yes. The BZSt helpline is **+49 228 406-1240**, available Monday to Friday, 08:00–17:00. They will ask you security questions to verify your identity before sharing any data.

## What People Get Wrong About the Steuer-ID

This is where most newcomers lose time or money:

- **Waiting to register.** Every week you delay your Anmeldung is a week without a Steuer-ID arriving. Register as soon as you have any address in Germany — even a sublet room.
- **Confusing Steuer-ID with Steuernummer.** Giving your employer the wrong number causes payroll errors. Double-check: the Steuer-ID is always exactly 11 digits and never starts with 0.
- **Not informing the employer.** If you've registered and told your employer the letter is coming, most HR departments will flag the payroll manually. Silence leads to Steuerklasse VI deductions.
- **Moving without re-registering.** Your Steuer-ID stays the same, but your address on file must always be current. If you move to a new apartment, do a new Anmeldung so future letters reach you.
- **Assuming it works like Morocco's system.** In Morocco, tax IDs are linked to employers or business activities. In Germany, the Steuer-ID is personal and permanent regardless of employment status.

## Using Your Steuer-ID Beyond Employment

Your 11-digit number is useful far beyond getting paid at work:

- **Opening a bank account:** Banks like Deutsche Bank, Commerzbank, N26, and DKB ask for it under EU anti-money-laundering rules.
- **Claiming tax refunds:** When you file a return via ELSTER or through a tax advisor (*Steuerberater*), you'll need it.
- **Child benefit (Kindergeld):** The Familienkasse asks for the Steuer-ID of both parents and each child.
- **Pension contributions:** Deutsche Rentenversicherung links your contributions to this number.
- **Health insurance:** Your Krankenkasse uses it for internal reporting.

Keeping a photo of your Steuer-ID letter on your phone (in a secure app) is a simple habit that saves a lot of headaches.

## Conclusion

Getting your Steuer-ID in Germany is simpler than it sounds — register your address, wait for the letter, and hand the number to your employer. The real risk isn't a complicated process; it's not knowing the steps exist and either delaying your Anmeldung or losing the letter when it arrives. Now you know exactly what to do.

If you're still navigating the paperwork side of moving to Germany — from your application documents to writing your first German CV — **book a free consultation to learn German and move to Germany successfully**. Our team helps Moroccan applicants get every document right from the start. Start with your CV at [/cv-builder](/cv-builder) or get a tailored cover letter at [/anschreiben-generator](/anschreiben-generator).

faqs.question: How long does it take to receive the Steuer-ID after Anmeldung?
faqs.answer: Typically 2–4 weeks. The Bundeszentralamt für Steuern sends it automatically by post to your registered address after your Anmeldung is processed. If it hasn't arrived after 4 weeks, request a reissue via www.bzst.de.

faqs.question: Can I start working in Germany without a Steuer-ID?
faqs.answer: Yes, but your employer must tax you at the maximum rate (Steuerklasse VI) until you provide the number. For a €2,500 gross salary, this can mean losing an extra €400–€500 per month in withholding. You get it back as a refund later, but it's better to register quickly and provide the number as soon as it arrives.

faqs.question: What if I lost my Steuer-ID letter?
faqs.answer: Request a reissue online at www.bzst.de using your name, date of birth, and German address. Alternatively, check your payslips, health insurance documents, or visit your local Finanzamt in person with your passport. You can also call the BZSt helpline at +49 228 406-1240.

faqs.question: Is the Steuer-ID the same as the Steuernummer?
faqs.answer: No. The Steuer-ID is a permanent 11-digit number that never changes, issued to individuals by the BZSt. The Steuernummer is 10–13 digits, assigned by your regional Finanzamt, and changes if you move to a different federal state. Your employer needs the Steuer-ID; your tax return may require the Steuernummer.

faqs.question: Do I need a new Steuer-ID if I move to a different German city?
faqs.answer: No. Your Steuer-ID stays the same for life, no matter how many times you move within Germany. However, you must do a new Anmeldung at your new address so that official correspondence reaches you and the tax office has your correct data on file.

new-lohnsteuerklasse-ausbildung-trainees.title: Lohnsteuerklasse Ausbildung: How to Pick the Right Tax Class as a Trainee in Germany
new-lohnsteuerklasse-ausbildung-trainees.summary: Confused about Lohnsteuerklasse during your Ausbildung? Learn which tax class applies to you, when switching saves real money, and how marriage or kids change things.
new-lohnsteuerklasse-ausbildung-trainees.content:
Starting your Ausbildung in Germany is exciting — but your first payslip can be a shock if you don't understand Lohnsteuerklasse. Most trainees are placed in a default tax class automatically, and many overpay taxes for months simply because they didn't know they could switch. Understanding how Germany's six tax classes work — and which one fits your situation — can put real money back in your pocket every single month.

## What Is a Lohnsteuerklasse and Why Does It Matter for Your Ausbildung?

A **Lohnsteuerklasse** (wage tax class) is a category the German tax system uses to calculate how much income tax is withheld from your salary every month. Your employer deducts this amount automatically before you ever see your money — it's called *Lohnsteuer* (wage tax).

As an Ausbildung trainee, your monthly training allowance (*Ausbildungsvergütung*) typically ranges from **€620 to €1,300**, depending on your sector and state. Even at these amounts, your tax class affects how much you actually take home. Choose the wrong class and you're handing over more than necessary to the Finanzamt (tax office) — sometimes €50–€100 extra per month.

The good news: Germany has a year-end tax return process (*Einkommensteuererklärung*) where you can reclaim overpaid taxes. But why overpay in the first place when you can optimize your class from the start?

## The 6 Steuerklassen Explained

Germany uses six tax classes. Here's a plain-English breakdown:

- **Steuerklasse I** — Single, separated, divorced, or widowed (after the year of death). No children accounted for in the class itself. This is the default for most single trainees.
- **Steuerklasse II** — Single parent raising at least one child who lives with you. You receive the *Entlastungsbetrag für Alleinerziehende* (single-parent relief), worth **€4,260 per year** (as of 2024). If you have a child and live alone with them, this class saves you real money monthly.
- **Steuerklasse III** — Married or in a registered civil partnership, and your spouse earns significantly more than you — or earns nothing. This class has the lowest tax deductions. Commonly paired with Class V for the spouse.
- **Steuerklasse IV** — Married or in a registered civil partnership, both partners earn roughly similar incomes. Both partners get Class IV by default when they marry.
- **Steuerklasse V** — The counterpart to Class III. Higher tax deductions. The lower-earning spouse takes this class when the other has Class III.
- **Steuerklasse VI** — Applied when you have a second job or second Ausbildungsstelle. Highest deductions, no basic allowance (*Grundfreibetrag*) applied. Avoid relying on this class if at all possible.

### The Grundfreibetrag: Your Tax-Free Base

Every person in Germany gets a basic tax-free allowance. In 2024 it stands at **€11,604 per year** (roughly €967/month). If your total annual income stays below this amount, you owe no income tax at all — and you should get back everything withheld via your tax return. Many first-year trainees earning around €700/month fall into this bracket entirely.

## Which Lohnsteuerklasse Applies to Ausbildung Trainees by Default?

When you start your Ausbildung and register with the Einwohnermeldeamt (residents' registration office), your tax class is automatically assigned based on your civil status. Here's what you'll get by default:

- **Single, no children → Steuerklasse I**
- **Single parent → Steuerklasse II** (but you usually have to apply for this proactively at the Finanzamt)
- **Married → Steuerklasse IV / IV** (both partners get Class IV automatically)

For most Moroccan trainees arriving in Germany, the default is **Steuerklasse I**. This is fine if you're single with no children — it applies the standard deductions and you'll likely get a refund at year-end if your income was below the Grundfreibetrag.

Your tax class data is stored digitally in the **ELSTAM system** (Elektronische LohnSteuerAbzugsMerkmale). Your employer retrieves your class automatically using your tax ID (*Steuer-Identifikationsnummer*), which you receive by post a few weeks after registering your address in Germany. If you haven't received it, contact the **Bundeszentralamt für Steuern** (BZSt) at bzst.de.

## How Marriage or Children Change Your Lohnsteuerklasse

### If You Get Married During Your Ausbildung

Getting married changes your default class to **IV/IV**. But if one partner earns significantly more — for instance, your spouse earns €3,000/month from a full-time job while you earn €800/month as a trainee — switching to the **III/V combination** can be smarter.

With III/V:
- The higher-earning spouse gets Class III (lowest deductions, more monthly take-home)
- You as the trainee take Class V (higher deductions)

**Example:** If your spouse earns €3,500/month and you earn €850/month, the III/V split could increase the household's combined monthly net income by €150–€250 compared to IV/IV. However, because Class V withholds more from you, you as the trainee will see less monthly. You balance this out at year-end with a joint tax return.

**Important:** With the III/V combination, filing a joint annual tax return (*gemeinsame Veranlagung*) is **mandatory**. Don't skip it.

### If You Have Children

Having children doesn't automatically change your class — you still start in Class I. But your employer applies the **Kinderfreibetrag** (child tax allowance) to reduce your taxable income. In 2024, the Kinderfreibetrag is **€6,384 per child per year** (combined for both parents).

If you're a single parent, apply at the Finanzamt for **Steuerklasse II** proactively. Bring your child's birth certificate, your rental contract showing you live with the child, and your tax ID. This change puts money in your pocket every month — not just at year-end.

## When Switching Your Steuerklasse Actually Saves Real Money

You can apply to change your Steuerklasse at your local **Finanzamt** (tax office) using the form **"Antrag auf Steuerklassenwechsel bei Ehegatten"** for married couples, or a general tax class change request for other situations. Since 2020, you can also submit changes digitally via **ELSTER** (elster.de) — Germany's official tax portal.

### Scenarios Where Switching Is Worth It

- **Single parent:** Switching from Class I → Class II saves roughly **€30–€80/month** depending on your income. Over a 3-year Ausbildung, that's up to €2,880 extra.
- **Married trainee with higher-earning spouse:** Switching from IV/IV → III/V can optimize monthly cash flow. Run the numbers at **bmf-steuerrechner.de** (the official Federal Ministry of Finance calculator).
- **Two incomes, roughly equal:** Stay in IV/IV or consider the **IV/IV with Faktor method**, which distributes deductions more precisely and avoids a big back-payment at year-end.

### When NOT to Switch

- Don't switch to Class III if both partners earn similar amounts — you'll owe a large tax bill in spring.
- Don't accept Class VI passively for a second job if you only have one employer — contact your Finanzamt if there's a data error.

## What People Get Wrong About Steuerklassen During Ausbildung

This is where most trainees lose money or create headaches:

- **"My class doesn't matter because I'll get it back anyway."** Partially true — but overpaying monthly means you're giving the government an interest-free loan. With trainee wages already tight, that €60/month matters.
- **"I can't change my class mid-year."** Wrong. Since 2020, married couples can switch **as many times as they want** per calendar year. Singles switching to/from Class II can also do this once per year.
- **"I don't need to file a tax return."** If you're in Class I with a single income and no special deductions, filing is optional — but almost always results in a refund. In your first year, you may reclaim several hundred euros if you started mid-year.
- **"My employer handles everything."** Your employer withholds based on whatever class is in the ELSTAM system. If the system shows the wrong class (common after a recent move or marriage), you must correct it at the Finanzamt. Your employer cannot override it.
- **"Class III is always better for the lower earner."** No — Class V has higher deductions. Class III benefits the higher earner. The trainee (lower earner) in a III/V setup takes home less monthly, not more.

## How to Apply for a Steuerklasse Change: Step by Step

1. **Identify your current class** — check your payslip (*Gehaltsabrechnung*). It's listed as "Steuerklasse" or "StKl."
2. **Determine your optimal class** using the scenarios above or the bmf-steuerrechner.de tool.
3. **Download the relevant form** from your local Finanzamt's website or ELSTER.
4. **Submit the form** — in person at the Finanzamt, by post, or digitally via elster.de. Bring your tax ID and, if married, your spouse's tax ID.
5. **Notify your employer** — your employer retrieves updated data from ELSTAM, usually within 1–2 weeks.
6. **File your annual tax return** — especially mandatory for married couples in III/V, and highly recommended for everyone else.

Changes typically take effect the **following month** after approval.

## Conclusion

Getting your Lohnsteuerklasse right during your Ausbildung isn't complicated once you understand the system — but it's easy to ignore until you realize you've overpaid for a year. Whether you're single and defaulting to Class I, a single parent who should be in Class II, or married and weighing III/V versus IV/IV, taking 30 minutes to review your situation can save you hundreds of euros.

If you're still navigating your first steps in Germany — from your residence permit to your Ausbildung application — don't go it alone. **Book a free consultation to learn German and move to Germany successfully**, and get expert help building the documents that make your application stand out, starting with your [CV builder](/cv-builder) or [cover letter generator](/anschreiben-generator).

faqs.question: Which Steuerklasse do most Ausbildung trainees get automatically?
faqs.answer: Most single trainees are automatically assigned Steuerklasse I when they register their address in Germany. This is the default for anyone who is unmarried and has no children. Your employer retrieves this class from the ELSTAM system using your tax ID.

faqs.question: Can I change my Steuerklasse during my Ausbildung, and how?
faqs.answer: Yes. You can apply for a change at your local Finanzamt or digitally via elster.de. Married couples can switch multiple times per year since 2020. Single parents switching to Class II can do so once per year. Changes typically take effect the following month.

faqs.question: Do I need to file a tax return as an Ausbildung trainee in Germany?
faqs.answer: It's not mandatory if you're in Class I with one income, but it's almost always worth doing. If your annual training allowance was below €11,604 (the 2024 Grundfreibetrag), you'll get back everything withheld. Many trainees reclaim €200–€600 per year this way.

faqs.question: What is Steuerklasse II and who qualifies for it during Ausbildung?
faqs.answer: Steuerklasse II is for single parents who live with at least one child. It includes the Entlastungsbetrag für Alleinerziehende — a tax relief of €4,260 per year in 2024. You must apply for it proactively at the Finanzamt with your child's birth certificate and proof of shared residence.

faqs.question: Is the III/V tax class combination a good idea if I'm a trainee and my spouse earns more?
faqs.answer: It can increase your household's combined monthly net income significantly. However, as the lower earner taking Class V, you personally take home less each month. You must also file a joint annual tax return. Run the numbers at bmf-steuerrechner.de before applying to confirm it benefits your specific situation.

new-postident-id-verification-germany.title: Postident ID Verification Germany: What Every Moroccan Applicant Needs to Know
new-postident-id-verification-germany.summary: Learn how Postident ID verification works in Germany, when to use VideoIdent, which documents are accepted, and how to avoid common rejection mistakes.
new-postident-id-verification-germany.content:
Opening a German bank account or signing up for an online service from Morocco — or right after arriving in Germany — almost always hits the same wall: you need to verify your identity first. Postident ID verification is Germany's most widely used system for this, and if you don't know exactly how it works, you can easily waste days on failed attempts. This guide walks you through every step, from choosing the right verification method to which documents actually work for non-EU citizens.

## What Is Postident and Why Does Germany Use It?

Germany has strict anti-money-laundering laws (Geldwäschegesetz) that require banks and many other services to confirm your real identity before letting you open an account or sign a contract remotely. Rather than building their own verification infrastructure, most providers outsource this to Deutsche Post's **Postident** system.

When you apply for a German bank account — say with N26, DKB, or ING — or register for certain government portals, the provider sends you a Postident coupon code or directs you to complete a Postident process. Deutsche Post then acts as a neutral third party, confirms your identity, and reports the result back to the provider.

You are essentially asking a post office clerk (or a video agent) to look at your original documents and confirm you are who you say you are. Simple in theory, but there are several ways it can go wrong — especially for Moroccan nationals with non-EU documents.

## Postident vs. VideoIdent: Which One Should You Choose?

The two main Postident methods are **Postident Classic** (in-person at a Postfiliale) and **Postident Video** (sometimes called VideoIdent, done on your phone or laptop). A third option, **Postident Digital**, uses the eID chip on German ID cards and is not relevant for most Moroccan applicants.

### Postident Classic — In-Person at a Post Office

This is the traditional route. You visit a Deutsche Post branch (Postfiliale), show your original identity document, and the clerk scans your Postident coupon and your document. The process takes about 5 minutes.

**Best for:** People already in Germany, or people who have a valid Moroccan passport and want a reliable, low-tech process.

**What you need:**
- Your Postident coupon (printed or shown on your phone from the provider's email)
- One valid original identity document (see the accepted documents section below)
- No appointment needed at most locations

You can find your nearest Postfiliale at [standorte.deutschepost.de](https://standorte.deutschepost.de). Type in your German city or postal code. In Berlin alone there are over 80 locations; Munich has more than 60.

### VideoIdent — Remote Verification from Anywhere

VideoIdent lets you complete the process from Morocco or from your apartment in Germany using a smartphone or laptop with a camera. A live Deutsche Post agent connects with you via video call and checks your document in real time.

**Best for:** People still in Morocco who need to open a German bank account before arriving, or people with mobility issues.

**What you need:**
- A smartphone or laptop with a working front-facing camera and microphone
- The Postident app (available free on iOS and Android) or a browser link from your provider
- A valid passport — more on document restrictions below
- A stable internet connection (weak WiFi causes the most failures)

**Important:** Not every bank or service offers VideoIdent. DKB, for example, currently only accepts Postident Classic for non-German ID documents. N26 uses its own VideoIdent system through IDnow, not Deutsche Post. Always check which method your specific provider supports before starting.

## Which Documents Are Accepted for Non-EU Citizens?

This is where many Moroccan applicants run into trouble. Germany's identity verification rules distinguish between EU and non-EU documents.

### Documents That Are Generally Accepted

- **Moroccan biometric passport** — accepted at Postfiliale locations and for VideoIdent in most cases. The document must be valid (not expired) and machine-readable (the MRZ strip at the bottom of the photo page must be intact and scannable).
- **German residence permit (Aufenthaltstitel)** — if you already have one, you can use it alongside your passport. Some providers require both.
- **German driving licence** — only valid if issued by a German authority, and not accepted for all providers.

### Documents That Are NOT Accepted

- A Moroccan national ID card (Carte Nationale d'Identité, CIN) — this is **not accepted** for Postident. Germany only accepts EU/EEA national ID cards from their respective countries for this process.
- An expired passport, even if it was valid when you entered Germany.
- Photocopies or digital scans — you must present the physical original document.
- A Moroccan driving licence.

**Practical tip:** If your passport expires in less than 6 months, renew it at the Moroccan consulate in Germany before starting your verification. Some providers reject passports with fewer than 3 months of remaining validity even if they are technically still valid.

## Step-by-Step: Completing Postident Classic at a Postfiliale

1. Receive your Postident coupon from your bank or service provider (usually by email as a PDF, or directly in their app).
2. Find your nearest Postfiliale using the Deutsche Post location finder. Look specifically for branches that show the "Postident" service tag — not all Paketshops or DHL service points offer it.
3. Go to the branch during opening hours. Most Postfiliale locations are open Monday–Friday 09:00–18:00 and Saturday 09:00–13:00.
4. Take a numbered ticket at the counter or join the queue.
5. Hand the clerk your coupon (printed or on-screen) and your original passport.
6. The clerk scans both, asks you to confirm some details, and the process is done. You receive a confirmation slip.
7. Your bank or provider is notified automatically — usually within 1–2 business days, though many providers confirm same-day.

Total cost to you: **€0**. Postident Classic is free for the applicant.

## Step-by-Step: Completing VideoIdent from Morocco

1. Download the **Postident app** from the App Store or Google Play, or click the VideoIdent link sent by your provider.
2. Enter your coupon code when prompted.
3. Grant the app permission to access your camera and microphone.
4. Wait to be connected to a live agent. Wait times are typically 2–10 minutes during business hours (German time, Monday–Friday 08:00–20:00).
5. The agent will ask you to hold your passport up to the camera, tilt it to show the hologram, and turn it to show the back. Follow their instructions carefully.
6. The agent may ask you basic questions to confirm your identity.
7. You receive an on-screen confirmation. Your provider is notified within minutes to a few hours.

**Cost:** Free for the applicant in most cases, though your mobile data usage applies.

## Common Pitfalls: What People Get Wrong

This is where most failed verifications happen. Avoid these mistakes:

- **Going to a Paketshop or DHL Packstation instead of a Postfiliale.** These do not offer Postident services. Only branches explicitly listed as "Postfiliale" or "Postbank Filiale" with the Postident service tag work.
- **Using a Moroccan national ID card (CIN).** As noted above, it is not accepted. Only your biometric passport works.
- **Starting VideoIdent with bad lighting.** The agent cannot read your document if your room is dark or the camera is low quality. Use natural daylight and a recent smartphone.
- **Trying VideoIdent through a VPN.** Deutsche Post's system sometimes rejects connections routed through VPNs. Turn it off before starting.
- **Waiting too long after receiving the coupon.** Postident coupons expire — typically after 60 days but sometimes sooner depending on the provider. Check the expiry date in your coupon email.
- **Assuming N26 uses Deutsche Post Postident.** N26 uses IDnow, a separate system. Searching for a Postfiliale for N26 verification is a common mistake that wastes time.
- **Not having a German address ready.** Most providers that use Postident also require a registered German address (Meldeadresse). If you have not yet done your Anmeldung (city registration), sort that first.

## Which German Banks Actually Use Postident?

Here is a quick reference for 2024:

- **DKB (Deutsche Kreditbank):** Uses Postident Classic. Non-EU passports accepted at the branch. Very popular with Moroccan students and Ausbildung trainees because there are no account fees.
- **Comdirect / Commerzbank:** Uses Postident Classic or VideoIdent.
- **ING Germany:** Offers VideoIdent via Deutsche Post for account opening.
- **Postbank:** Uses Postident Classic at its own branches (Postbank Filialen also serve as Postfilialen for this purpose).
- **N26:** Uses IDnow VideoIdent — not Deutsche Post. Do not look for a Postfiliale for this one.
- **Bunq:** Uses its own in-app verification and does not use Postident.

If you are opening an account specifically to receive your Ausbildung salary or to set up direct debits, DKB is a particularly practical choice because it has no monthly fee and accepts Moroccan passports reliably at Postfiliale branches.

## Conclusion

Postident ID verification in Germany is straightforward once you know which method your provider supports, which documents work as a Moroccan national, and which locations actually offer the service. The single most important thing: always use your biometric Moroccan passport, always go to a proper Postfiliale (not a Paketshop), and double-check whether your bank uses Deutsche Post Postident or a different system like IDnow.

If you are preparing your move to Germany for an Ausbildung or job and need help building a strong CV and cover letter that gets you to the banking and registration stage in the first place, [book a free consultation and use our CV builder](/cv-builder) to start your application the right way.

faqs.question: Can I use my Moroccan national ID card (CIN) for Postident verification?
faqs.answer: No. Deutsche Post's Postident system only accepts EU/EEA national ID cards from their issuing countries. As a Moroccan citizen, you must use your biometric Moroccan passport. Make sure it is not expired and that the MRZ strip on the photo page is undamaged.

faqs.question: Can I complete Postident VideoIdent while still in Morocco before moving to Germany?
faqs.answer: Yes, in most cases. VideoIdent works from anywhere with a stable internet connection and a functioning camera. However, not all banks offer VideoIdent for non-EU documents — DKB, for example, currently requires Postident Classic in person. Check your specific provider's requirements before starting.

faqs.question: How do I find a Postfiliale near me that offers Postident?
faqs.answer: Go to standorte.deutschepost.de, enter your German city or postal code, and filter for "Postident" under the services menu. Look for branches labeled "Postfiliale" — Paketshops and DHL Packstations do not offer this service. In major cities like Frankfurt, Hamburg, or Cologne, there are usually dozens of qualifying branches.

faqs.question: How long does it take to get my identity confirmed after Postident Classic?
faqs.answer: The clerk transmits the data immediately. Most banks and providers receive the confirmation the same day or within 1–2 business days. You usually get an email from your provider once the verification is processed and your account is activated.

faqs.question: Does N26 use Deutsche Post Postident?
faqs.answer: No. N26 uses IDnow, a separate video identification system built into the N26 app. You do not need to visit a Postfiliale for N26. The IDnow process is done entirely in-app with a live video agent, and it accepts Moroccan passports in most cases.

new-niederlassungserlaubnis-pr-after-aus.title: Niederlassungserlaubnis After Ausbildung: Your Fast-Track to Permanent Residency in Germany
new-niederlassungserlaubnis-pr-after-aus.summary: Learn how to get permanent residency in Germany after your Ausbildung — the 2-year fast-track, B1 requirement, pension months, and exact documents needed.
new-niederlassungserlaubnis-pr-after-aus.content:
Getting permanent residency in Germany after completing your Ausbildung is one of the most direct paths available to non-EU nationals — and most people don't realize just how fast it can happen. If you finish your vocational training, land a job in your field, and meet a few concrete requirements, you could hold a Niederlassungserlaubnis (settlement permit) in as little as two years after graduating. This guide breaks down exactly how the fast-track works, what you need to prepare, and the mistakes that derail applications at the last minute.

## What Is a Niederlassungserlaubnis and Why Does It Matter?

A Niederlassungserlaubnis (NE) is Germany's permanent residence permit. Unlike your Aufenthaltserlaubnis (temporary residence permit), it has no expiry date, doesn't need to be renewed every one or two years, and gives you the right to live and work anywhere in Germany in any job you choose. You're also free to travel outside Germany for longer periods without losing your status.

For Moroccans who come to Germany on a vocational training visa, the NE is the logical next step after finishing the Ausbildung. It gives you security — you're no longer dependent on your employer for your residence status, and you can change jobs, move cities, or take career risks without worrying about your permit.

## The Two-Year Fast-Track: Who Qualifies?

The legal basis for the fast-track Niederlassungserlaubnis after Ausbildung is **§ 18b Abs. 1 AufenthG** (Residence Act). Under this paragraph, you can apply for permanent residency after just **two years of employment** following your Ausbildung — instead of the standard five years required under the general rule (§ 9 AufenthG).

To qualify under this fast-track, you must meet **all** of the following:

- You completed a state-recognised vocational training (Berufsausbildung) or a university degree in Germany
- You have been employed in a job related to your qualification for at least **24 months** since completing your training
- You hold a valid Aufenthaltserlaubnis for skilled employment purposes (issued under §§ 18a or 18b AufenthG)
- Your livelihood is secure — meaning your income covers your living costs without relying on social benefits
- You have paid into the **German statutory pension insurance (Rentenversicherung) for at least 24 months**
- You meet the **German language requirement at B1 level**
- You have not been convicted of a criminal offence

One important clarification: the 24 months of employment and 24 months of Rentenversicherung contributions essentially run at the same time if you're working full-time in a qualified position. You don't need to accumulate them separately.

### What Counts as "Related Employment"?

The job doesn't have to be an exact match to your training title. If you trained as a Kaufmann/-frau für Büromanagement (office management specialist) and then work as a project coordinator, that's generally accepted. What doesn't work: completing an Ausbildung as an Elektroniker and then working full-time in a supermarket. The connection between your qualification and your job must be defensible. When in doubt, ask your Ausländerbehörde in advance or get a written confirmation from your employer describing how your role relates to your training.

## The B1 Language Requirement: What You Actually Need

The language requirement for the Niederlassungserlaubnis after Ausbildung is **German at B1 level** — not B2, not C1. This is lower than what many people expect, and it's good news because you've likely already reached B1 during your Ausbildung itself.

Accepted proof of B1 includes:

- **Goethe-Institut B1 certificate** (Goethe-Zertifikat B1)
- **telc Deutsch B1 certificate**
- **ÖSD Zertifikat B1**
- **German secondary school diploma** (not typically applicable for Moroccans in this process)
- **Successfully completing an Ausbildung conducted in German** — in some Ausländerbehörden, this alone is accepted as evidence of B1

That last point is worth emphasising. Many Ausländerbehörden in cities like Munich, Frankfurt, and Hamburg accept the Ausbildungszeugnis (training certificate) or Berufsschulzeugnis as indirect proof of B1. However, this is not universal. In some cities — particularly smaller ones — they will explicitly ask for a formal language certificate. The safest approach is to have a recognised B1 certificate ready regardless. Exams cost between **€150 and €230** depending on the provider and city.

If you took a B1 exam during your Ausbildung and passed, keep that certificate somewhere safe. You will need it at the Ausländerbehörde.

## Rentenversicherung Months: How to Check and What to Submit

The requirement for **24 months of statutory pension insurance contributions** (Rentenversicherung) is one that trips people up — not because it's hard to meet, but because applicants don't have the right paperwork.

Your Rentenversicherung record is maintained by the **Deutsche Rentenversicherung (DRV)**. Here's how to get your documentation:

1. Go to **www.deutsche-rentenversicherung.de**
2. Create an online account (you'll need your Sozialversicherungsnummer, which is on your payslips)
3. Download your **Rentenauskunft** or request a **Versicherungsverlauf** (insurance history statement)
4. Alternatively, visit your nearest DRV regional office in person — free of charge

The Versicherungsverlauf shows every month during which contributions were made and by whom. When you apply for the NE, bring a printed copy. Some Ausländerbehörden will accept payslips as secondary evidence, but the official DRV statement is always cleaner.

Note: months during your Ausbildung itself also count toward your Rentenversicherung total if your employer was making contributions — which they are legally required to do. So if your Ausbildung lasted three years and you moved straight into employment, you likely already have 36+ months of contributions before you even reach the two-year employment threshold.

## Full Document Checklist for Your Application

When you go to the Ausländerbehörde, bring originals and copies of everything. Missing one document means a wasted appointment — and in cities like Berlin or Cologne, getting a new appointment can take months.

**Required documents (standard):**

- Valid passport (with at least 6 months remaining validity)
- Current Aufenthaltserlaubnis
- Biometric passport photo (35mm × 45mm format, recent)
- Completed application form (available on your city's Ausländerbehörde website or at the office)
- Employment contract and current payslips (last 3 months)
- Employer confirmation letter describing your role and its relation to your qualification
- Ausbildungszeugnis (training completion certificate) and Abschlusszeugnis der Berufsschule
- **Versicherungsverlauf** from Deutsche Rentenversicherung
- Proof of B1 German language level (certificate or Ausbildungszeugnis)
- Proof of accommodation (rental contract or Wohnungsgeberbestätigung)
- Proof of health insurance (current insurance card or confirmation from Krankenkasse)
- No criminal record — this is checked automatically via the Bundeszentralregister; you don't need to provide this yourself in most cases

**Optional but useful:**

- Income tax assessment (Einkommensteuerbescheid) from the last year
- Confirmation from employer that you're employed indefinitely (unbefristet) or at least for the foreseeable future

The application fee is **€113** as of 2024.

## Timing Your Application: When to Apply

Don't wait until the last day your current Aufenthaltserlaubnis is valid. Apply **3 to 4 months before** it expires. This gives the Ausländerbehörde time to process your application, and while it's being processed, your current permit is automatically extended by law (Fiktionsbescheinigung).

In practice:

- Check your current permit's expiry date
- Count back 3–4 months
- Book an appointment at your local Ausländerbehörde as soon as possible (in large cities, book 4–6 months in advance if possible)
- Gather all documents in the weeks before the appointment

If you're in Berlin, use the **Berlin.de service portal** to book. In Munich, it's the **KVR online appointment system (muenchen.de)**. In Frankfurt, appointments are via **frankfurt.de/buergeramt**.

## What People Get Wrong About Niederlassungserlaubnis After Ausbildung

**Assuming the job doesn't need to match the Ausbildung.** Some applicants change careers completely after training and are surprised when the Ausländerbehörde questions the connection. Always verify with your local office before switching fields.

**Not having a B1 certificate ready.** Even if your Ausländerbehörde sometimes accepts the Ausbildungszeugnis as proof of language level, yours might not. Don't gamble on this — get the certificate.

**Forgetting to request the Rentenversicherung statement in advance.** The DRV can take 2–3 weeks to send the Versicherungsverlauf by post if you request it that way. Use the online portal, or visit in person if you're short on time.

**Applying too late.** If your Aufenthaltserlaubnis expires before you apply, you enter a legal grey zone. Your stay isn't automatically illegal (there's a 3-month tolerance period under § 81 AufenthG), but it creates unnecessary stress and documentation headaches.

**Miscounting the 24 months of employment.** The clock starts from the date you took up employment after your Ausbildung — not from the date you graduated. If you took 3 months off between finishing training and starting work, those months don't count.

## Conclusion: Your Path to a Secure Future in Germany

The Niederlassungserlaubnis after Ausbildung fast-track is one of the most accessible routes to permanent residency in Germany for non-EU nationals. Two years of qualified employment, 24 months of Rentenversicherung contributions, a B1 certificate, and the right paperwork — that's genuinely all it takes. The process is bureaucratic, but it's manageable if you plan ahead and gather your documents systematically.

Start preparing early, book your Ausländerbehörde appointment well in advance, and don't leave language certification to the last minute. Germany rewards those who do their Ausbildung properly and commit to staying — the permanent residency fast-track is proof of that.

Want help preparing your documents, writing a professional cover letter, or building a CV that supports your next career step? [Book a free consultation and use our CV builder](/cv-builder) to move forward with confidence.

faqs.question: Can I apply for Niederlassungserlaubnis after Ausbildung if I change employers during the two years?
faqs.answer: Yes. Changing employers is allowed as long as you stay in employment related to your qualification throughout the 24-month period. The Ausländerbehörde looks at the total duration and relevance of your employment, not whether it was with one employer.

faqs.question: Does the Ausbildung period itself count toward the 24 months of employment required for the fast-track?
faqs.answer: No. The 24 months of qualified employment starts after you complete your Ausbildung and begin working as a skilled employee. However, Rentenversicherung contributions made during your Ausbildung do count toward the 24-month pension contribution requirement.

faqs.question: What happens if my B1 certificate is from before my Ausbildung — is it still valid for the NE application?
faqs.answer: Generally yes, there is no expiry date on Goethe-Institut, telc, or ÖSD language certificates. As long as you have a recognised B1 certificate, the date it was issued is not typically an issue. Bring the original to your appointment.

faqs.question: How long does it take for the Ausländerbehörde to process a Niederlassungserlaubnis application?
faqs.answer: Processing times vary significantly by city. In smaller cities it can be 4–8 weeks. In larger cities like Berlin or Munich it can take 3–6 months. Book your appointment early and apply well before your current permit expires to avoid gaps.

faqs.question: Can my spouse or children also get a Niederlassungserlaubnis once I receive mine?
faqs.answer: Yes. Once you hold a Niederlassungserlaubnis, your spouse and minor children who are legally resident in Germany can apply for their own NE under family reunification rules (§ 9a AufenthG), provided they meet basic requirements like a sufficient command of German and financial independence.

new-change-address-ummeldung-germany.title: Ummeldung Change Address Germany: The Complete Guide for Moroccan Newcomers
new-change-address-ummeldung-germany.summary: Learn how to complete your Ummeldung (change address) in Germany, what documents you need, the 14-day deadline, and how it updates your taxes, car, and bank.
new-change-address-ummeldung-germany.content:
Moving to a new flat in Germany comes with more than just unpacking boxes — it comes with a legal obligation most newcomers don't know about until they're already late. The Ummeldung (address registration change) is one of Germany's most important bureaucratic rituals, and missing the deadline can cost you real money. Whether you're moving across the street or from Munich to Hamburg, this guide walks you through every step, every document, and every downstream effect on your life in Germany.

## What Is Ummeldung and Why Does It Matter in Germany?

The German registration system — called the **Melderegister** — is the backbone of almost every official process in the country. When you first arrived in Germany, you did an **Anmeldung** (initial registration). Every time you move to a new address afterward, you must do an **Ummeldung** — registering your new address with the local registration office (*Einwohnermeldeamt* or *Bürgeramt*).

This isn't optional. Under the **Bundesmeldegesetz (BMG)** — Germany's Federal Registration Act — every person living in Germany must register their current address within **14 days** of moving in. It doesn't matter if you're a German citizen, an EU national, or a Moroccan resident with a visa or permanent residence permit. The rule applies to everyone.

Why does it matter so much? Because your registered address in the Melderegister flows into almost everything: your tax file number, your health insurance records, your driver's license, your car registration, your bank account, and your ARD/ZDF broadcasting fee (known as the **Rundfunkbeitrag** or formerly GEZ). If your address is wrong, payments get lost, official letters go to the wrong place, and in the worst case, you miss critical deadlines from the immigration office (*Ausländerbehörde*).

## The Wohnungsgeberbestätigung: The Document Your Landlord Must Give You

Before you can do anything, you need one critical piece of paper: the **Wohnungsgeberbestätigung** (landlord confirmation of residence). This is a written confirmation from your landlord — or the person who is legally allowed to let you live in the property — confirming that you have moved into their flat on a specific date.

### What it must contain

The Wohnungsgeberbestätigung is not a free-form letter. It must include:

- Full name and address of the landlord (the *Wohnungsgeber*)
- The complete address of the flat (street, number, postal code, city)
- The exact move-in date
- The full name(s) of all people moving in
- The landlord's signature

Many German landlords provide a standard template. You can also download official templates from your city's Bürgeramt website — for example, the **Munich city portal (muenchen.de)**, **Hamburg's service portal (hamburg.de)**, or **Berlin's Bürgeramt (berlin.de)** all offer free downloadable PDF forms.

### What if your landlord refuses?

This is a real problem, especially in shared flats (*Wohngemeinschaften*, or WGs). Under the BMG, the landlord is legally **obligated** to provide this document within two weeks of you moving in. If they refuse without a valid reason, you can report this to the registration office, and the landlord can be fined up to **€1,000**.

If you're in a sublet situation (e.g., renting from another tenant who is the main tenant), the main tenant acts as your *Wohnungsgeber* and must sign the confirmation.

## Step-by-Step: How to Do Your Ummeldung

Once you have your Wohnungsgeberbestätigung, the process is straightforward.

### Step 1: Book an appointment

Most German cities require you to book a slot at the Bürgeramt online. Appointments can fill up fast — especially in Berlin, Hamburg, and Munich. Book as soon as you know your move-in date. Search "[your city] Bürgeramt Termin online" or go directly to your city's official portal.

In smaller cities like **Erfurt**, **Freiburg**, or **Augsburg**, you can often walk in without an appointment during open office hours (*offene Sprechstunden*).

### Step 2: Gather your documents

Bring the following to your appointment:

- **Wohnungsgeberbestätigung** (completed and signed by your landlord)
- **Your current passport** (and for non-EU nationals, your residence permit card)
- **Completed Anmeldeformular** (the registration form) — most offices have these at the counter, but you can also fill it in advance from your city's website
- If you are registering a spouse or children: their passports and any relevant documents

### Step 3: Attend the appointment and receive your Meldebestätigung

The appointment itself takes about 10–15 minutes. The officer will verify your documents and update the register. At the end, they hand you a **Meldebestätigung** — a small printed confirmation of your new registered address. Keep this document safe. You will need it for banks, insurance companies, and many other institutions.

### Step 4: What it costs

The Ummeldung itself is **free** in almost all German cities. There is no fee for registering a change of address.

## The 14-Day Deadline: What Happens If You Miss It?

You have **14 days** from your official move-in date to complete the Ummeldung. If you move in on the 1st of the month, you must register by the 15th.

Missing this deadline is an administrative offence (*Ordnungswidrigkeit*). The fine varies by city, but typically ranges from **€20 to €500**, depending on how late you are and whether the office considers it a repeated offence. In practice, first-time offenders who are only a few days late rarely receive a fine — but this is not guaranteed. Don't count on leniency.

One important tip: if you book a Bürgeramt appointment within the 14-day window but the earliest available slot is later (which happens often in Berlin), keep the booking confirmation as evidence that you tried to comply in time.

## How Ummeldung Cascades: Taxes, Car, GEZ, Banks

Your new address in the Melderegister doesn't automatically update everywhere. Here's what you need to update manually — and how your Ummeldung helps you do it.

### Tax office (Finanzamt)

Your Finanzamt is determined by your address. When you move, your tax case is transferred to the Finanzamt in your new district. You should inform your current Finanzamt of your new address in writing or via **ELSTER** (the German tax portal at elster.de). Your tax ID number (*Steueridentifikationsnummer*) stays the same — it's linked to you for life, not to your address.

### Car registration (*Kfz-Zulassung*)

If you own a car registered in Germany, you must update your vehicle registration documents (*Fahrzeugschein*) within **one year** of moving. You do this at the local **Kfz-Zulassungsstelle**. Some cities, like Hamburg, allow online address updates via i-Kfz (internet-based car registration). If your new city has a different area code for licence plates, you may receive new plates — cost: around **€30–€50** for admin fees plus plate manufacturing.

### Rundfunkbeitrag (formerly GEZ)

Every German household pays **€18.36 per month** in broadcasting fees. You need to notify the ARD ZDF Deutschlandradio contribution service at **rundfunkbeitrag.de** of your new address. You can do this online in under five minutes using your contribution number (*Beitragsnummer*). If you were sharing a contribution with a flatmate and now have your own flat, you need to register a new account.

### Banks and health insurance

Banks in Germany are required by law to have your current address on file. Contact your bank (e.g., Deutsche Bank, Commerzbank, N26, DKB) directly — most allow address changes via their online banking portal or app. Your health insurance provider (*Krankenkasse*), such as TK (Techniker Krankenkasse) or AOK, must also be notified separately, usually via their member portal or a written form.

## What People Get Wrong About the Ummeldung

This is where many newcomers — and even long-term residents — trip up:

- **Waiting for the landlord to remind you.** They won't. It's your legal responsibility, not theirs.
- **Thinking the old Anmeldung still counts.** It doesn't. Every move requires a new registration.
- **Not updating banks and insurance after Ummeldung.** The Bürgeramt does not automatically notify your bank, health insurer, or employer. You must do this yourself.
- **Assuming subtenants don't need to register.** They absolutely do. Even if you're staying for just a few months in a shared flat, you must register if you live there.
- **Forgetting to update immigration documents.** If you have a residence permit tied to a specific city's *Ausländerbehörde*, moving to a new city means transferring your file to the new local authority. Failure to do this can cause serious complications with your visa renewal.
- **Not getting the Meldebestätigung.** Some people walk out without asking for this confirmation slip. Always ask — you'll need it immediately for opening bank accounts or signing up for services.

## Conclusion

The Ummeldung is one of those tasks that sounds trivial but has real consequences if you ignore it. With the right preparation — getting your Wohnungsgeberbestätigung from your landlord, booking your Bürgeramt appointment early, and understanding what to update after — you can get it done smoothly within your 14-day window. Once your address is registered correctly, everything else in German bureaucracy becomes easier: your taxes align, your bank stays happy, and the *Ausländerbehörde* knows where to find you.

If you're still in the process of planning your move to Germany and need help preparing your application documents, [build a professional German-style CV](/cv-builder) or [generate a tailored cover letter](/anschreiben-generator) to give your Ausbildung search the best possible start. Book a free consultation to learn German and move to Germany successfully.

faqs.question: How long do I have to complete my Ummeldung after moving to a new flat in Germany?
faqs.answer: You have exactly 14 days from your official move-in date. Missing this deadline is a legal offence and can result in a fine of up to €500, depending on the city and how late you register.

faqs.question: What is the Wohnungsgeberbestätigung and who provides it?
faqs.answer: It's a written confirmation from your landlord (or main tenant, in a sublet) proving that you have moved into the property. It must include your name, the property address, the move-in date, and the landlord's signature. Your landlord is legally required to provide it — and can be fined up to €1,000 if they refuse.

faqs.question: Does my bank automatically get updated when I do my Ummeldung?
faqs.answer: No. The Bürgeramt only updates the official Melderegister. You must separately notify your bank, health insurance provider, employer, the Rundfunkbeitrag service, and your Finanzamt. Most banks allow address updates through their online banking app.

faqs.question: I live in a shared flat (WG) — do I still need to do an Ummeldung?
faqs.answer: Yes, absolutely. Every person living in a flat in Germany must register their address, regardless of whether it's a WG, a sublet, or a private flat. The main tenant or landlord acts as your Wohnungsgeber and must sign the confirmation form.

faqs.question: Does the Ummeldung affect my residence permit if I move to a different city?
faqs.answer: Yes, significantly. Your residence permit (*Aufenthaltstitel*) is tied to the local Ausländerbehörde that issued it. If you move to a new city, you must transfer your case to the new city's Ausländerbehörde. Failing to do this can cause problems when you next need to renew your permit. Always inform both the old and new Ausländerbehörde of your move.

new-family-reunification-visa-morocco-ge.title: Family Reunification Visa Morocco Germany: How to Bring Your Spouse Without Delays
new-family-reunification-visa-morocco-ge.summary: Learn exactly how to get a family reunification visa from Morocco to Germany — A1 German test, income proof, apartment rules, and Casablanca consulate tips.
new-family-reunification-visa-morocco-ge.content:
Bringing your spouse or family member from Morocco to Germany is one of the most emotionally charged bureaucratic processes you will ever navigate — and one of the most misunderstood. The family reunification visa (Familiennachzug) has strict legal requirements that catch thousands of applicants off guard every year, turning a joyful reunion into months of frustrating back-and-forth. If you understand the rules before you start, you can avoid the most common delays and get your family together faster.

## What Is the Family Reunification Visa (Familiennachzug)?

The Familiennachzug is a German residence permit category that allows the foreign-national spouse, registered partner, or minor child of a person living legally in Germany to join them. It is regulated primarily under §§ 27–36 of the German Residence Act (Aufenthaltsgesetz).

There are two main scenarios depending on who is already in Germany:

- **German citizen sponsor**: Your spouse applies under § 28 AufenthG. The rules are slightly more relaxed — no minimum income threshold applies in the same strict way.
- **Non-EU foreign national sponsor** (e.g., a Moroccan with a German work or Ausbildung residence permit): The application falls under § 30 AufenthG, which has tighter requirements including a minimum income rule and a valid residence permit of at least one year.

Most Moroccan families dealing with this process fall into the second category — one partner has moved to Germany for an Ausbildung, a job, or a Blue Card, and they want to bring their spouse over. This article focuses on that scenario.

## The A1 German Language Requirement: What You Actually Need

This is the rule that surprises people the most. Before your spouse can even submit their visa application at the German consulate in Casablanca, they must prove basic German language skills at the **A1 level** according to the Common European Framework of Reference (CEFR).

### Which certificate is accepted?

Germany accepts certificates from officially recognized testing institutions. The main options available in Morocco are:

- **Goethe-Institut Morocco** (offices in Casablanca and Rabat) — Goethe-Zertifikat A1: Start Deutsch 1
- **telc GmbH** — telc Deutsch A1
- **ÖSD** (Österreichisches Sprachdiplom) — available at some authorized centers

The Goethe-Institut in Casablanca is the most straightforward choice. Registration opens online at **goethe.de**, exam fees are approximately **€130–€160**, and exam slots fill up fast — book 6–8 weeks in advance.

### Who is exempt from the A1 requirement?

There are legal exemptions under § 30 Abs. 1 Satz 3 AufenthG:

- Your spouse holds a university degree that qualifies them for a German Blue Card
- Your spouse can demonstrate they are unable to reach A1 level due to a physical or mental disability
- The sponsor holds a settlement permit (Niederlassungserlaubnis) and has been living in Germany for at least three years
- Other exceptional hardship cases

If none of these apply, the A1 certificate is mandatory. Period.

## Income Proof: The Numbers You Need to Hit

The German immigration authorities want to know that you can financially support your spouse without relying on public benefits (Sozialleistungen). This means the sponsor — the person already in Germany — must demonstrate sufficient income.

### What counts as "sufficient"?

The general rule of thumb used by most Ausländerbehörden (local immigration offices) is:

- Your **net income must cover** your own living expenses plus those of your spouse after deducting rent
- A widely used benchmark: at least **€1,200–€1,400 net per month** remaining after rent for a couple with no children in most German cities
- In high-cost cities like Munich or Frankfurt, this threshold is interpreted more strictly

**Practical example**: If you earn €2,100 net per month in Nuremberg and your rent is €750, you have €1,350 remaining — that typically passes the check. If your rent is €1,100, you may fall short and need additional documentation.

### What documents prove income?

Prepare these for your sponsor in Germany:

- Last 3 months of payslips (Gehaltsabrechnungen)
- Employment contract (unbefristet = unlimited preferred; Ausbildungsvertrag is accepted too)
- Last tax assessment (Steuerbescheid) if available
- Bank statements showing regular income deposits

If you are still in Ausbildung earning roughly €800–€1,100/month, income requirements can be harder to meet. In that case, consult an immigration lawyer — some Ausländerbehörden in smaller cities have more flexibility.

## The Apartment Size Rule: Do You Have Enough Space?

Germany requires that the shared apartment meets the **adequate housing standard** (angemessener Wohnraum). This does not mean you need a luxury flat, but there are real minimums.

A common standard applied across Germany:

- **12 m² of living space per additional person** beyond the first occupant
- Some Ausländerbehörden cite a minimum of **45–50 m²** total for a couple

**Real example**: You are renting a 35 m² studio in Cologne. That is unlikely to pass the housing check for a couple. A 55 m² one-bedroom apartment for €900/month in Leipzig, however, would comfortably qualify.

You will need to provide your current **rental contract (Mietvertrag)** listing the apartment's total size in square meters. Make sure the apartment size is explicitly stated — older contracts sometimes omit this detail.

## The Casablanca Consulate: Step-by-Step Application Process

The German Consulate General in Casablanca handles visa applications for most of Morocco (Rabat handles the north). Here is how the process works in practice.

### Step 1: Book an appointment

Appointments are made online through the **AIS system** (Auswärtiges Amt appointment portal) at **service2.diplo.de**. Casablanca slots are notoriously scarce — check early in the morning and be persistent. Waiting times for an appointment can range from **4 to 12 weeks** depending on the season.

### Step 2: Compile your document checklist

- Valid Moroccan passport (at least 6 months validity beyond the planned stay)
- Completed and signed visa application form (download from the Casablanca consulate website)
- Two biometric passport photos
- Proof of civil status: marriage certificate (acte de mariage), apostilled and translated into German by a certified translator
- A1 German language certificate (original)
- Proof of sponsor's legal residence in Germany: residence permit copy (Aufenthaltstitel)
- Proof of sponsor's income: payslips, employment contract
- Rental contract showing apartment size
- Health insurance confirmation (the spouse will be enrolled once in Germany, but some consulates ask for evidence)
- Visa fee: **€75** (non-refundable)

### Step 3: Attend the interview

The consulate may ask your spouse basic questions about the relationship, where you met, your daily life, etc. This is standard and not adversarial — just prepare your spouse to speak honestly and calmly.

### Step 4: Wait for processing

Processing time at the Casablanca consulate is typically **6–12 weeks** after the appointment, though it can stretch to 4–5 months in complex cases. The consulate may request additional documents (Nachforderung) via email — respond immediately and completely to avoid further delays.

### Step 5: After arrival in Germany

Within 14 days of arrival, your spouse must register their address (Anmeldung) at the local Einwohnermeldeamt. Then apply for the actual residence permit at your Ausländerbehörde. Bring all original documents from the consulate process.

## What People Get Wrong: Common Pitfalls

- **Starting the A1 preparation too late**: Exam slots in Casablanca fill up months in advance. If your spouse starts studying now, they may still be 3–4 months away from being exam-ready. Start immediately.

- **Submitting uncertified translations**: Your marriage certificate must be translated by a **sworn (beeidigter) translator** recognized in Germany. A bilingual friend's translation will be rejected.

- **Not checking the apostille requirement**: Moroccan documents often need an apostille from the Moroccan Ministry of Foreign Affairs before the German consulate will accept them. Build this into your timeline — it can take 2–4 weeks.

- **Ignoring the Ausländerbehörde in Germany**: Some applicants focus entirely on the consulate and forget that the sponsor must also prepare documentation at their local immigration office in Germany first. The Casablanca consulate will communicate with your Ausländerbehörde.

- **Using a tourist visa as a shortcut**: Some couples try to get the spouse in on a tourist visa and then apply for residency from inside Germany. This is legally risky and can result in refusal and deportation. Always use the correct visa category from the start.

- **Underestimating processing time**: If you are targeting a start date — for example, your spouse wants to arrive before a baby is born or before a job starts — apply at least **6 months before that date**.

## Conclusion: Get Your Family to Germany Without the Headaches

The family reunification visa from Morocco to Germany is absolutely achievable, but it requires preparation well in advance — ideally 9–12 months before your target reunion date. Nail the A1 certificate, get your income and housing documents in order, and respect the consulate process in Casablanca.

If you are unsure about your specific situation — especially if you are in Ausbildung, have an unusual residence permit type, or your spouse has special circumstances — professional guidance makes a real difference. Book a free consultation to learn German and move to Germany successfully, and explore our tools at [/cv-builder](/cv-builder) to also prepare your professional documents for a strong start in Germany.

faqs.question: Does my spouse have to pass the A1 German test before applying for the family reunification visa in Morocco?
faqs.answer: Yes, in most cases. If you are a non-EU foreign national living in Germany (e.g., on an Ausbildung or work permit), your spouse must present a valid A1 German certificate — such as the Goethe-Zertifikat A1 — at the Casablanca consulate appointment. Without it, the visa will be refused. Exemptions exist for Blue Card holders' spouses and certain hardship cases.

faqs.question: How long does the family reunification visa process take from Morocco to Germany?
faqs.answer: From start to finish, expect 6–12 months in a best-case scenario. Getting an appointment at the Casablanca consulate can take 4–12 weeks, consulate processing takes another 6–12 weeks, and preparing documents (A1 exam, apostilles, certified translations) adds more time. Start the process at least 9 months before your target arrival date.

faqs.question: What is the minimum income I need to earn in Germany to sponsor my Moroccan spouse?
faqs.answer: There is no single fixed number, but most Ausländerbehörden want to see that your net income covers living costs for two people after rent. A practical benchmark is roughly €1,200–€1,400 net remaining after rent. If you earn €2,000 net and pay €700 rent, you have €1,300 left — that generally passes. Ausbildung trainees earning €900/month may face difficulties and should consult an immigration lawyer.

faqs.question: Does the apartment I rent in Germany need to meet a minimum size for the family reunification visa?
faqs.answer: Yes. Most German immigration offices require at least 12 m² of living space per additional person, with a practical minimum of around 45–50 m² total for a couple. You must submit your rental contract (Mietvertrag) showing the apartment size. A 35 m² studio is unlikely to qualify; a 55 m² one-bedroom apartment typically will.

faqs.question: Can my Moroccan spouse apply for the family reunification visa if I am still doing an Ausbildung in Germany?
faqs.answer: Yes, it is possible, but more challenging. An Ausbildung contract is an accepted form of employment, but the income (typically €800–€1,100/month) may not meet the financial sufficiency threshold on its own.
