- **[Eltern stärken](https://www.elternstaerken.de)** — A national program offering parenting and school support in Arabic and other languages.
- **[Make it in Germany](https://www.make-it-in-germany.com)** — The federal government's official portal for immigrants, with a section dedicated to education.
- **Local mosques and cultural associations** — In cities like Cologne, Frankfurt, Berlin, and Munich, Moroccan community groups often run informal tutoring and mentoring for children.

### Private Tutoring Costs

If your child needs extra help after school, private tutoring (Nachhilfe) in Germany typically costs **€15–€40 per hour**, depending on the city and subject. Platforms like [Schülerhilfe](https://www.schuelerhilfe.de) or [Nachhilfevermittlung.de](https://www.nachhilfevermittlung.de) let you find tutors near you.

## The Path to Abitur for Foreign Children

Getting your child to the Abitur — Germany's university-entrance qualification — is absolutely possible, even if they arrive with no German. Thousands of children from Morocco, Syria, Afghanistan, and other countries have done it. But it takes planning.

A realistic timeline for a child who arrives at age 10 with no German:

- **Year 1:** Willkommensklasse, intense German acquisition.
- **Year 2:** Enters regular Gymnasium or Gesamtschule from Grade 5 or 6.
- **Years 3–8:** Regular school pathway.
- **Abitur exam:** Around age 18–19.

Children who arrive older — say, at 14 or 15 — face a tighter window. In this case, a **Gesamtschule** is usually the most practical option because it allows more time and flexibility. Some states also offer **Abendgymnasium** (evening Gymnasium) for older students who want to earn the Abitur while working.

The Abitur opens the door to German universities, where tuition at public institutions is mostly free or very low (€150–€350 per semester in student fees).

## What People Get Wrong About the German School System

Many Moroccan families make avoidable mistakes in the first weeks. Here is what to watch out for:

- **Waiting too long to enroll:** School is compulsory. Delays can create legal issues and social problems for your child. Enroll within the first two to four weeks of arrival.
- **Assuming the school will automatically place the child in the right track:** You can and should advocate for your child. If a school recommends Hauptschule but your child is academically strong, ask about Gesamtschule or Gymnasium with DaZ support.
- **Underestimating the power of Gesamtschule:** Many families fixate on Gymnasium from day one. Gesamtschule is often a smarter entry point for foreign children because it allows track changes based on performance.
- **Not getting documents translated:** Schools may not be able to formally assess your child's academic history without translated records. Spend the €50–€100 on a certified translation early.
- **Assuming German schools teach English the same way Moroccan schools do:** The curriculum will be different. Your child may need to restart certain subjects from scratch, especially math notation and science terminology.
- **Ignoring the Willkommensklasse phase:** Some parents worry their child is "falling behind" in a welcome class. In reality, this phase is critical — children who go through it integrate far more successfully.

## Conclusion

The German school system for foreign children has a clear structure once you understand it. From the Willkommensklasse to Grundschule and all the way to Abitur, there is a real pathway — and genuine support along the way. The key is to act quickly after arrival, know which documents you need, and advocate confidently for your child's placement.

If you are still preparing your move to Germany and want to make sure your family's transition goes smoothly — from your own job application to your children's schooling — book a free consultation to learn German and move to Germany successfully. Our team can help you build a strong CV and cover letter at [/cv-builder](/cv-builder) so you hit the ground running from day one.

faqs.question: At what age do children start school in Germany?
faqs.answer: Children in Germany start Grundschule (primary school) at age 6. School attendance is compulsory from that point. If your child is already older when you arrive, they will be placed in the grade matching their age.

faqs.question: What is a Willkommensklasse and how long does my child stay in one?
faqs.answer: A Willkommensklasse is an intensive German-language class for newly arrived children who do not yet speak German. Most children spend 6 to 18 months in one before joining a regular class full-time. The exact duration depends on language progress and the school's policy.

faqs.question: Can a foreign child in Germany still reach Gymnasium and get the Abitur?
faqs.answer: Yes, absolutely. Many children who arrive with no German go on to complete the Abitur, especially if they enter the system by age 10–12. Children arriving older can use Gesamtschule or Abendgymnasium as flexible pathways to the Abitur.

faqs.question: What documents do I need to enroll my child in a German school?
faqs.answer: You need your child's birth certificate, previous school reports (ideally with a certified German translation), a passport or travel document, your residence permit, proof of address (Meldebescheinigung), and a vaccination booklet. Certified translations cost roughly €30–€80 per page.

faqs.question: Is there financial support for school materials and costs in Germany?
faqs.answer: Public schools in Germany are free, including Willkommensklassen. For school supplies, low-income families can apply for the Bildungs- und Teilhabepaket (BuT), which provides up to €116 per year for materials plus support for school trips and extracurricular activities. Ask your Jobcenter or Sozialamt about eligibility.

new-probezeit-ausbildung-trial-period.title: Probezeit Ausbildung: Your Trial Period Rights and What to Expect in Germany
new-probezeit-ausbildung-trial-period.summary: Learn how the Probezeit Ausbildung trial period works, how long it lasts, termination rules, and how to protect your rights as a trainee in Germany.
new-probezeit-ausbildung-trial-period.content:
Starting your Ausbildung in Germany is exciting — but the first few months come with rules that many international trainees don't fully understand. The Probezeit Ausbildung trial period is a legally defined phase at the beginning of every apprenticeship, and knowing your rights during this time can save you from a nasty surprise. Whether you're just arriving from Morocco or already settled in Munich or Hamburg, this guide breaks down exactly how the trial period works, what your employer can and cannot do, and how to navigate it confidently.

## What Is the Probezeit in an Ausbildung?

The **Probezeit** (trial period) is the opening chapter of every German apprenticeship contract. It's the phase where both you and your employer get to decide whether the training relationship is a good fit. Think of it as a mutual test drive — you're evaluating the company just as much as they're evaluating you.

This period is governed by **§ 20 of the Berufsbildungsgesetz (BBiG)** — Germany's Vocational Training Act. The law sets clear boundaries on how long the trial period can last and what either side can do during it.

### How Long Does the Probezeit Last?

The Probezeit must last **at least one month** and **no more than four months**. Most Ausbildung contracts set it at exactly **three months**, which has become the standard across industries like retail, healthcare, IT, and hospitality.

Your employer cannot legally extend the Probezeit beyond four months, even if you were sick for part of it. Some trainees mistakenly believe absences automatically extend the trial — this is **not true** under BBiG unless a very specific exception applies and it's written into your contract.

Practical example: If your Ausbildung starts on **1 September 2024**, a standard three-month Probezeit ends on **30 November 2024**. From **1 December 2024** onward, you have significantly stronger job protection.

## Termination During the Probezeit: What the Law Actually Says

This is the part that surprises most trainees. During the Probezeit, **both parties can terminate the training contract at any time, without giving a reason (ohne Grund)**. That means your employer can end your Ausbildung in week two simply because they feel it's not working — and you can do the same.

This sounds harsh, but it works both ways. If you decide after four weeks that the company is not a good fit, you can walk away without having to justify yourself.

### The 2-Week Notice Rule — and When It Doesn't Apply

Even during the Probezeit, there is **no notice period (Kündigungsfrist) required** by law. Termination can be immediate — effective the same day, if both parties agree or if there is a serious cause.

However, many Ausbildung contracts include a **voluntary 2-week notice clause** during the trial period. Always check your individual contract. If your contract says "zwei Wochen Kündigungsfrist während der Probezeit," then both sides must give two weeks' notice before the termination takes effect.

After the Probezeit ends, the rules change dramatically:
- You can only be terminated **for a specific, documented reason**
- Your employer must give you **4 weeks' written notice**
- Termination without cause after the Probezeit is **legally invalid**

## Your Rights During the Probezeit Ausbildung Trial Period

Just because the employer can terminate more easily doesn't mean you have zero rights. Several important protections still apply during the trial period.

### You Must Receive Proper Training

The purpose of the Probezeit is to assess fit — not to use you as free cheap labour. Your employer is legally obligated to train you according to the **Ausbildungsrahmenplan** (training framework plan) from day one. If you're spending your first three months cleaning the warehouse or doing tasks unrelated to your trade, that is a violation you can report to the **Industrie- und Handelskammer (IHK)** or **Handwerkskammer (HWK)**.

### You Must Be Paid

Your **Ausbildungsvergütung** (training allowance) is due from the first day, including during the Probezeit. As of 2024, the minimum training allowance in Germany is **€ 649 per month in the first year** (set by the Mindestausbildungsvergütungsgesetz). Many companies pay more — IT Ausbildung trainees in Frankfurt often earn €800–€1,000/month even in their first year.

### You Are Entitled to a Beurteilung (Performance Review)

You have the right to receive **feedback on your performance**. What counts as fair feedback? It should be:
- **Specific** — relating to actual tasks or behaviour
- **Timely** — not saved up for termination day
- **Documented** — ideally in writing or noted in your training record (Berichtsheft)

If your employer only ever tells you "it's fine" and then terminates you at the end of week ten, you can challenge whether proper training supervision took place — though reversing a Probezeit termination is still difficult in practice.

### Sick Leave During the Probezeit

If you get sick, you must notify your employer **before your shift starts** (or as early as possible) and submit a **Krankenschein (sick note from a doctor)** on the first day of illness, or by the third day — check your contract as rules vary. Illness does not automatically end your Probezeit, but repeated absences could give your employer grounds to terminate, so make sure everything is documented properly.

## What Counts as Unfair or Illegal Termination?

Even during the trial period, some terminations are **prohibited by law**:

- **Discriminatory termination** — ending your contract because of your nationality, religion, gender, or disability is illegal under the **Allgemeines Gleichbehandlungsgesetz (AGG)**
- **Termination due to pregnancy** — a pregnant trainee cannot be dismissed during or after the Probezeit; this protection kicks in automatically when the employer is informed
- **Retaliation termination** — if you reported a safety violation or contacted the IHK, your employer cannot legally terminate you as punishment

If you believe your termination falls into one of these categories, contact the **Antidiskriminierungsstelle des Bundes** (Federal Anti-Discrimination Agency) or speak to a **Gewerkschaft (trade union)** like ver.di or IG Metall. Many unions offer free legal advice to apprentices.

## Common Pitfalls — What People Get Wrong About the Probezeit

**1. "I can't be fired without notice."**
Wrong. During the Probezeit, immediate termination is possible unless your contract specifically includes a notice clause.

**2. "My illness extended my Probezeit."**
Not automatically. Only if your contract explicitly says so, and only under very specific conditions.

**3. "Verbal promises count."**
They don't in German law. If your Ausbilder (trainer) told you verbally that everything is fine, that holds no legal weight. Get feedback in writing.

**4. "I can quit without any consequences."**
Mostly true during Probezeit, but check your contract for any clause about repaying training costs — this is sometimes included and may be enforceable.

**5. "The Probezeit can be 6 months."**
No. Four months is the absolute legal maximum. If your contract says six months, that clause is invalid under BBiG, and the Probezeit automatically ends at four months.

**6. "I don't need to attend Berufsschule during the Probezeit."**
False. Berufsschule (vocational school) is compulsory from the first week of your Ausbildung, trial period or not.

## How to Make the Most of Your Probezeit

Here's what actually works during these critical first weeks:

- **Ask for feedback proactively** — don't wait for your employer to come to you. Request a short weekly or biweekly check-in
- **Keep your Berichtsheft (training record) up to date** — it's your paper trail
- **Note everything** — if your trainer gives you feedback (positive or negative), write it down with the date
- **Build relationships** — in German workplace culture, showing up reliably and communicating problems early is valued highly
- **Use your Berufsschule network** — other trainees in your class may have faced similar issues and can point you to union resources or the IHK

If things feel wrong early — tasks don't match the training plan, you're being bullied, or communication is poor — contact the **IHK or HWK hotline** sooner rather than later. Waiting until after termination makes everything harder.

## Conclusion

The Probezeit Ausbildung trial period is a short but pivotal window. It gives both you and your employer the flexibility to test the relationship, but it comes with real legal structure — minimum duration of one month, maximum of four months, no mandatory notice period unless your contract says otherwise, and zero tolerance for discriminatory termination. Understanding these rules puts you in a much stronger position, whether you're trying to succeed in your apprenticeship or recognising when something is going wrong.

If you're preparing your application documents or need help crafting a strong Anschreiben before your Ausbildung begins, [book a free consultation and use our Anschreiben Generator](/anschreiben-generator) to move to Germany with confidence.

faqs.question: How long does the Probezeit in an Ausbildung legally last?
faqs.answer: Between one and four months. Most contracts set it at three months. Your employer cannot extend it beyond four months, even if you were sick during part of it.

faqs.question: Can my employer fire me during the Probezeit without giving a reason?
faqs.answer: Yes. During the trial period, both the employer and the trainee can terminate the contract without stating a reason. However, termination for discriminatory reasons (nationality, religion, pregnancy) is always illegal under the AGG.

faqs.question: Do I get paid during the Probezeit Ausbildung trial period?
faqs.answer: Absolutely. Your Ausbildungsvergütung starts from day one. As of 2024, the legal minimum is €649 per month in the first training year, and many employers pay significantly more depending on the sector and region.

faqs.question: Is a 2-week notice period required during the Probezeit?
faqs.answer: Not by law — termination during the Probezeit can be immediate. However, many individual contracts voluntarily include a 2-week notice clause. Always check your specific Ausbildungsvertrag to know which rules apply to you.

faqs.question: What should I do if I think my Probezeit termination was unfair or discriminatory?
faqs.answer: Contact the Antidiskriminierungsstelle des Bundes (Federal Anti-Discrimination Agency) or a trade union like ver.di or IG Metall. Many unions offer free legal advice to apprentices. You can also reach out to your local IHK or HWK for guidance.

new-urlaubsanspruch-vacation-days-ausbil.title: Urlaubsanspruch Ausbildung: How Many Vacation Days Do You Get as a Trainee in Germany?
new-urlaubsanspruch-vacation-days-ausbil.summary: Learn how many vacation days you're entitled to during your Ausbildung in Germany, how collective agreements can increase that number, and how to plan time off.
new-urlaubsanspruch-vacation-days-ausbil.content:
Starting your Ausbildung in Germany is exciting — but after weeks of early mornings, Berufsschule schedules, and new workplace routines, you're going to need a break. Understanding your Urlaubsanspruch (vacation entitlement) as a trainee is not just about knowing when you can rest; it's about knowing your legal rights so no employer can shortchange you. The rules around vacation days during an Ausbildung are more generous than many trainees expect, and they vary depending on your age, your industry, and your specific training contract.

## What Does Urlaubsanspruch Mean for Ausbildung Trainees?

Urlaubsanspruch simply means your legal entitlement to paid vacation days. During your Ausbildung, you are covered by the **Berufsbildungsgesetz (BBiG)** — Germany's Vocational Training Act — which guarantees you paid leave just like any regular employee.

The key thing to understand is that your vacation days are **paid**. Your training allowance (Ausbildungsvergütung) continues to be paid while you're on vacation. You don't lose money by taking time off — it's your right.

### Who Sets the Rules?

Three layers determine how many days you actually get:

- **The BBiG (federal law):** Sets the statutory minimum based on your age.
- **Tarifvertrag (collective bargaining agreement):** Your industry's union agreement, which often gives you more days than the legal minimum.
- **Your individual Ausbildungsvertrag (training contract):** Must be at least as generous as the law — never less.

## The Statutory Minimum: 24 Days for Young Trainees

Under § 19 BBiG, your minimum vacation entitlement during Ausbildung depends on your age at the **start of the calendar year**:

- **Under 16 years old:** 30 vacation days per year
- **16 years old:** 27 vacation days per year
- **17 years old:** 25 vacation days per year
- **18 years old and older:** 24 vacation days per year

These are **working days**, not calendar days. Since most Ausbildung schedules run Monday to Friday (5 working days per week), 24 working days equals about **4.8 weeks** of vacation per year. That's already solid — but many trainees end up with even more.

> **Important:** The age that counts is how old you are on **January 1st** of that year. If you turn 18 in March, you still get the 25-day entitlement for the full calendar year because you were 17 on January 1st.

### What Counts as a Vacation Day?

Only days you would normally have been working count against your vacation quota. This means:

- Berufsschule days do **not** use up your vacation days (more on this below)
- Public holidays do **not** count as vacation days
- Sick days (with a doctor's note after the third day) do **not** reduce your vacation entitlement
- Weekends are never deducted

## How a Tarifvertrag Can Increase Your Vacation Days

If your training company is bound by a **Tarifvertrag** (a collective agreement negotiated between employers' associations and trade unions), you likely get more than the legal minimum. This is where it gets interesting.

Here are real examples from common Ausbildung sectors:

| Sector | Typical Vacation Days |
|---|---|
| Retail (Einzelhandel) | 28–30 days |
| Banking & Finance | 30 days |
| Construction (Bau) | 30 days |
| Healthcare (Pflege) | 29–30 days |
| IT & Tech | 27–30 days |
| Public sector (TVöD) | 30 days |

For example, if you're doing an Ausbildung as a **Bankkaufmann/-frau** in Frankfurt, your Tarifvertrag will typically give you **30 vacation days** — that's 6 full weeks per year, far above the legal minimum.

To find out if your employer is bound by a Tarifvertrag, check the website of the relevant trade union. For retail, that's **ver.di** (verdi.de). For metalworking and IT, it's **IG Metall** (igmetall.de). For construction, check **IG BAU** (igbau.de).

## Planning Your Vacation Around Berufsschule

One of the most confusing parts of taking vacation during an Ausbildung is figuring out when you can actually take it, given that you split your time between your training company and the **Berufsschule** (vocational school).

### The Basic Rule

Your employer is responsible for granting your vacation. You should always check your company's policies, but here's the general framework:

- Vacation is ideally taken during **school holidays** (Schulferien) when possible, because your absence from the workplace is easier to manage.
- However, your employer **cannot force** you to take all vacation during school holidays. You have a right to take vacation at other times too, as long as it doesn't conflict with urgent business needs.
- If Berufsschule days fall within your approved vacation period, those school days are **not counted** as vacation days. For example, if you take a week off and two of those days are Berufsschule days, only three days are deducted from your vacation quota.

### How to Request Vacation

1. Submit a written vacation request (Urlaubsantrag) to your Ausbilder or HR department — many companies have a standard form or an online system.
2. Give as much notice as possible — at least 2–4 weeks, more if you want time off during popular periods like summer.
3. Coordinate with colleagues and fellow trainees to avoid everyone being absent at once.
4. Get written confirmation of your approved vacation before booking any flights or accommodation.

### City-Specific Tip: School Holiday Dates Differ by State

Germany's school holidays vary by **Bundesland**. If you're doing your Ausbildung in **München (Bavaria)**, summer holidays typically run from late July to early September. In **Hamburg**, they often fall in June and July. Check the official holiday calendar for your state at **kmk.org** (the Standing Conference of the Ministers of Education).

## Carrying Over Unused Vacation Days

What happens if you don't use all your vacation days by December 31st? The rules are stricter than many people assume.

- In principle, vacation must be taken within the **same calendar year**.
- Carrying days over to the following year is only allowed if you had a legitimate reason for not taking them — such as illness or employer refusal.
- If carried over, these days must generally be taken by **March 31st** of the following year, after which they legally expire.
- Your employer cannot simply pay you out for unused vacation days while the employment (or training) relationship is ongoing.

**Exception:** If your Ausbildung ends mid-year (for example, you finish in July after passing your exams), you are entitled to a **pro-rated** number of vacation days for the months you worked. If you couldn't take them before the contract ended, your employer must pay them out at your daily training allowance rate.

## What People Get Wrong About Vacation During Ausbildung

This is where many trainees — especially those new to German workplace culture — run into problems.

**Mistake 1: Assuming Berufsschule days are vacation.**
Many trainees mistakenly believe that if they're not at the company, they're "off." Berufsschule is part of your Ausbildung — it's not free time, and it doesn't count as vacation.

**Mistake 2: Not requesting vacation in writing.**
A verbal agreement from your Ausbilder is not enough. Always get approval in writing. If a dispute arises later, you need documentation.

**Mistake 3: Booking travel before vacation is approved.**
This one is costly. Never buy non-refundable flights or book hotels before you have written confirmation. Your employer can reject your request if business needs require it.

**Mistake 4: Not knowing your Tarifvertrag rights.**
Many trainees don't realize their industry agreement gives them more than 24 days. Check your contract and ask your company's HR or works council (Betriebsrat) whether a Tarifvertrag applies.

**Mistake 5: Letting days expire.**
If you reach late November with 10 unused vacation days, don't wait — request them immediately. Employers sometimes resist, but you have a legal right to take them within the calendar year.

**Mistake 6: Thinking sick days reduce your vacation.**
If you become ill during your approved vacation and have a medical certificate (Krankschreibung) from a doctor, those sick days must be restored to your vacation account. You don't lose them.

## Your Vacation Rights Are Protected — Know Them

Your Urlaubsanspruch during your Ausbildung is protected by federal law. No training contract can give you fewer days than the BBiG requires, and no employer can pressure you into forfeiting earned days. If you ever feel your rights are being violated, you can contact the **Agentur für Arbeit**, the relevant trade union, or a free legal advice service like **Caritas** or **AWO**, which many cities offer to immigrants and newcomers.

Understanding these rules before you start your Ausbildung puts you in a much stronger position — you know what to expect, what to ask for, and when to push back.

If you're still in the process of applying for your Ausbildung and need help crafting the perfect cover letter or CV, [book a free consultation and use our CV builder](/cv-builder) to move one step closer to starting your career in Germany.

faqs.question: How many vacation days do I get during my Ausbildung in Germany?
faqs.answer: By law, you get at least 24 working days per year if you are 18 or older at the start of the calendar year. Younger trainees get more: 25 days at 17, 27 days at 16, and 30 days if you are under 16. Many industries give additional days through Tarifvertrag agreements, often reaching 28–30 days total.

faqs.question: Do Berufsschule days count as vacation days during my Ausbildung?
faqs.answer: No. Berufsschule days are part of your official training and are never counted against your vacation entitlement. If your approved vacation period overlaps with Berufsschule days, only the days you would have been at your training company are deducted from your quota.

faqs.question: Can my employer force me to take vacation only during school holidays?
faqs.answer: Your employer can encourage you to take vacation during Schulferien to minimize disruption, but they cannot legally require you to use all your days during school holidays. You have the right to request vacation at other times, and the employer can only refuse if there are urgent, documented business reasons.

faqs.question: What happens to unused vacation days at the end of the year?
faqs.answer: Unused vacation days generally expire on December 31st unless you had a valid reason for not taking them, such as illness or employer refusal. If carried over, they must be used by March 31st of the following year. Your employer cannot simply cancel them without justification, and you should actively request any remaining days before the year ends.

faqs.question: What if my Ausbildung ends before I have used all my vacation days?
faqs.answer: If your Ausbildung ends mid-year — for example after passing your final exams in July — you are entitled to a pro-rated share of your annual vacation. Any days you were unable to take before the contract ended must be paid out by your employer at your daily training allowance rate.

new-krankschreibung-sick-rules-ausbildun.title: Krankschreibung Sick Days Ausbildung Rules: What Every Moroccan Trainee Needs to Know
new-krankschreibung-sick-rules-ausbildun.summary: Learn the exact rules for calling in sick during your Ausbildung in Germany — from eAU notes to sick pay — and avoid costly mistakes.
new-krankschreibung-sick-rules-ausbildun.content:
Getting sick is never convenient, but when you're in the middle of your Ausbildung in Germany, a simple cold can feel stressful if you don't know the rules. Understanding Krankschreibung sick days Ausbildung rules isn't just about staying out of trouble — it's about knowing your rights and protecting your training contract. Many Moroccan trainees lose pay, get warnings, or even face contract issues simply because nobody explained the process to them clearly. This guide fixes that.

## What "Krankschreibung" Actually Means in the Ausbildung Context

The word **Krankschreibung** literally means "sick note" or "medical certificate." In Germany, it's the official doctor's confirmation that you are unfit to work or train on a given day or period. During your Ausbildung, you are treated much like a regular employee when it comes to sickness — which is both good news and bad news depending on the situation.

The good news: German law gives you strong protections. The bad news: the rules are specific and must be followed exactly, or you risk disciplinary consequences.

Your legal basis is the **Entgeltfortzahlungsgesetz (EFZG)** — the Continued Pay Act — and your Ausbildung contract (Berufsausbildungsvertrag). Both set out exactly what you must do when you can't come in.

## The First Rule: Call Your Training Company Before Your Shift Starts

This is the single most important action. If you wake up sick, you must notify your Ausbildungsbetrieb (training company) **before your shift begins** — not during, not after. In Germany, this is called the **Meldepflicht** (duty to report).

Here's what a correct notification looks like in practice:

- **Call by phone** — don't just send a WhatsApp or email unless your company explicitly says that's OK. A phone call is the standard.
- Call your **direct supervisor or the HR department**, not just a colleague.
- Tell them you are sick and cannot come in, and give a rough idea of how long you expect to be absent (even if you're not sure yet).
- If you're sick on the first day of the working week (e.g., Monday), call early — ideally 30 minutes before your shift starts.

A simple script in German:
*"Guten Morgen, ich bin leider krank und kann heute nicht zur Arbeit kommen. Ich werde einen Arzt aufsuchen und mich um eine Krankmeldung kümmern."*

Missing this step — even if you later bring a doctor's note — can result in a written warning.

## When Do You Need a Doctor's Note?

This question trips up a lot of trainees, because the rules changed in recent years and vary slightly by employer.

### The General Legal Rule

By law, your employer can require a **Arbeitsunfähigkeitsbescheinigung (AU-Bescheinigung)** — a certificate of incapacity for work — from the **first day of absence**. However, most employers only require it from the **third day** (so if you're sick Monday, you need the note by Wednesday morning at the latest).

Check your **Ausbildungsvertrag** carefully. Some companies write in that they want the note from day one. This is legal and binding.

### The eAU — The Digital Sick Note

Since January 2023, Germany uses the **elektronische Arbeitsunfähigkeitsbescheinigung (eAU)**. This means:

- Your doctor sends the sick note **digitally** directly to your health insurance (Krankenkasse).
- Your Krankenkasse then makes it available to your employer electronically.
- You no longer need to hand in a yellow paper slip in most cases.

**Important:** You still need to go to the doctor and get the AU issued. The process is just paperless now. Your employer will retrieve the data digitally. If something goes wrong technically, you may still be asked for the paper version as a backup.

### When You're Sick and Have Berufsschule (Vocational School)

Being sick also means you must inform your **Berufsschule** separately. Your training company and your school are two different institutions. Missing school without notification can count as unauthorized absence, which has its own consequences including repeated failure affecting your exam eligibility.

## Sick Pay During Your Ausbildung: How Much Do You Get?

Here is where the **Entgeltfortzahlungsgesetz** really protects you. As long as you have been in your Ausbildung for **more than four weeks**, you are entitled to **100% of your Ausbildungsvergütung (training allowance)** for up to **six weeks** per illness.

### Real Numbers

Let's say you're in the second year of your Ausbildung as a Kaufmann für Büromanagement in Frankfurt and you earn **€900/month**. If you're sick for three weeks with the flu, your employer must pay you the full €900 for those three weeks — you don't lose a single euro.

After six weeks of the same illness, payment switches to **Krankengeld** — sick pay from your health insurance (Krankenkasse). Krankengeld is approximately **70% of your gross income**, paid by your health insurance for up to 78 weeks.

### The Four-Week Waiting Period

In your very first four weeks of Ausbildung (the **Wartezeit**), you are not yet entitled to continued pay. If you get sick in week two of your training, your employer is not legally required to pay you. This is rare but worth knowing.

## What Happens If You're "Sick Too Often"?

This is the topic that worries most trainees. There is **no fixed number of sick days** in German law that automatically triggers termination. It's not like "10 days and you're out." But there are real-world consequences to frequent sick leave.

### Patterns That Raise Red Flags

- Repeatedly being sick on Mondays and Fridays
- Being sick right after your vacation is denied
- Short absences that add up to 30+ days per year without a clear medical reason

These patterns can lead to:

1. **A personal conversation (Gespräch)** with your supervisor or HR
2. **A written warning (Abmahnung)** if the behavior continues
3. In extreme cases, **termination** — but only after a formal process

### "Personenbedingte Kündigung" — Termination Due to Illness

A training company can in theory terminate your contract if your illness makes it impossible for them to plan staffing and it's reasonably expected to continue. But this requires:

- A pattern of absences documented over a long period
- A formal process including warnings
- A proportionality check

For a first or second sick episode, this is almost never a concern. Don't panic.

## What People Get Wrong About Sick Days in Ausbildung

This section could save you from a serious mistake.

**Mistake 1: Sending a WhatsApp to your buddy instead of calling HR.**
Your message may never reach the right person. Always call the official contact.

**Mistake 2: Waiting until you feel better to go to the doctor.**
If your employer requires the note from day three, you must have seen a doctor by day three — even if you feel better. Don't go to the doctor on day five and ask them to backdate the certificate. Doctors generally refuse to do this, and attempting it is a legal gray area.

**Mistake 3: Thinking the eAU means you don't need to do anything.**
You still need to physically (or by phone/video, depending on the practice) consult a doctor. The eAU is just the transmission method, not a replacement for the medical consultation.

**Mistake 4: Forgetting to notify the Berufsschule.**
Many trainees notify their company but forget the school. Both need to hear from you.

**Mistake 5: Not tracking your own sick days.**
Keep a personal record. After six weeks of the same illness, your pay structure changes. Knowing where you stand helps you plan.

**Mistake 6: Assuming "sick leave resets every year."**
The six-week continued pay entitlement applies per illness episode. If you're sick with the same diagnosed illness twice in 12 months, the second episode may not restart the six-week clock.

## Practical Tools and Contacts to Know

- **Your Krankenkasse (health insurance):** AOK, TK, Barmer, DAK are the most common. Log into your online account to see your AU records.
- **Your Ausbildungsvertrag:** Re-read the clauses about sick leave obligations. They vary.
- **Telefonische Krankschreibung:** Some doctors now allow phone consultations for mild illnesses (up to 5 days). Check with your Hausarzt (GP).
- **Bundesministerium für Gesundheit (BMG):** [www.bundesgesundheitsministerium.de](https://www.bundesgesundheitsministerium.de) — official source for health-related legal questions in Germany.

## Conclusion

Knowing the Krankschreibung sick days Ausbildung rules protects both your health and your career. The core principle is simple: call in before your shift, see a doctor within the required timeframe, and make sure the eAU is issued and transmitted. Your pay is protected by law for up to six weeks, and occasional illness will not end your training contract. What causes real problems is ignoring the notification duty or missing the Berufsschule without informing them.

If you're still preparing for your Ausbildung — working on your application letter or building your CV — **book a free consultation to learn German and move to Germany successfully**. Our [Anschreiben Generator](/anschreiben-generator) and [CV Builder](/cv-builder) are designed specifically for Moroccan applicants navigating the German system.

faqs.question: Do I need a sick note from day one of my Ausbildung absence in Germany?
faqs.answer: It depends on your training contract. By law, employers can demand a note from day one, but most require it from the third day of absence. Always check your Ausbildungsvertrag for the exact rule your company applies.

faqs.question: What is the eAU and do I still need to visit a doctor?
faqs.answer: The eAU (elektronische Arbeitsunfähigkeitsbescheinigung) is a digital sick note introduced in January 2023. Your doctor sends it electronically to your health insurance, which forwards it to your employer. You still need a medical consultation — the eAU just removes the paper handover step.

faqs.question: How much sick pay do I receive during my Ausbildung in Germany?
faqs.answer: After your first four weeks of training, you receive 100% of your Ausbildungsvergütung for up to six weeks of the same illness. After six weeks, your health insurance (Krankenkasse) pays Krankengeld — roughly 70% of your gross income — for up to 78 weeks.

faqs.question: Can my training company fire me for being sick too often?
faqs.answer: There is no fixed number of sick days that triggers automatic termination. A so-called personenbedingte Kündigung due to illness requires a documented long-term pattern, formal warnings, and a proportionality review. A single sick episode or occasional absences will not put your contract at risk.

faqs.question: Do I need to inform my Berufsschule separately when I am sick?
faqs.answer: Yes, absolutely. Your training company and your vocational school (Berufsschule) are separate institutions. You must notify both on the first day of absence. Failing to inform the school can result in unauthorized absences that may affect your exam eligibility.

new-mobbing-workplace-rights-germany.title: Mobbing in the Workplace Germany: Your Rights and Exactly What to Do
new-mobbing-workplace-rights-germany.summary: Find out what counts as mobbing under German law, how to document it, and the exact steps to take — from talking to your boss to calling a labor lawyer.
new-mobbing-workplace-rights-germany.content:
Being targeted at work is one of the most draining experiences a person can go through — and when you're new to Germany, it can feel even more isolating. Mobbing in the German workplace is not just unpleasant; it is legally recognised, and you have concrete rights and a clear path for fighting back. This guide walks you through exactly what counts as mobbing under German law, how to collect evidence that actually holds up, and the full escalation chain from your first conversation with a manager all the way to a labour court.

## What Counts as Mobbing Under German Law

In Germany, "Mobbing" is a specific legal concept, not just a general word for rudeness. German courts — particularly the Federal Labour Court (Bundesarbeitsgericht) — define mobbing as **a systematic, repeated pattern of hostile behaviour** directed at one person over an extended period, with the effect of harming their dignity, health, or ability to work.

The key word is *systematic*. A single bad day, one rude comment, or an unfair performance review on its own does not legally qualify. Courts typically look for behaviour that:

- Happens **repeatedly** (at least several times) over **weeks or months**
- Is directed at **one specific person**
- Is **intended or clearly likely** to humiliate, isolate, or psychologically harm

### Behaviours That Qualify as Mobbing

German courts have ruled the following as mobbing in real cases:

- Deliberately excluding you from team meetings or group chats
- Spreading false rumours about your competence or private life
- Constantly criticising your work in front of colleagues with no constructive purpose
- Giving you meaningless, below-level tasks to humiliate you (called *Schikane*)
- Shouting, insults, or threats made repeatedly
- Blocking your career progression deliberately (e.g. refusing to pass on your promotion application)
- Ignoring you completely — the "silent treatment" — for weeks on end

### What Does NOT Qualify

It is equally important to know the limits:

- A genuinely harsh performance review that is factually correct
- A colleague who is simply unfriendly or difficult
- One heated argument
- Being asked to do tasks you dislike, as long as they fall within your job description

German law gives employers the right to direct and manage staff (*Direktionsrecht*). Not every conflict or uncomfortable situation crosses the legal threshold.

## Your Legal Protections as an Employee in Germany

Even without a dedicated "anti-mobbing law," you are protected by several overlapping legal frameworks.

**§ 75 BetrVG (Works Constitution Act):** Employers and works councils (*Betriebsrat*) are jointly obliged to protect the dignity of every employee.

**§ 241 BGB (German Civil Code):** Your employment contract carries an implied duty of care. Your employer must protect you from harm — including mobbing by colleagues or managers.

**AGG (General Equal Treatment Act):** If the mobbing is linked to your nationality, religion, ethnicity, or gender, the AGG provides additional protections and gives you a 2-month window to make a formal complaint after each incident.

**Occupational Health and Safety Act (ArbSchG):** Employers have a legal duty to assess and eliminate psychosocial risks, which includes workplace mobbing.

As a Moroccan employee in Germany, the AGG is particularly relevant if any of the hostile behaviour targets your background, language, or religion.

## How to Collect Evidence That Holds Up

Before you escalate anything, you need a paper trail. German labour courts place a heavy burden of proof on the person making the claim — which means your documentation is everything.

### Keep a Mobbing Diary (Mobbingtagebuch)

Start a detailed written log immediately. For every incident, record:

- **Date and time**
- **Exact location** (meeting room, open office, canteen, chat platform)
- **Exactly what was said or done** — use direct quotes where possible
- **Who was present** as a witness
- **Your reaction and how it made you feel**
- **Any physical symptoms** (sleep problems, headaches, anxiety)

Keep this diary somewhere private — not on your work laptop. A handwritten notebook or a personal cloud document works well.

### Save Written Evidence

- Screenshots of hostile emails, Slack/Teams messages, or WhatsApp messages
- Any written instructions that show deliberately humiliating tasks
- Emails where you were cc'd out after previously being included, showing a pattern of exclusion

### Get Medical Documentation

If you have seen a doctor or therapist for stress, anxiety, or burnout related to the situation, ask them to document that the symptoms are work-related. This is powerful evidence in court and also relevant for sick pay (*Krankengeld*) if you need to take leave.

### Find Witnesses

Think about colleagues who have seen incidents. You cannot force anyone to testify, but knowing who was present is valuable when you escalate formally.

## The Escalation Chain: Step by Step

Follow this order. Skipping steps can weaken your legal position later.

### Step 1: Talk to Your Direct Manager

If your manager is not the person mobbing you, start there. Keep the conversation factual — refer to your diary, not your emotions. Ask specifically: "What steps will you take to address this behaviour?" Follow up the conversation with an email summarising what was said. This creates a written record.

### Step 2: Go to HR (Personalabteilung)

If the manager does nothing, or if the manager is the person doing the mobbing, go directly to HR. Submit a **formal written complaint** — not a verbal one. Specify the incidents, dates, and witnesses. Ask HR to confirm receipt in writing.

### Step 3: Contact the Works Council (Betriebsrat)

If your company has a Betriebsrat (required in companies with 5+ permanent employees), this is one of your strongest allies. Under § 84 BetrVG, every employee has the right to file a formal complaint with the Betriebsrat. The council is legally obliged to investigate and report back. They can also call for mediation and, in serious cases, pressure the employer to act. This step is **free** and confidential.

### Step 4: Call the DGB Hotline or Seek Union Support

The **Deutscher Gewerkschaftsbund (DGB)** — Germany's main trade union federation — runs a free advice hotline: **0800 4 DGB DGB (0800 4 342 342)**, available Monday to Friday. If you are already a union member, contact your union directly (IG Metall, ver.di, and others all provide legal support). Even if you are not a member yet, joining now means you can access legal help after a waiting period (usually 3 months).

### Step 5: Consult a Labour Lawyer (Fachanwalt für Arbeitsrecht)

If internal routes have failed, it is time for a specialist. A *Fachanwalt für Arbeitsrecht* can:

- Assess whether your case meets the legal standard
- Send a formal cease-and-desist letter (*Abmahnung*) to your employer
- File a claim for damages or compensation
- Represent you in the labour court (*Arbeitsgericht*)

An initial consultation typically costs **€90–€190**. If you have legal expenses insurance (*Rechtsschutzversicherung*), it will usually cover this. Labour court fees in Germany are relatively low — and in the first instance there are **no court fees** for the claimant. Find a qualified lawyer via the German Bar Association's portal: **anwaltauskunft.de**.

## What People Get Wrong About Mobbing Claims in Germany

**"I'll just wait and see if it gets better."** Every week you delay is a week without documentation. Courts look at the full timeline, and gaps make your case weaker.

**"I complained verbally, so they know."** Verbal complaints are almost impossible to prove. Everything must be in writing — email is fine, but written is essential.

**"I signed a settlement and that ends it."** Not necessarily. Depending on what you signed, you may still be able to claim for health damage or psychological harm. A lawyer can advise.

**"Because I'm on a work visa, I can't make trouble."** This is a myth. Your employment rights in Germany apply regardless of your residency or visa status. Making a legal complaint about mobbing does not threaten your right to stay in Germany.

**"I need to prove intent."** You do not always need to prove the person intended to harm you — courts can find mobbing based on the objective effect of the behaviour, especially where a pattern is clear.

**"The company is too small to have rules."** Even without a Betriebsrat, your employer still has legal duties under BGB and ArbSchG. Small companies are not exempt.

## Conclusion

Mobbing in the German workplace is serious, but German law gives you a clear set of tools to fight it. The formula is simple: document everything, escalate step by step, and do not wait too long. Start your diary today, put your complaint in writing, use the Betriebsrat, call the DGB hotline, and get a labour lawyer if you need one. You have more protection than you think — and you deserve to use it.

If you are still building your career in Germany and want to make sure your application documents are strong before your next move, [book a free consultation and use our CV builder](/cv-builder) to present yourself professionally and protect your position from day one.

faqs.question: How long does mobbing have to go on before I can take legal action in Germany?
faqs.answer: German courts generally look for a pattern over several weeks to months. There is no fixed minimum, but isolated incidents rarely qualify. Start documenting immediately and consult a labour lawyer once you have a clear pattern — don't wait months before acting.

faqs.question: Can I be fired for making a mobbing complaint in Germany?
faqs.answer: Retaliatory dismissal is illegal in Germany. If your employer fires you shortly after you file a formal mobbing complaint, this can itself be challenged in labour court. Keep records of the timeline so any retaliation is clearly visible.

faqs.question: Does the Betriebsrat have to keep my complaint confidential?
faqs.answer: The Betriebsrat is legally bound by confidentiality rules under the BetrVG. They cannot share your identity without your consent during an investigation. You can also ask them explicitly to protect your anonymity when they approach your employer.

faqs.question: What compensation can I receive if my mobbing claim succeeds in German labour court?
faqs.answer: Compensation typically covers documented financial losses (e.g. lost wages if you were forced to quit), and in some cases damages for psychological harm (Schmerzensgeld). Awards vary widely — cases have ranged from €1,000 to over €20,000 depending on severity and duration. A Fachanwalt für Arbeitsrecht can give you a realistic estimate for your situation.

faqs.question: I don't speak German fluently. Can I still file a formal complaint?
faqs.answer: Yes. You have the right to submit a complaint in writing and, if needed, bring an interpreter to any meeting. The DGB hotline also has advisors who speak multiple languages. For legal proceedings, the court can arrange interpretation. Your language level does not affect your legal rights.

new-betriebsrat-works-council-trainee.title: Betriebsrat & Works Council as a Trainee: How It Protects Your Ausbildung in Germany
new-betriebsrat-works-council-trainee.summary: Learn how the Betriebsrat protects Auszubildende in Germany, what the JAV does, and how to raise concerns confidentially as a trainee.
new-betriebsrat-works-council-trainee.content:
Starting your Ausbildung in Germany is exciting — but what happens when something goes wrong at work? Maybe your trainer is asking you to do tasks outside your training plan, or you're being pressured to work overtime without pay. This is exactly where the Betriebsrat, Germany's workplace works council, steps in to protect you. Understanding your rights and knowing who to turn to can make the difference between a miserable training year and a successful one.

## What Is the Betriebsrat and Why Does It Matter for Your Ausbildung?

The **Betriebsrat** (works council) is an elected employee body that exists inside German companies with five or more permanent employees. It operates independently of the employer and has real legal powers — not just advisory ones. Its rights and responsibilities are defined by the **Betriebsverfassungsgesetz (BetrVG)**, Germany's Works Constitution Act.

For you as an Auszubildender (trainee), the Betriebsrat is one of the most important protections you have at your training company. It monitors whether your employer is sticking to the rules, and it has co-determination rights — meaning the employer legally cannot make certain decisions without consulting it first.

### Key Rights the Betriebsrat Holds

- **Co-determination on working hours**: If your company wants to change shift patterns or overtime rules, the Betriebsrat must agree.
- **Co-determination on training content**: The works council can push back if your training deviates significantly from the approved Ausbildungsplan (training plan).
- **Right to be informed**: The Betriebsrat must be notified before any trainee is hired or dismissed.
- **Protection against unfair dismissal**: If your employer wants to dismiss you before your Ausbildung ends, the Betriebsrat must be formally consulted under § 102 BetrVG. Without this, dismissal is invalid.

Not every small business has a Betriebsrat — companies with fewer than five employees are not required to have one. But if you're training at a supermarket chain, a manufacturing plant, a hospital, or any mid-to-large company, there's a good chance one exists.

## The Jugend- und Auszubildendenvertretung (JAV): Your Direct Representative

Within the Betriebsrat structure, there is a special body created specifically for young employees and trainees: the **Jugend- und Auszubildendenvertretung**, or **JAV** (Youth and Trainee Representation). This exists in companies where there are at least five employees under 18 or in Ausbildung.

The JAV is elected by trainees and young workers, and it acts as your direct voice. JAV members are typically trainees themselves — people who understand exactly what you're going through because they're in the same situation.

### What the JAV Can Do for You

- **Bring your concerns to the Betriebsrat**: The JAV doesn't have independent co-determination rights, but it can submit proposals and requests to the full Betriebsrat, which is then obligated to address them.
- **Attend Betriebsrat meetings**: JAV representatives are invited to Betriebsrat meetings when topics affecting trainees are discussed.
- **Monitor training conditions**: The JAV checks that your training matches what's written in your Ausbildungsvertrag (training contract).
- **Support individual trainees**: If you have a complaint or concern, you can go directly to a JAV member for help and guidance.
- **Participate in takeover negotiations**: At the end of your Ausbildung, the JAV can push for the Betriebsrat to negotiate trainee takeover agreements with the employer.

JAV elections happen every two years. If your company has a JAV, you'll usually see a notice board or internal announcement about who the current representatives are.

## How the Betriebsrat Protects You Day-to-Day

Let's get concrete. Here are real situations where the Betriebsrat makes a direct difference for Auszubildende:

### Protection Against Exploitation

German law is clear: you are at your company to learn, not to be used as cheap labor. Under the **Berufsbildungsgesetz (BBiG)**, your employer must provide training according to your approved Ausbildungsplan. If you spend your entire week doing tasks completely unrelated to your trade — like a retail trainee being used exclusively as a cleaner — this is a violation.

The Betriebsrat can intervene and formally demand the employer return to the agreed training content. In serious cases, it can involve the **Industrie- und Handelskammer (IHK)** or **Handwerkskammer (HWK)**, the chambers that officially oversee your Ausbildung.

### Overtime and Pay Issues

Your working hours as a trainee are governed by the **Arbeitszeitgesetz (AZG)** and, if you're under 18, the **Jugendarbeitsschutzgesetz (JArbSchG)**. If you're over 18, your maximum working week is 48 hours. If you're under 18, it's 40 hours, and you cannot work nights, Sundays, or most public holidays.

If your employer is routinely asking you to stay late without compensation, the Betriebsrat can act. Overtime must be agreed upon by the works council before it is introduced systematically — the employer cannot simply decide alone.

### Protection Against Dismissal

During your Ausbildung's probation period (usually one to four months), either side can terminate without notice. After that, the rules change dramatically in your favor:

- Your employer can only dismiss you for serious cause (fristlose Kündigung) after the probation period.
- The Betriebsrat must be consulted **before** any dismissal. If this step is skipped, the dismissal is legally void.
- The JAV is also notified separately.

If you receive a dismissal letter unexpectedly, go to the Betriebsrat immediately. You have only **three weeks** to challenge an unfair dismissal at a labor court (Arbeitsgericht), so time matters.

## How to Bring a Concern Confidentially

Many trainees worry: "If I complain, will my trainer turn against me?" This is a valid concern, and German law takes it seriously. Here's how to raise issues confidentially:

1. **Speak to a JAV representative privately**: JAV members have a duty of confidentiality. You can share your situation without it going directly to your trainer or manager.
2. **Request a Betriebsrat meeting**: You have the legal right to speak with the Betriebsrat — your employer cannot prevent this or demand to know why.
3. **Use anonymous feedback channels**: Some larger companies have ombudsperson systems or anonymous complaint boxes specifically for this.
4. **Contact the IHK or HWK directly**: These chambers have advisory offices (Beratungsstellen) and can help trainees independent of the company. The IHK München, for example, offers a free trainee hotline at 089 5116-0.
5. **Reach out to the DGB (Deutscher Gewerkschaftsbund)**: Germany's main trade union federation has local youth offices that advise Auszubildende free of charge.

Retaliation against a trainee for contacting the Betriebsrat or JAV is illegal. If it happens, that itself becomes a new complaint the Betriebsrat can act on.

## What If Your Company Has No Betriebsrat?

Roughly half of German employees work at companies without a works council — this is especially common in small businesses and some sectors. If this is your situation:

- **Your IHK or HWK is your primary contact**. They are legally responsible for overseeing your Ausbildung.
- **A trade union (Gewerkschaft) can support you**. For example, IG Metall supports trainees in manufacturing, and ver.di covers retail and services. Membership fees for apprentices are often as low as €3–5 per month.
- **Legal aid services**: Germany has free legal consultation days (Beratungstage) run by bar associations in most cities.

Don't make the mistake of thinking you have no options just because there's no Betriebsrat at your company.

## Common Pitfalls: What Trainees Get Wrong About the Betriebsrat

**"The Betriebsrat works for the employer."** No — it is legally independent. Members cannot be fired for their Betriebsrat work and are protected during their term and for one year after.

**"Only German trainees can use the Betriebsrat."** Absolutely not. Your rights under BetrVG apply regardless of your nationality or language level. The Betriebsrat must serve all employees and trainees equally.

**"If I complain, my Ausbildungszeugnis (training certificate) will suffer."** Your employer is legally required to give you an objective Zeugnis. Influencing it negatively as retaliation is illegal and challengeable in court.

**"I should wait until the problem is very serious."** Don't wait. Small issues — like a pattern of missed training days or unpaid overtime — are much easier to resolve early. Once a pattern is established, it's also better documented.

**"The JAV has no real power."** It has more than you think. Through the Betriebsrat, JAV proposals carry legal weight. Many companies have significantly improved their trainee conditions after sustained JAV pressure.

## Conclusion

The Betriebsrat and the JAV exist precisely because the power balance between a trainee and an employer is unequal. Germany's labor law system has built these structures over decades to give workers — including you — a real voice. Whether you're dealing with unfair tasks, overtime pressure, or a sudden dismissal threat, you have more support than most trainees realize.

As you prepare for your Ausbildung in Germany, understanding these rights is just as important as mastering your technical skills. If you need help writing a strong application or navigating the German workplace system, [book a free consultation and use our CV builder](/cv-builder) to put your best foot forward from day one.

faqs.question: Does the Betriebsrat apply to me as a foreign trainee on a visa?
faqs.answer: Yes. Your rights under the Betriebsverfassungsgesetz (BetrVG) apply regardless of your nationality or residence status. The Betriebsrat and JAV must represent all trainees equally, including those from Morocco or other non-EU countries.

faqs.question: What is the difference between the Betriebsrat and the JAV?
faqs.answer: The Betriebsrat is the main works council for all employees and has binding co-determination rights. The JAV (Jugend- und Auszubildendenvertretung) is a sub-body elected specifically by trainees and young workers. The JAV submits proposals to the Betriebsrat, which then acts on them with full legal authority.

faqs.question: My company has no Betriebsrat. Who protects my Ausbildung?
faqs.answer: Your IHK (Industrie- und Handelskammer) or HWK (Handwerkskammer) is responsible for overseeing your training. You can also contact a trade union like IG Metall or ver.di — trainee membership fees are often just €3–5 per month. Both routes can help resolve disputes with your training company.

faqs.question: Can my employer fire me for going to the Betriebsrat?
faqs.answer: No. Contacting the Betriebsrat is a protected legal right. Retaliation — including negative performance reviews or dismissal — is illegal. If retaliation occurs, it becomes a new formal complaint that the Betriebsrat can escalate to the labor court (Arbeitsgericht).

faqs.question: How do I find out if my company has a JAV?
faqs.answer: Check the company's internal notice board, intranet, or ask HR for the name of the Betriebsrat or JAV contact. In larger companies, this information is often posted in common areas like break rooms. If you can't find it, your IHK or HWK can confirm whether a JAV is registered at your training company.

new-discrimination-foreign-trainees-germ.title: Workplace Discrimination Against Foreign Trainees in Germany: Your AGG Rights Explained
new-discrimination-foreign-trainees-germ.summary: Foreign trainees in Germany have strong legal protection under the AGG. Learn your rights, how to document discrimination, and where to get free help.
new-discrimination-foreign-trainees-germ.content:
Starting an Ausbildung in Germany as a Moroccan trainee is a huge step — but what happens when your workplace doesn't treat you the same as your German colleagues? Discrimination against foreign trainees in Germany is more common than people admit, and many victims don't act simply because they don't know the law protects them. The Allgemeines Gleichbehandlungsgesetz (AGG) — Germany's General Equal Treatment Act — gives you concrete rights, clear deadlines, and access to free legal support, and this guide will walk you through all of it.

## What Is the AGG and How Does It Protect Foreign Trainees in Germany?

The AGG (Allgemeines Gleichbehandlungsgesetz) came into force in 2006 and implements four major EU anti-discrimination directives into German law. It applies to **everyone working or training in Germany**, regardless of nationality or immigration status. You do not need to be a German citizen to use it.

The law prohibits unequal treatment based on six protected characteristics:

- **Ethnic origin and race** — the most relevant ground for many Moroccan trainees
- **Religion or belief**
- **Sex and gender identity**
- **Disability**
- **Age**
- **Sexual orientation**

The law covers the entire employment relationship — job applications, Ausbildung contracts, daily working conditions, pay, promotions, and dismissal. If your trainer, supervisor, or even a colleague subjects you to disadvantage because of your origin, skin color, accent, or religion, that behavior potentially falls under the AGG.

### Direct vs. Indirect Discrimination

**Direct discrimination** is straightforward: your supervisor assigns you the worst cleaning shifts every week while German trainees rotate, and you're told "that's just how it is for foreigners." Direct, clear, and illegal.

**Indirect discrimination** is subtler: a company policy requires "native-level German spoken at home" as a selection criterion for a promotion — a rule that disproportionately disadvantages people of foreign origin without objective justification. This is also illegal under the AGG.

### Harassment and Instructions to Discriminate

The AGG also covers **workplace harassment** based on a protected characteristic. Repeated racist jokes, exclusion from team activities, or offensive comments about your Moroccan background create a hostile work environment — which is a specific form of discrimination under § 3 Abs. 3 AGG. Even a single severe incident can be enough.

## Real Examples: What Discrimination Can Look Like in an Ausbildung

Many trainees don't recognize discrimination when it's happening because it's normalized. Here are concrete situations that may constitute violations of the AGG:

- Your German colleagues receive their Ausbildungsvergütung (training allowance) on time every month, but yours is routinely paid 10–14 days late with no explanation.
- Your Ausbildungsleiter gives you a formal written warning for speaking Arabic with a Moroccan friend on your lunch break.
- You apply for the same apprenticeship as a German applicant with identical qualifications and are rejected — the company later confirms it preferred "German-speaking households."
- You are excluded from after-work team events and told "it's better for integration" that you don't attend.
- Your trainer mocks your accent in front of the entire team on a regular basis.

None of these situations require you to simply "accept it." Each one could be the basis of a formal complaint.

## The AGG's Critical 2-Month Deadline — Don't Miss It

This is where many foreign trainees lose their rights: **the AGG sets a strict 2-month deadline** to assert your claims after the discriminatory act occurred (§ 15 Abs. 4 AGG). Miss this window and you generally cannot demand compensation or damages, even if your case is strong.

The 2-month clock starts from the moment you became aware of the discriminatory act. So:

- Racist comment on March 1 → you must formally assert your AGG claim **by May 1** at the latest.
- Unfair rejection from a promotion on April 15 → deadline is **June 15**.

"Formally asserting" means sending a written statement — ideally a letter or email — to your employer stating that you consider their behavior a violation of the AGG and that you are claiming your rights. You don't need to file a lawsuit at this stage; you just need to put it in writing and keep proof.

**Tip:** Send the letter by registered mail (Einschreiben mit Rückschein, around €3–5 at any Deutsche Post branch) so you have documented proof of delivery.

## How to Collect Evidence and Find Witnesses

Discrimination cases in Germany follow a special evidentiary rule under § 22 AGG: you only need to **establish a plausible case** (Glaubhaftmachung). You don't have to prove discrimination beyond doubt — once you present credible indications, the burden shifts to your employer to prove no discrimination occurred. This makes evidence-gathering more manageable.

### What to Document

Start keeping a written record the moment something feels wrong:

- **Date, time, location** of every incident
- **Exact words used** — write them down within hours while they're fresh
- **Names of people present** — these are potential witnesses
- **Screenshots** of WhatsApp messages, emails, or any written communication
- **Copies of written warnings, payslips, and your Ausbildungsvertrag** — keep personal copies at home, not only on company devices

### Witnesses

A colleague or fellow trainee who witnessed an incident can be enormously valuable. Ask them — privately and outside the workplace — if they would be willing to confirm what they saw. Even a written statement from them that you can present to a counselor strengthens your position significantly.

Note that witnesses are not required to go to court immediately. A written account they provide you privately is already useful at the complaint and counseling stage.

## Where to Get Free Help: Antidiskriminierungsstelle des Bundes and Other Resources

You don't have to navigate this alone, and you don't have to pay for initial advice. Germany has a federally funded anti-discrimination body and a network of local counseling centers.

### Antidiskriminierungsstelle des Bundes (ADS)

The **Antidiskriminierungsstelle des Bundes** (Federal Anti-Discrimination Agency) is your first stop. It is completely free and independent.

- **Website:** [www.antidiskriminierungsstelle.de](https://www.antidiskriminierungsstelle.de)
- **Phone:** 0800 546 546 0 (free, Monday–Friday 9am–4pm, Thursday until 6pm)
- **Email and online contact form** available on the website
- They offer advice in multiple languages and can refer you to local legal counseling centers (Beratungsstellen)

The ADS cannot take legal action on your behalf, but they will explain your rights, help you assess your situation, and connect you with lawyers or advocacy groups that can.

### Local Counseling Centers (Beratungsstellen)

Across Germany, there are regional discrimination counseling centers funded by state governments and NGOs. In cities with large communities — Berlin, Munich, Frankfurt, Cologne, Hamburg, Düsseldorf — you can find walk-in advice in Arabic or French. Search for "Antidiskriminierungsberatung [your city]" or use the ADS website's directory.

### Trade Unions (Gewerkschaften)

If you're in a sector covered by a union — retail (ver.di), manufacturing (IG Metall), healthcare (ver.di) — your union membership entitles you to free legal advice and representation. Membership costs between €5 and €25 per month for trainees, depending on your Ausbildungsvergütung.

### Labor Court (Arbeitsgericht)

If counseling and employer negotiations don't resolve the issue, you can file a claim at the Arbeitsgericht (Labor Court). In Germany, the first instance at the Arbeitsgericht does not require a lawyer, and court costs for trainees earning under €1,500/month are typically waived or minimal. Under the AGG, you can claim **damages for material loss** (e.g., unpaid allowance) and **compensation for non-material harm** (pain and suffering), which courts have awarded between €1,000 and €10,000 in discrimination cases, depending on severity.

## What People Get Wrong About Workplace Discrimination Claims in Germany

**Mistake 1: Waiting too long.** The 2-month deadline under § 15 AGG is absolute. People often spend weeks "hoping things improve" and miss their window entirely. Document and act immediately.

**Mistake 2: Assuming verbal complaints count.** Telling your supervisor verbally that you feel discriminated against is not enough to assert your AGG rights. Everything must be **in writing**.

**Mistake 3: Thinking you need a lawyer first.** You don't. The ADS and local Beratungsstellen offer free guidance and can help you write the initial assertion letter to your employer.

**Mistake 4: Believing discrimination only counts if it's extreme.** The AGG protects you from repeated low-level hostility (harassment) and even single severe incidents. You don't need to wait until the situation becomes unbearable.

**Mistake 5: Not keeping copies of documents at home.** Once a conflict becomes open, employers sometimes restrict access to company systems. Always keep your Ausbildungsvertrag, payslips, and any relevant correspondence saved privately.

**Mistake 6: Confusing the AGG deadline with the general statute of limitations.** Some trainees think they have three years (the general German limitation period) to act. For AGG compensation claims, you have only two months to formally assert the claim — even if the lawsuit itself can be filed later.

## Conclusion

Germany has strong legal protection for foreign trainees facing discrimination — but those protections only work if you know them and act within the deadlines. The AGG is on your side: it shifts the burden of proof, covers a wide range of discriminatory behavior, and gives you access to free counseling through the Antidiskriminierungsstelle des Bundes. Document everything, assert your claim in writing within two months, and reach out to the free support network available to you.

If you're still planning your move to Germany or preparing your Ausbildung application, it helps to start with strong documents. [Book a free consultation and use our CV builder](/cv-builder) to put your best foot forward — and arrive in Germany prepared for every situation, including knowing your rights.

faqs.question: Does the AGG protect me as a non-EU trainee doing Ausbildung in Germany?
faqs.answer: Yes. The AGG applies to all workers and trainees in Germany regardless of their nationality or visa status. Whether you are from Morocco, Tunisia, or anywhere else, you have the same anti-discrimination rights as a German trainee.

faqs.question: What is the exact deadline to make a discrimination complaint under the AGG?
faqs.answer: You must formally assert your AGG compensation claim in writing within 2 months of the discriminatory act (§ 15 Abs. 4 AGG). This means sending a written letter or email to your employer stating you consider their behavior a violation of the AGG. Missing this deadline generally means losing your right to financial compensation.

faqs.question: How much compensation can I receive if my AGG discrimination claim is successful?
faqs.answer: German labor courts have awarded between €1,000 and €10,000 for non-material harm in discrimination cases, depending on severity and duration. You can also claim material damages — for example, unpaid training allowance or a lost promotion bonus — on top of that amount.

faqs.question: Is the Antidiskriminierungsstelle des Bundes really free to contact?
faqs.answer: Yes, completely free. You can call 0800 546 546 0 at no charge, use their online contact form, or visit www.antidiskriminierungsstelle.de. They provide independent advice, help you understand your rights, and refer you to local legal counseling centers if needed.

faqs.question: Can I be fired for making an AGG discrimination complaint against my employer?
faqs.answer: No. The AGG explicitly prohibits retaliation against employees who assert their rights under the law (§ 16 AGG). If your employer retaliates — for example, by dismissing you or worsening your working conditions after you complain — that retaliation itself becomes an additional legal violation you can challenge.

new-overtime-ausbildung-germany-rules.title: Overtime Ausbildung Germany Rules: Limits, Pay, and Your Rights
new-overtime-ausbildung-germany-rules.summary: Learn the exact overtime rules for Ausbildung trainees in Germany — legal hour limits, compensation rights, and what to do if your employer pushes too far.
new-overtime-ausbildung-germany-rules.content:
Starting your Ausbildung in Germany is exciting, but when your trainer asks you to stay late for the third time this week, you need to know exactly where the legal line is. Overtime rules in Germany are strict, especially for trainees, and the law treats minors and adults very differently. Understanding the overtime Ausbildung Germany rules before a conflict arises could save your training contract — and your sanity.

## The Legal Foundation: Which Laws Apply to You

Germany does not have a single "overtime law." Instead, several laws stack on top of each other depending on your age and your specific training agreement.

### The Vocational Training Act (BBiG)

The **Berufsbildungsgesetz (BBiG)** is the backbone of every Ausbildung. Section 17 BBiG says your employer must pay you fairly, and Section 19 says you must be paid even if work is not available — but it also implies you must not be exploited. Critically, §17 BBiG gives trainees the right to receive their training allowance regardless of hours, but extra hours must be compensated separately.

### The Working Hours Act (ArbZG) — For Adults 18+

If you are 18 or older, the **Arbeitszeitgesetz (ArbZG)** governs your hours:

- Maximum **8 hours per working day**, extendable to **10 hours** if the average over 6 calendar months stays at or below 8 hours/day
- Maximum **48 hours per week** (averaged over 6 months)
- Mandatory rest break of **30 minutes** if you work 6–9 hours, **45 minutes** if you work more than 9 hours
- Minimum **11 consecutive hours of rest** between shifts

So if your Ausbildung contract says 40 hours/week and your employer asks for 45, those extra 5 hours are overtime — and they must be compensated.

### The Youth Labour Protection Act (JArbSchG) — For Minors Under 18

If you are under 18 when your Ausbildung starts, the **Jugendarbeitsschutzgesetz (JArbSchG)** applies, and the rules are significantly stricter:

- Maximum **8 hours per day**
- Maximum **40 hours per week** — no exceptions, no averaging
- Work is only allowed between **6:00 AM and 8:00 PM** (with limited sector exceptions)
- No work on Saturdays, Sundays, or public holidays in most sectors
- Mandatory break of **30 minutes** after 4.5 hours of work, **60 minutes** after 6 hours

The JArbSchG limits are absolute. An employer **cannot legally ask a minor to exceed them**, even with the trainee's agreement in writing.

---

## What Counts as Overtime in Ausbildung?

This is where many trainees get confused. Overtime is any working time **beyond what your training contract specifies**, not just beyond the legal maximum.

**Example:** Your contract says 37.5 hours/week. Your employer schedules you for 42 hours. The extra 4.5 hours are overtime — even though the legal maximum for adults is 48 hours. Your contract is the ceiling that matters first.

Overtime also includes:
- Staying late to finish a customer order
- Coming in early before your official shift
- Working through your lunch break (if your break was supposed to be 30+ minutes)
- Attending mandatory after-hours training sessions not listed in your contract

One grey area: **Berufsschule hours**. School days count as working time. If you attend Berufsschule for 8 hours, your employer cannot also require you to work a full shift at the company on the same day.

---

## How Overtime Must Be Compensated

German law and your training contract determine how overtime is paid. There are two standard compensation methods:

### 1. Time Off in Lieu (Freizeitausgleich)
